Epistola Joannis Tritemii abbatis spanhemenk: in opusculu de triplici regione claustralii. Euerendis in christo patribus, dnis presidibus, diffinitoribus, et ceteris abbatis bus capli annalis, ordinis sancti benedicti, vnionis et obseruatie burkfeldensis: frater joannes tritemius vocatus abbas in span hem: eiusdem ordinis et congregationis. maguine diocelis: reuerentia et charitate. Parui pceps tis viris colendiffimi patres: et opusculu de triplici regio ne claustralii vnacu exercicio spuali monachop. p vence rabilem patre dhn joannem abbatē burkfeldenscm nua per editum: sicut mibi pcepsitis assumpli corrigendum. Ecreuera nisi me auctoritas vra compulisset nunquá ad tanti patris pclarum opus manu fuisset ausus a pone re: que constat me longe doctiorem t sanctiorem optime scriplisse. Quid em corrigerem: vbi omnia probatissima inueniuntur: Uir bonus t deuotus: no aliter scripsit q̄ vuit et decuit. Uerũtamen ut satisfacerem tā vro impen rio t̄ precibus ipius auctoris: totum opusculu breuiori bus quidem licet non pauitoribus sententijs reddidi: et illud accentibus deseruiens in meũ scribendi morem t̄ sti lum quantũ potui reduci. Ordinem vero et materiã prion ris voluminis tenui: formã et dicendi cõsuetudinem pe nitus immutaui. Multa que mihi videbantur utilia pen ne in omibus locis addidi: paucã subtraxi: verba nõ sen lus in singulis alterauai. Hoc em ut auderem et iussio vra cõtulit: et prefaci patris importuna petitio pluasit. Uo luistis namq̄ ut ex veteri materia opus nouũ facerem: adderem quelibet mihi visa congrua: reseccarem supfluã: alterarem immutãda. Feci q̄ potui: mandatis vris obe divi: opus iniuctum pro viribus ingenij mei que tenues sunt rescribingo cõlummaui. Letter of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the little work concerning the threefold region of cloistered persons.

To the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents, definitors, and the other abbots of the annual chapter of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the union and observance of Bursfelde: Brother Johannes Trithemius, called abbot in Sponheim, of the same order and congregation, in the diocese of Mainz, offers reverence and charity.

I have obeyed your commands, most venerable fathers, and, as you instructed me, I undertook to correct the little work on the threefold region of cloistered persons, together with the spiritual exercise of monks, recently published by the venerable father lord Johannes, abbot of Bursfelde. Indeed, unless your authority had compelled me, I would never have dared to set my hand to the distinguished work of so great a father, who, it is certain, wrote most excellently, being far more learned and holier than I. For what was I to correct, where everything is found most approved? The good and devout man wrote in no other way than he wished and than was fitting.

Nevertheless, in order to satisfy both your command and the prayers of the author himself, I rendered the whole little work in briefer, though not fewer, statements, and, adapting it to accents, I brought it as far as I could into my own manner and style of writing. I kept the order and matter of the former volume, but I entirely changed the form and customary mode of speaking. I added many things that seemed useful to me in almost every place; I removed a few; I altered the words in individual passages, not the sense. That I dared to do this was due both to your command and to the urgent request of the aforementioned father. For you wished me to make a new work out of old material, to add whatever seemed suitable to me, to cut away what was superfluous, and to alter what needed changing. I did what I could; I obeyed your commands; according to the strength of my talent, which is slight, I completed the task enjoined on me by rewriting it.

Receive now, therefore, most beloved fathers, a work not mine but yours, not composed by me but rather rewritten. If it pleases you, praise the talent of the first father; but if, because of its worthlessness, it displeases you, correct my imperfection, since I, who had from another man’s expenditure the best material for a spiritual building, have through my own lack of skill constructed an inept structure. If I have become foolish, you compelled me. Therefore, whether the work pleases or displeases, it has been easier for me, by writing foolishly, to accept your command obediently than, contrary to obedience, to keep silence. Yet I trust not in my own powers but in another’s merits, for a work which charity has produced will displease no one who loves God.

I desire your paternities always to remain happy in Christ. From Sponheim, the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1498.

Here begins the book on the threefold region of cloistered persons and on the spiritual exercise of novices.

When I call to mind the whole condition of monastic life in these days, I feel intense grief for its calamity, because the fervor of spiritual exercise, which once produced most abundant fruits in the order of our holy father Benedict, has now for the most part failed among monks. We see cloistered persons returning in their morals to the world; we see the institution of regular observance despised by many; and religion, which from the beginning had been instituted for contempt of the world, is by wicked monks being called back again to the pomps of the world. The crown has fallen from our head; the integrity of regular discipline has been corrupted; and the former fervor of holy conduct is perishing. We perceive that many monasteries of our order lie buried in the worst deformity, while we see very few reformed to the purity of the Rule.

The cause of this destruction of regular institution is negligence in spiritual exercises; for as soon as the spirit of fervor has lost its savor in the minds of cloistered persons, the flesh, previously dead through self-denial, has risen again, and the world, which before appeared dry and contemptible to devout hearts, has begun to bloom again in carnal minds. For truly the thought of the human heart, prone to evil from youth, unless it is daily stirred to fervor of spirit by the bridle of spiritual exercise, falls back again in its usual way into its former negligences and grows lukewarm from its holy purpose.

For just as a fallow field, deprived of the diligent care of cultivation, with thorns springing up, quickly returns to its former desolation, so the human mind, however pure or holy it may be, is quickly reduced to thickets of vices unless it is renewed to fervor of spirit by the daily exercise of devotion. Led by this consideration, the fathers of our observance of Bursfelde, devout cultivators, entrusted to us and to posterity, by word and example, that since through our own frailty we cannot remain constant in fervor of spirit, we should at least, by evening recollection after Compline, accuse our daily negligences.

Be prima regione aie in qua cum bestũs monachi verũantur carnales: multus passion nibus inordinati: in regione infimia sensualiter conuer a fantes. O Rima igitur anime regio sensualis infima ec animalis dicitur: in qua radices omniũ ma loũ cõtincetur. In hac regione tenebrosa cõ stuti homines cu bestũs in genere suo parti elpant: quũpe qui mores (ut ita dicam) bestiales obser uant: dum rationi aut nihil aut parũ deferũ: sed omia sensualitati ut bestie concedũt. Nam in ista regione infi ma tres aie vires sensuales president: quarũ prima sensi bilis circa obiecta quinc sensuũ exteriorũ diffundit: con cupiscibilis altera in carnaliũs delectat: tercla irascibilis

[unclear] may we be renewed from the state of our mind to the fervor of our holy purpose? But whoever neglects the exercise of daily discipline falls into the depth of the body, as the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “If you do not keep yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, the Lord will quickly overturn your house,” which he understands as a good conscience. For the provision of this exercise, so useful and so necessary, the Rule of our most holy father Benedict for monks seems to suffice, since it is clear that it contains all the material of exercises, both spiritual and bodily, necessary for monks to preserve regular discipline. And therefore all monastic exercises must be humbly submitted to the ordinances of the Rule, since whatever is prescribed either by us or by others for the instruction of monks is wholly directed to observing the monastic norm. For the whole sum of our religious life, which is acquired by the continual practice of spiritual exercise, is contained in the Rule of monastic tradition as in one root, in brief compass.

Therefore every spiritual or bodily exercise of monks, by which the mind is led by love to humble obedience and self-denial, is conformed to the institutions of the holy Rule, which is known to present the monk first to God as good and humble, and so much the more opposes the effort of proud contempt. The holy mysteries of this exercise, by an invisible teaching in the mind of their cultivator, direct him by a safe path to the love of God as to his due end; they wonderfully acquire the grace of inward devotion, and make the monk count all earthly things as nothing and sweetly burn at all times in fervor of spirit. The animal man does not grasp this saving exercise of devotion; the vain and curious monk does not understand this pursuit; the proud man does not admit this knowledge, which is to be preferred to all things. Happy is he who has learned to penetrate the secrets of this exercise; happy is he who has deserved to receive this gift of holy compunction from the Lord, for whoever has once attained it perfectly will fear no adversity of this world. But that exercise which, bereft of its due end, does not direct the minds of cloistered men to the observance of the commandments of the Rule, does not pour in the Holy Spirit of discipline; for where the obedience of subjection is despised, no gift is accepted by almighty God.

For it is written: “Obedience is better than victims, and to listen is better than to offer the fat.” And although many little works of spiritual exercise are found composed by different men, yet not all things suit everyone. Therefore it has seemed good also to us to publish something in accordance with the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, by which we may be able to stir ourselves more closely and more nearly toward the purity of regular observance. And so we have divided the present little work, collected from the exercises of the excellent father Theoderic, once abbot of the monastery of Bursfelde, into two principal parts. The first is placed in the consideration of monastic institution; the second is occupied with the exercise of the spiritual life. In the first it commands you to know yourself; in the second, to raise the mind from earthly things to heavenly things.

Therefore, approaching the proposed consideration according to our strength, we have divided the first treatise into three parts, according to the threefold state of cloistered men, whom we may call first sensual, second rational, and third spiritual. From this threefold state of men we take a fitting title for this work, which we call On the Three Regions of Cloistered Men. In these three regions the whole crowd of monks is included, as will be said in what follows.

On the first region of the soul, in which carnal monks live with beasts, disordered by many passions, dwelling sensually in the lowest region.

The first region of the soul, then, is called sensual, lowest, and animal; in it the roots of all evils are contained. Men established in this dark region share in their own kind with beasts, since they observe, so to speak, beastly habits, while they give either nothing or little to reason, but grant everything to sensuality like beasts. For in that lowest region three sensual powers of the soul preside. The first, the sensitive power, is spread about the objects of the five exterior senses; the second, the concupiscible power, delights in carnal things; the third is the irascible power.

Ue omibus in hac regione te nebrosa manentibus: q̄m nũlet penitentiã egerint: cui illis deputãdi sunt q̄ tenebras exteriores inhabitãt: ubi nulet lus ordo sed ppetuet horror inhabitat. Ha sicut monachi secundũ regulũ spiritu ambulãtes in celo cui sanctis ange lis sine fine feliciter coronãdi sunt: ita cõtra normã insti tucũnis monastice in hac infima regione carnis vqũs ad mortẽ pseuerãtes: pagãnis deteriores cui demonibus in inferno eternaliter sunt cruciandi. Ueraciter eni dicit ille beatus. Sicut nunũs vidi meliores his q̄ in cenobio pfe cerũt: ita nũlet sum exptus deteriores illis q̄ in monasterio defecerũt. Professio em monastica spũalis vite pfectionẽ exiguit: et ad sumũnã virtutũ quasi ad suũ finẽ debitu tenẽ dit. Quũto autẽ quisqet ab hoc conatu pfiendi in moa

fleeing things contrary to the pleasures of the flesh, he pursues.

And this lowest region is compared to the airy heaven; for just as hail, snow, lightning, and various storms are generated in the air, so also various storms of vices follow in the minds of carnal men who inhabit this dark region. Woe to carnal monks who inhabit this dark region, in which there is frequent movement of crimes and a continual storm of pleasures. These are monks given over to animal passions, who subject reason to sensuality, who live according to the flesh in beastly desires.

Now the works of the flesh dwelling in this lowest region are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, immodesty, lust, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, rivalries, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, feasting, and things like these. Concerning them the holy apostle proclaims that those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God. These are the signs of the works of the lowest region; these are the deadly storms of the minds of carnal monks, who live irreligiously in religion, who despise the traditions of the holy fathers, who with polluted presumption scorn the commands of the elders. These are the unclean worshipers of the lowest region, given over to vices and carnal desires, who do not care to have God in their knowledge, who serve the pleasures of the flesh, who stubbornly break the vow of holy religion which they have professed, who, despising the salvation of their souls, disdain to follow the grace of God calling them.

Therefore he handed them over to a reprobate sense and to false judgment, so that they think evil good, and falsely suppose that the things which are in truth the worst are themselves the best. These are the carnal monks of whom the holy apostle spoke: whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, insulting, proud, puffed up, inventors of evils, disobedient to superiors, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy, filled with all iniquity, malice, wickedness, contention, deceit, and malignity. Though they know the justice of God, they refuse to understand that those who do such things are worthy of eternal death; and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them, and those who, by duty of office, in no way oppose the pursuits of evil men.

For indeed, when the ruler of souls does not correct delinquent subjects, he entangles himself in the crimes of others and becomes liable to condemnation; by keeping silence he becomes the companion of those whose faults condemnation will pursue. For any pastor of souls who, though placed in office, neglects to amend sinners according to the canonical rule, even if he is free from the offense itself, will nevertheless be condemned before the strict judge for the fault of another. For the supreme shepherd says to the prophet: “Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel; and you shall hear the word from my mouth, and shall announce it to them from me. If, therefore, when I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, nor speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man indeed shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand.”

And our blessed father says in the Rule: “Let the abbot know that the fault of the shepherd will fall upon him, if the father of the household is able to find any lack of profit in his sheep.” O sentence to be feared by all spiritual pastors, by which not only the depraved conduct of subjects is ascribed to the ruler, but he is also held guilty before the inward judge for their lesser progress. O what shall we wretched pastors say in that strict examination, who neglect to amend according to the Rule the monks entrusted to us when they fall in many ways? We do not call those lying in the lowest region to higher things, but, carnal with the carnal, we grow sluggish in the shadow of death with destructive idleness.

Woe to all who remain in this dark region; for unless they do penance, they must be assigned with those who inhabit the outer darkness, where no order but everlasting horror dwells. For just as monks who walk according to the Rule in the spirit are to be happily crowned without end in heaven with the holy angels, so those who, against the norm of monastic institution, persevere in this lowest region of the flesh all the way to death, worse than pagans, are to be eternally tormented in hell with demons. For that blessed man truly says: “As I have never seen better men than those who have made progress in the cenobium, so I have never experienced worse than those who have failed in the monastery.” For the monastic profession demands the perfection of spiritual life, and tends toward the summit of virtues as toward its proper and due end. How the carnal monks of this lowest region are disordered in many respects.

Although the description of this lowest region generally applies to any carnal people at all who live in sins and crimes with the habits of beasts, nevertheless, so that we may attend to our own, we intend to speak of lukewarm and carnal cloistered monks, doing absolutely no injury to the good and devout. For always and in all things we wish the conduct of good cloistered monks to remain untouched and unharmed whenever we discuss the evil pursuits of the wicked. We reproach the bad cloistered monks and their corrupt ways; the good we honor and praise everywhere, as is fitting. And what else but evil can we say of the evil, in whom we find nothing good to say? They live disorderly in a holy order; they despise the traditions of the elders; they do not receive words of salvation.

So great, indeed, is the disorder of the monks of the lowest region that, in my judgment, it would be easier to convert a publican than to call a disorderly monk back to repentance. We include this disorder of carnal monks under eight headings, although we know that they are disorderly in many other ways as well. First, the citizens of this lowest region, beastlike monks, are disordered toward God; then toward their own prelate; third, prelates toward their subjects; fourth, members toward one another; again, fifth, they are disordered toward themselves; then toward the goods of the monastery; seventh, toward contempt of the world; and finally toward repentance for sin. These are the principal disorders of the citizens of the lowest region; these are the beastlike affections of carnal monks, who dwell in the depths in mind and heart, because they do not hasten to press on to the summit. I shall take care to set out briefly, in order, these disordered conditions of the lowest region, and to show, as far as I can, how far carnal monks are from God. For thus, as the prophet says, salvation is far from sinners.

How the citizens of this lowest region are disordered toward God. Article One.

Therefore the carnal monks of this lowest region, its mad inhabitants, are disordered toward God in many ways: they do not now taste the sweetness of his love; they admit no compunction of divine fear; swollen and beastlike in their affections, they are at all times unclean in their carnal pleasures.

First, their disorder toward God takes its origin from ignorance, since, given over to animal passions, they do not care to have God in their knowledge, nor do they consent to think upon those things that lead the soul to fear him; but, blinded by evil desires, they become vain in their thoughts. But what does Scripture say? “He who is ignorant shall be ignored.” They do not wish to understand so that they may do good; they do not tremble before the face of the strict judge; without repentance they continually persevere in evils. For the man swollen in his own manner of life does not fear to rot away in his pleasures; they do not heed the patience of God calling them to repentance; they seek nothing except the comforts of their flesh. At all times they walk in the greatest sins without any fear; they stubbornly refuse to know the ways of the Lord. Of the future judgment they think either nothing or very little; they do not fear the punishments prepared for sinners in hell; no grace of compunction now pierces their hearts, because the love of God does not kindle their minds. They have no care for God; no dread of death. They obey the belly more than God; at all times they desire to live according to the flesh; and while they shamefully neglect their own salvation, they descend to hell with the demons. For those who, having forgotten God, keep badly the vow of holy monastic profession do not attain the rewards of heavenly life that are to be given to the just.

Second, carnal monks are disordered toward God by a foolish profession, because they promise to live according to the Rule, yet do not truly care to fulfill it. And what is more disorderly than to promise to the one God a consecrated life, and yet remain in the foulness of one’s former life? It is a mockery of almighty God, is it not, for anyone in the monastery to live otherwise than the monastic Rule teaches?

Semp em apud reprobas mentes vita bonoy in suspi tionem trahitur: semp alienis virtutibus invidia torque tur; et monachus qui se vicijs peccans voluntarie subg

We see that today many among cloistered men live in a secular fashion: many seem to neglect the state of their profession, violating the observance of regular discipline in various ways, knowingly ignoring the goodness of God, and shrinking back from doing penance.

Third, many cloistered men of this lowest region are disordered toward God through careless neglect of the service due to him. They serve their own affections and fleshly desires in various ways, and always come to God’s service with a distracted mind. Of these, some run to choir lukewarm, without any devotion; others come unwillingly, compelled by necessity; some, scattered by outward thoughts, are present at the divine offices in body, but in mind wander outside through various workshops. Others are not afraid to seek out false occasions by which they may, as it were, lawfully absent themselves from choir. They pretend a severe headache; now they allege this, now that, deceitfully; and while they fraudulently withdraw the service owed to almighty God, they incur the reproach of eternal malediction due to the negligent.

Fourth, there are very many who are disordered toward God through the working of habit. Even if they sometimes avoid the malediction of the negligent, still they never draw near to the fruit of inward devotion. For they come to the service of God from habit alone, and are not moved to any good work by devotion. Others, placed under grave necessity, obey the commands of their superiors unwillingly enough, and bear temporal penalties rather than fear the judgment of God. These carry the cross of the Lord under compulsion with Simon, and, like Ephraim, a heifer trained for threshing, apply themselves to good works by habit alone. But they never do good well who come to the service of God with an improper intention. They also perform a just thing without the reward of justice, because in good and just works they do not assume a good will.

Fifth, the citizens of the lowest region are disordered toward God through the vice of ingratitude, which is the greatest crime of a disordered will. And indeed a man is often exposed, by his own deserving, to be scourged by various and very grave temptations when he is found ungrateful to the Lord for the benefits he has received. Therefore he deserves to lose the benefit he has received who neglects to show himself grateful to so great a benefactor. And what greater ingratitude can there be than to live irreligiously in religion, to break one’s vow, shamefully to violate the purpose solemnly undertaken? The monk who entangles himself in fleshly vices, who neglects to live according to the rule he has professed, voluntarily incurs the very great vice of ingratitude.

How the monks of this lowest region are disordered toward their prelate.

Article II.

Carnal monks are disordered in many ways toward their prelate. They tear apart his life with constant detractions; with a stubborn heart they disparage his pastoral office; they refuse, according to the Rule, to show their shepherd the affection of filial love. For the monks of this lowest region, blinded by various pleasures of the flesh, disdain to consider whose place the abbot holds in the monastery; and the one whom they ought humbly to venerate as Christ’s vicar they regard, because of weakness, as one like themselves and worthy of no honor. Under the snare of this disordered conduct the ancient enemy deceives carnal monks, whom he leads in various ways into displeasure with their shepherd. For the greatest power of raging against the monastic flock is granted to the devil when the one who presides is hated by his subjects. For just as a sick man cannot be healed if, by detesting the physician, he does not allow him to come near, so a monk cannot be saved who, because of aversion, is unwilling to disclose his temptations to his shepherd. For how will anyone be able to escape the savage teeth of the ravening wolf if he cannot endure the presence of the shepherd?

First, therefore, disordered monks criticize the life of their shepherd; they stubbornly accuse both his deeds and his words, because, when they consider that their ruler walks according to the traditions of the holy fathers, they fear being corrected in their own depravity. For among reprobate minds the life of the good is always drawn into suspicion; envy is always tormented by the virtues of others; and the monk who voluntarily subjects himself to vices by sinning [unclear].

Secundo autem ciues huius tenebrose regionis inordinati sunt ad suos prelatos, cui eius officio derogant: quem ad presidendum in monasterio a deo ordinatum no ignorat. Contra eum facili occasione murmurat: eius mandata no observat: et qui se armis sancte obedientie et deo amore tampridem subdiderant: nunc more sarabaturi cotem et pta obedientia, voluntati suarui sibi pniciosum dominium usurpat. Abbatem pruus suis convenientem moribus habere desiderant: sancti et utilem recusant. Si remissum et inerte pastorem inuenerint, multos eum venenis aduando intoxicant: patre optimu et piumu vocant: eis se non humiliter sed libenter subiicunt: a quo nulla pruavitatis sue correptionem pertimescunt. Tercio monachi carnales inordinatos se ad suos pastores exhibent: qui eis affectu filialis amoris subtrahunt: et obedientie secundu regulu contemnunt. Verutamen cum monachus abbatem suos tantos christi vicarii sincero affectu teneatur diligere: non poterit eum sine grauissimo scelere odire. Eniucro qui pastores suos amore christi no diliget: verus amator dei no eruit. Nam christus qui etiam inimicos vult diligi: suos vicarios quomodo pmitteret odi ri: Illu itaqs intende qui tibi abbate pesse vice sua vo luit: et causa dispucentie contra eum iã deinceps non erit. Quarto ciues inordinati vallis umbrose pastoris sui reverentie derogant: qui ei honoris ex regula debitu non solu cotemnunt impendere: sed qo peus est no metuue etia cotuemiam irrogare. Regula em phibet abbatevis ces christi in monasterio gerere: cui oes monachi tantos ipi christo debet humiliter obedientie: qm obedientia que maioribus impenditur: christo exhibetur. Sed peruerfi claustrales de psidentia plato, semp ingrati: ordinacio ni divine contumaciter obuiare non metuunt: mandatis sancte regule obedientie contemnunt: abbates suui cui oma nem reverentia exhibere debuerant: odio et detracioni bus lacerantes inhonoran. Quicquid fecerit, quicquid ordinauerit, quicquid dixerit, tantus male factus est disipli et qui conversationi eius cotempro officio, nihil magis confusione sui pas storis oues morbidely inquirit. Ex his nonulli abbatem suum in occulto iudicatet despiciunt: alij in faciem ei co tradicunt: qui dum reverentia suo pastori exhibere negleg gunt: omne discipline observantia cofundunt. His semper est familiaris elatio: carnis amica turpitudo: quoniam qui se ab affectu pastoris voluntarie subtrahunt: in tenta tiones abominabiles et sceleras pessima cadunt. Quisquis eim christi vicarii in monasterio despicit: seuiedi in se po testate diabolo tradit: et unionem corporis mystici cofundit. Quinto monachi carnales inordinati ad suum pastorem eius auctoritati derogant: du nihil ei licere nisi con fenserint ipi in cenobio putant. Virtute humilitatis elan ta ceruice despiciunt: subjectionem regularis spernunt: cen dere melioribus contemnunt. Omnibus negociis et caus sis se voluit immittere: fibis consilii principatum usurpa re: ut abbas nihil agere vel disponere audeat: nisi prius de eorum consensu negocii procedat. Sed quid dicit le gislator benedictus in regula? Audiens inquit abbas consilia fratrum, tractet apud se: et quod utiuis indicauer rit faciat. Et iterum, Sic autem dent fratres consilia cui omni humilitatis subjectione: ut non psamant procaci ter defendere quod eis visum fuerit: sed magis in abba tis pendeat arbitrio: ut quod salubrius esse iudicauerit: ei cuicui obedient. Et rursus de ordinado opposito dicit. Nos, quidemus expedire ppter charitatis pacis custo diam: in abbatis pendere arbitrio ordinationem mona sterij sui. Hec vtis ordinatio institutionem deinstitutionem omnia officialium monasterij respicit: que non consensum fratrum sed consilium deum timenti requirit. Denigis omnibus regula mandat agendu secundu volun tatem abbatis: nihilus penitus esse psamendu: qo ab eo no fuerit iniunctu. Hanc eius auctoritate monachi car nales, prius voluntatis temerarii usurpatores, varijs mo

Thus they always hate a pastor of purified conduct.

Secondly, the citizens of this dark region are disorderly toward their prelates, whose office they disparage, though they know that he has been appointed by God to preside in the monastery. On any easy occasion they murmur against him; they do not observe his commands; and those who long ago had submitted themselves with the weapons of holy obedience and for love of God now, in the manner of Sarabaites, despising obedience, usurp for their own will a dominion ruinous to themselves. They desire to have an abbot suited to their own depraved ways; they reject one who is holy and useful. If they find a lax and sluggish pastor, they intoxicate him with many poisons by flattering him; they call him an excellent and most loving father; they submit themselves to him not humbly but willingly, since they fear from him no correction of their depravity.

Thirdly, carnal monks show themselves disorderly toward their pastors when they withdraw from them the affection of filial love and despise obedience according to the Rule. Yet since a monk is bound to love his abbot sincerely as Christ’s vicar, he cannot hate him without the gravest crime. For truly, whoever does not love his pastor for the love of Christ will not be a true lover of God. For Christ, who wills even enemies to be loved, how would he permit his vicars to be hated? Therefore look to him who willed your abbot to preside over you in his place, and from then on there will be no cause of displeasure against him.

Fourthly, the disorderly citizens of the shadowy valley disparage the reverence due to their pastor; they not only scorn to render him the honor owed by the Rule, but, what is worse, they do not fear even to inflict contempt on him. For the Rule teaches that the abbot holds the place of Christ in the monastery, and all monks owe him humble obedience as to Christ himself, since the obedience rendered to superiors is shown to Christ. But perverse cloisterers, always ungrateful toward the prelate set over them, do not fear contumaciously to resist the divine ordinance; they despise the commands of obedience in the holy Rule; and they dishonor their abbots, to whom they ought to have shown all reverence, tearing them apart with hatred and detraction. Whatever he does, whatever he ordains, whatever he says, the disciple is so ill-disposed that, despising the office in his conduct toward him, he seeks nothing more, like a diseased sheep, than the confusion of his pastor. Of these, some judge and despise their abbot in secret; others contradict him to his face; and when they neglect to show reverence to their pastor, they throw the whole observance of discipline into confusion. Pride is always familiar to them, and foulness, the friend of the flesh; for those who voluntarily withdraw themselves from affection for their pastor fall into abominable temptations and the worst crimes. For whoever despises Christ’s vicar in the monastery hands himself over to the devil’s power to rage against him, and confounds the unity of the mystical body.

Fifthly, carnal monks are disorderly toward their pastor when they disparage his authority, thinking that nothing is lawful for him in the monastery unless they themselves have consented. With necks raised high they despise the virtue of humility; they spurn regular subjection; they scorn to yield to their betters. They wish to thrust themselves into all business and causes, to usurp for themselves the primacy of counsel, so that the abbot may dare to do or arrange nothing unless the matter first proceeds with their consent. But what does the blessed lawgiver Benedict say in the Rule? “After hearing,” he says, “the counsel of the brethren, let the abbot consider the matter within himself, and do what he judges more useful.” And again: “Let the brethren give their counsel with all humble subjection, so that they do not presume insolently to defend what has seemed good to them; rather, let it depend on the abbot’s judgment, so that all may obey what he has judged more salutary.” And again, concerning the appointment of a prior, he says: “We judge it expedient, for the preservation of charity and peace, that the ordering of his monastery depend on the abbot’s judgment.” This useful ordinance concerns the appointing and removing of all officials of the monastery; it requires not the consent of the brethren, but the counsel of those who fear God. Finally, in all things the Rule commands action according to the will of the abbot, and that nothing at all be presumed which has not been enjoined by him. Carnal monks, rash usurpers of their own will, disparage this authority of his in various [unclear].

Ergo cu voluntate abbatis omnia fiunt: et nullus in monasterio prius cordis sen quatur voluntate. Quod si no videatur ad ordinatione monasterij prudentia rectoris sufficiens: monachis carnalibus imputandu est: qui sibi no idoneu volutarie pfe cerut. Semp odio habet stulticia prudentia: et abbate monachi pruai detestant sapientem. Qui ergo libi stuls tum scienter preficiut: eius ordinaconi et voluitati necesse rio subiacebit. Preceptis abbatis in omnibus obedientia est: etia si ipse qo absit aliter agat. Sed nobis inobedientia redarguentibus monachi carnales obiuciit. Recta inquiuit et bona intencone hec facimus: qui perire substantia monasterij p malu regimen videm? Sed vobis cotradicit aplus: qui no sunt facienda maola ut veniat bona: nec pter damnu rei temporalis: dea serenda est subiectio humilitatis. Nam vbi inter damnu substantie temporalis et regularis obedientie periculum aliqz subeundu occurrerit: melius est perire substantia: qz ledi obedientie puritate. Non em pecunias de manibus nostris deus requiret sed animas. Enuero qui versus monachus est: omnibus rebus mudi virtutem obedientie prefert. Civis autet huius infime regionis monachi carnales varijs modis virtute obedientie lacerat: arma sancte humilitatis impugnant: vt mihilfacillus vla deatur nouii de seculo monachii instituere: q̄ istoet igna utiam posse emendare. Sed ex fructibus eoet quales sine manifeste cognoscimus: quiet qui pacem et charitatem in monasterio violant: concordia unicitatis turbant: inter fra tres et abbatem discordia seminant: obedientia mādatis re gule cōtumaciter recusant. Hec sunt opa maloet claustra lium: hec sunt indicia civili infimoet: quiet prīc volūtatiet improbissimi defensores arma sancte obedientie proiicunt: carne non spiritu viuunt: patrũ statutis aut nihil aut paet deferunt: sanis consiliiet non acqescunt: quoet damnatio lusta est. Nam sic ut impossibile est ignem flammantem non sursum ascēdere: ita non est possibile monachum sine obe dientia celis secreta penetrare. Nam si pastor infirmus adhuc in infima regione cui ouibus habitat: den biles negligendo interficit non confortat. Cecus enim si ou catũ cecco pbeat: necesse est vt cum eo simul in fonteiam can bat. Pastor autem q̄ se ordinatũ erga subditos suos secũ dum regulam non exhibet: non pastor sed mercennarius dicendus est: et in domo domini non manebit inetermü. Multe autem sunt inordinationes prelatorum carnaliũ: que tanto amplius ouibus nocent: quanto rarus emen dantur. Conditiones mercennarii si ordinatũ Conditiones boni pastoris

they try to break [unclear], to disturb the order and charity of the whole monastery; they think nothing is to be left to the rector in matters to be done, nothing except what they themselves think right.

But tell me, proud inhabitants of the lowest region, you who always make decrees according to your own will, you who usurp another’s right: is this the virtue of obedience, to refuse to yield to the command of a superior, but stubbornly to cling to your own judgment? Did the holy father establish for you in the Rule such a way of living, when he commanded you to follow the abbot’s will in all things? For the greatest virtue of a monk is obedience, which our holy father wished to commend so highly that he says a good work done without the abbot’s will lacks merit. Therefore, giving instruction, he concludes thus: let all things be done with the abbot’s will, and let no one in the monastery follow the will of his own heart.

But if the rector’s prudence seems insufficient for ordering the monastery, this must be imputed to the carnal monks, who willingly set over themselves one who was not fit. Folly always hates prudence, and foolish monks detest a wise abbot. Therefore those who knowingly set a fool over themselves must necessarily be subject to his ordering and will. Indeed, no insufficiency of the pastor ought to extinguish obedience in the subject, since the Rule commands us to obey even an unprofitable one. For it says: obedience is to be given to the abbot’s commands in all things, even if he himself, which God forbid, acts otherwise.

But when we rebuke disobedience, carnal monks object: “We do these things with right and good intention, because we see the substance of the monastery perishing through bad governance.” But the Apostle contradicts you: evils must not be done so that good may come; nor, on account of damage to temporal property, must the subjection of humility be abandoned. For where one must undergo either the loss of temporal substance or danger to regular obedience, it is better for the property to perish than for the purity of obedience to be harmed. For God will not require money from our hands, but souls. Indeed, one who is a true monk prefers the virtue of obedience to all the things of the world.

But the citizens of this lowest region, carnal monks, tear apart the virtue of obedience in various ways; they attack the weapons of holy humility, so that it seems to me nothing is easier than to train monks newly come from the world, [unclear] than to be able to amend that sloth of theirs. But from their fruits we plainly know what sort they are: they violate peace and charity in the monastery; they disturb the concord of unity; they sow discord between the brethren and the abbot; they stubbornly refuse obedience to the commands of the Rule. These are the works of evil cloisterers; these are the marks of the lowest citizens, who, as most wicked defenders of their own wills, cast away the weapons of holy obedience, live according to the flesh and not the spirit, give either no deference or very little to the statutes of the fathers, do not acquiesce in sound counsels, and their condemnation is just. For just as it is impossible for a blazing fire not to rise upward, so it is impossible for a monk without obedience to penetrate the secrets of heaven.

In What Way the Pastors of This Lowest Region Are Disordered

Article Three

Since, then, we have shown that many monks of the lowest region are disordered toward their pastors, why should we, as though sparing prelates, not show the disorders of prelates toward their subjects? For the name of abbot sanctifies no one, nor does the dignity of pastoral care save the undeserving. Therefore, since many among the prelates dwell on the mountain of the lowest region with the beasts of the earth, they must by no means be passed over by us in silence. For many rectors of cloistered men show themselves disordered toward their subjects: they not only neglect to feed according to the Rule the souls committed to them, but tear them apart and kill them in various ways.

And whenever anyone from the lowest region is taken up as pastor, the pursuits of the wicked are strengthened for the worse. Therefore a good man and a diligent lover of God must be promoted to the office of abbot: one who has long since overcome this lowest region; one who has known how to tame the passions of the flesh; one who both wills and is able to ascend to that highest region of the spirit. For the abbot of monks ought to be of higher merit than the monks, since whoever is established as ruler of souls must necessarily be adorned with many virtues. For if the pastor, still weak, dwells in the lowest region with the sheep, by neglecting the weak he kills them; he does not strengthen them. For if a blind man offers guidance to the blind, he must necessarily fall into the ditch together with him. But a pastor who does not show himself ordered toward his subjects according to the Rule must be called not a pastor but a hireling, and he will not remain forever in the house of the Lord. Now the disorders of carnal prelates are many, and they harm the sheep all the more because they are more rarely amended.

The Conditions of the Disordered Hireling

The Conditions of the Good Pastor

Secundo pastor animae inordinatus erga subditos efficieitur: si animus cuius nimis aude in rebus temporalibus occupetur: si maiorem sollicitudinem gerat p negotiis secularibus: & pro cõmissis sibi a iabus. Hanc vero numi am rerum temporalium cura sanctus pater benedictus in regula phibet: animas et rationales omnibus rebus secu li merito iudicat pferendas. Ante omnia inquit ne diffimuo lans aut paruipendes salutae aia et sibi cõmissae et plus gen rat sollicitudine abbas de rebus trãsitorijs terrenis atqs caductis: sed semp cogitet qm aias suscepit regendas: pro quibus est ratione redditurus. Cõsequenter cu de necessa rys corporis pius pater certificat: si deum amans pura mente colat. Et ne forte inquit causetur de minore substã cia: meminerit scriptum. Primum querite regnum dei et iusticiae eius: et bec omnia adiçientur vobis. Et iterum. Ahiil deest timentibus dei. Sed pastor monachus in ordinatus avaricie p feducitur: mente tanç non sentiae exceccatur: dñi a setimorem proijac: cum achab venunda tus sub peccato ad auxilium sceleris currit: promissa per sanctũ patre de consequedis necessarijs confidentia desti cultur: plus et decet monachum in exterioribus occupat. Impulsus iam deinceps avaricie stimulis mandata dei et sancte matris ecclesie despicit: dies festos nõ custoditae rebus terrenis totus immergit: nibil aliud et palia medi catur. Dandatũ dñi stultus cum saule tranfreditur: ex piari se victimis contra obedientiam fatuus arbitratur. Denigoe aut rebus aut curis secularibus incrasfatus et di latatus in omnae lasciviam et dissolutionem plerũq labis tur: regularis discipline obseruatiam detestatur: et dum coberceri a malis studiis auctoritate capi metuit: diffon lutionem sancte vnionis querit. Deinde reprobus cum saule effectus phytoniffe consilium innocat: obedientiam reformationis suo monasterio damnabilem clamat: ab solui quãtocius a submissione sancte confederationis de siderat: ad hoc multa falso et mendaciter narrat. Sed cu auctoritas capituli annalis impune despicitur: restae vt observantia monastica non fragetur: quoniam amor Dei bonos in disciplina regulariter continet: et timor correctionis praos a malis operibus cohercit. Qusquis autem subterfugere unitatem capituli nittitur: diabolum imitatur. Sic imperator bulgaroy subditos sibi christia nos convetum in ecclesia celebrare sub pena capitis, pha ber: quibus tamem credendi quicqad voluerint licentia ins dulget. Houit emi callidus homo sinceritatei christiane fidei no diu posse subfustere: si cotigerit publici exhortatio nis officii deesse. Huc christiane fidei aduersarii inordi natus et carnalis abbas quantu potest imitari nittitur: q madatis ta necessarii capituli reluctatur. Sola em capi tuli auctortas est que regularis discipline observantia in ordine continuat: que si cotempta fuerit: nulla cōversatio nis monastice integritas pmanebit. Sed infimere regionis culcor. abbas inordinatus contra regularē observantia causas fingit innumerab: cōditiones monasterij sui mens titur contrarias: antiqua privilegia supprimi cōqueritur: subdi suũ cenobiũ alicui deignatur. Sed ve inordinas tis hoibus: p quos ab hac sanctissima congregatione vel vnũ cotigerit cenobiũ amitei. Deniqs hec avaricie pestis abbate non solũ inordinatũ facit ad subditos: sed etiã sibi metipi contrariũ: et a deo penitus auersum. Cupiditas em oim maloy radic est: que tollens seruium christi: min strũ facit esse diaboli. Abbas ergo qui mente suam huic vicio submuserit: non pastore led mercensriũ se ostendit. Semp lucris terreinis inhiat: de profectu aia s nihil cu rat: sacre lectionis codex raro vel nunqũ in manibus eius conficit: registra cenuũ crebrius reuoluuntur. Agrum agro copulat: auy, et argentum semp in thecam sepeliens dum comportat: et dum abundare monasteriũ suũ rebus temporalibus nimũ desiderat: preda raptoribus parat. Frequentet emi fiscus dominij palis pecunias monaste rioũ deuorat: quas nimia cupido monachoy cenobiũ importat. Uetibi pastor auare claustraliũ: q maiorem ge ris follicitudine de brucis aialibus: s de commissis tibi

Secondly, the pastor of souls becomes disordered toward his subjects if his mind is too boldly and excessively occupied with temporal affairs, if he has greater concern for secular business than for the souls committed to him. This excessive care for temporal things the holy father Benedict forbids in the Rule, and he rightly judges rational souls to be preferred to all worldly things. “Above all,” he says, “let the abbot not, by feigning ignorance or making light of it, neglect the salvation of the souls entrusted to him, and take greater care for transient, earthly, and perishable things; but let him always think that he has undertaken to govern souls, for which he will have to render an account.” Accordingly, concerning the necessities of the body, the loving father gives assurance, if one loves God and worships him with a pure mind. “And lest perhaps,” he says, “he complain of too little substance, let him remember what is written: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you.’ And again: ‘Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.’”

But the disordered monastic pastor is seduced by greed; yet, blinded in mind, he does not perceive it. He casts away the fear of the Lord, and, like Ahab sold under sin, he runs to the aid of wickedness; he is deprived of the confidence promised by the holy father concerning the obtaining of necessities, and he is occupied outwardly more than befits a monk. Driven thereafter by the goads of greed, he despises the commandments of God and of holy mother Church; he does not keep feast days, but plunges himself wholly into earthly affairs; he thinks and meditates on nothing else. Like Saul, the fool transgresses the commandment of the Lord, and stupidly supposes that he can be cleansed by victims offered against obedience. Finally, fattened and swollen with secular affairs or cares, he generally slips into every kind of wantonness and laxity; he detests the observance of regular discipline, and, since he fears being restrained from evil pursuits by the authority of the chapter, he seeks the dissolution of holy union. Then, having become reprobate like Saul, he calls upon the counsel of the witch; he cries out that obedience to reform is damnable for his monastery; he desires to be released as quickly as possible from submission to the holy confederation, and to this end he tells many things falsely and mendaciously.

But when the authority of the annual chapter is despised with impunity, it remains that monastic observance should not be broken, since the love of God keeps the good regularly within discipline, and fear of correction restrains the wicked from evil works. Whoever tries to escape the unity of the chapter imitates the devil. Thus the emperor of the Bulgars forbade the Christians subject to him, under penalty of death, to hold an assembly in church, though he granted them freedom to believe whatever they wished. For the cunning man knew that the sincerity of the Christian faith could not long endure if the office of public exhortation happened to be lacking. The disordered and carnal abbot, an adversary of the Christian faith, strives as much as he can to imitate him, because he resists the commands of so necessary a chapter. For the authority of the chapter alone is what preserves the observance of regular discipline in the order; if it is despised, no integrity of monastic life will remain.

But the disordered abbot, a cultivator of the lowest region, invents innumerable reasons against regular observance; he falsely claims that the conditions of his monastery are contrary to it; he complains that ancient privileges are being suppressed; he deems it beneath him that his monastery should be subject to anyone. But woe to disordered men, through whom even one monastery may happen to be lost from this most holy congregation. Finally, this plague of greed makes the abbot disordered not only toward his subjects, but also opposed to himself and utterly turned away from God. For covetousness is the root of all evils; taking away the servant of Christ, it makes him a minister of the devil. Therefore the abbot who has subjected his mind to this vice shows himself to be not a pastor but a hireling. He always gapes after earthly gains; he cares nothing for the progress of souls. The book of sacred reading rarely or never rests in his hands; registers of revenues are turned over more often. He joins field to field, always burying gold and silver in his chest as he gathers it; and while he desires too much for his monastery to abound in temporal goods, he prepares prey for robbers. For often the treasury of secular lordship devours the monies of monasteries, which the excessive greed of monks brings into the monastery. Woe to you, greedy pastor of cloistered men, who have greater concern for brute animals than for the souls committed to you.

13
animabus. Infirmatur equus et mor paras remediis: pericilia et nulli putas imminere periculum. Egrotat bos et asinus tuos compatris: absorbetur tristicia frater et non occurris. Tu ergo mercenario non pastor qui fratri tuo infirmitates contumaci pectore despicis: qui constitutus in amaritudine non succurris: non plumas te manus dini posse effugere: cuius oves permittis ta nequiter interire. Tercio inordinatus est rector ad subditos, cum eos quos intra septa monasterii sollicitate servare debuerat: non sine periculo in exterioribus locat. Eniuero dum cenobii ca infirmus ad regimen monialii vel ad ecclesias seculan res exponitur: regularis observatii integritas violatur: qui qui adhuc in regione infima consistens spiritui carni subijcere non didicit: psidere alij sine suo periculo nescit. Pastor aut inordinatus qui,pter cōmodum rei temporis monachos suos tanto periculo nō timet exponere: omnii anima p tali occasione percunctii reus est: t apud internii iudice ad restitutione oim obligatur. Non est de professione monachi secularii ecclesias regere: non expedie infirmo cenobite monialibus psidere. Sed quid: Ergo ne monachus imperio se pastoris debet opponere: si eum voluerit cu monialibus aut in ecclesias secularii residere: Dandat em regula: nihil obedientie pferendii. Aescio sane quid huic interrogationi respondeam: vt periculum qō vtrobic imminere cernitur non incurram. Nam si ve ritatem dicer subjectionis obedientiā videboz infringere re: si monachos periculo exponendo psefsero fatcor me peccare. Dicam tamen paucis quod sentio: quāqz paritu ram odiu veritatem nō ignoro. Sicut monachus de ne cessitate sue professionis in omnibus q sunt secundii regulam monastica suo simpliciter tenetur obedienti pastor: ita platus compellere monachii ad ea que sunt supra regulā maxime salutis periculo interveniēte nō potest sine ipius voluntate. Sed ecclesias regere: mulieribus pesse: extra cenobium residere: non est secundii regulā obedienti. Non irascamini nubi patres si veritate dixi: nolite frontē conn trahere si quod mihi videtur expressi vos nihilominus quod vobis videtur etiam me reclamante estis facturi. Verum tamen oro nolite moachos vestros periculo castitatis ex ponere: nolite aliquid ad monialium et ecclesiam, parrochian liu regimien violenter compellere: cui plures qui hec officia ambiciose appetant posse invenire. Bona quidem est obedientia: sed veritati et aie salutis nullatenus est pseren da. Cui emi de salutis periculo agitur: melius est obedientia humiliter excusando postponere: quod castitatis naufrago subire. Ve monachos platis qui cenobitis suis ecclesias secularium incorporant: qui avaricie facibus sinu cupi dinis laxant: quod se benefacere posteritati existimant: multos per occasionem damnant. Quarto rector monachorum inordinatus ad subditos suos efficit: si turbulentus et anxius inueniat. In pastore aia pia et prudens discretio valde necessaria est: ne aut zelus discipline sit nimius: aut modus copatiendi nimia laxitate remissus. Sed rector inordinatus qui per ina discretum furem tyrannum se monachis exhibet: qui per dissoluta copatione ad grauissima scelera velut insensibilis tacet. Aescit iusti moderamen regiminis: feruore in se non experitur fraterne charitatis: semper dum se monachorum exultimat: patre et sociis humiliis ignozat. Quid hoc regumie ferocius: quid sceleratius potestate, ubi non Deus, non ratio, non intellectus, sed bestia principat? Eniuero ubi Deus et intellectus gubernat imperium: a rectitudine legis nature presidentiis iudicia non recedunt. Inordinatus vero et anxius rector variis passionibus bestia et inficitur: semper male de monachis suspicatur: qui dum regiminis mon duni perperam dirigit: anxius semper amittere regnum cui herode pertinecit. Quinto pastor claustralium inordinatus ad monachos dicit: si in erogatis monasterii rebus aut nimius aut obsti tinatus babeatur. Nimius autem dicendus est si in distri buendo fuerit prodigus: aut indiscreta largitione diffusa sus. Obstinatus vero dicitur si que dada lunt oportune

...souls. Your horse grows weak and you prepare remedies; you think dangers are near, and yet that no danger threatens anyone. Your ox and your ass fall sick, and you feel for them; your brother is swallowed up by sorrow, and you do not come to his aid. You, therefore, are a hireling and not a shepherd, you who with a stubborn heart despise your brother’s infirmities; you do not help him when he is set in bitterness. Do not think that you can escape the hands of the Lord, whose sheep you allow to perish so wickedly.

Third, a ruler is disordered toward his subjects when those whom he ought to have kept with solicitude within the enclosure of the monastery he places, not without danger, in external affairs. For indeed, when a weak member of the monastery is set over the governance of nuns or assigned to secular churches, the integrity of regular observance is violated; and he who, still remaining in the lower region, has not learned to subject the flesh to the spirit, does not know how to preside over others without danger to himself. A disordered shepherd, who for the advantage of temporal property is not afraid to expose his monks to such great danger, is guilty of all the souls that perish through such an occasion, and before the inward judge he is bound to make restitution for them all. It does not belong to the profession of a monk to govern secular churches; it is not expedient for a weak cenobite to preside over nuns.

But what then? Should a monk oppose the command of his shepherd if he wishes him to reside with nuns or in secular churches? The Rule commands that nothing be preferred to obedience. Truly, I do not know what I should answer to this question, so as not to incur the danger that is seen to threaten on both sides. For if I speak the truth, I shall seem to break the obedience of subjection; if I encourage monks to expose themselves to danger, I confess that I sin. Yet I shall say briefly what I think, although I know that the truth will bring forth hatred. Just as a monk, by the necessity of his profession, is simply bound to obey his shepherd in all things that are according to the monastic rule, so a prelate cannot compel a monk, without his own consent, to things that are beyond the rule, especially when danger to salvation intervenes. But to govern churches, to preside over women, to reside outside the monastery, is not according to the rule of obedience.

Do not be angry with me, fathers, if I have spoken the truth; do not knit your brows if I have expressed what seems right to me. Nevertheless, you will do what seems right to you, even if I protest. Yet I beg you: do not expose your monks to danger against chastity; do not violently compel anyone to the governance of nuns and parish churches, since you can find many who ambitiously seek these offices. Obedience is indeed good, but it must in no way be preferred to truth and the salvation of the soul. For when danger to salvation is at issue, it is better humbly to excuse oneself and set obedience aside than to suffer shipwreck of chastity. Woe to the prelates of monks who incorporate secular churches into their monasteries, who loosen the torches of avarice in the lap of desire; because they think they are benefiting posterity, they damn many through the occasion.

Fourth, the ruler of monks becomes disordered toward his subjects if he is found turbulent and anxious. In a shepherd, pious and prudent discretion is very necessary, lest either zeal for discipline be excessive, or the measure of compassion be relaxed by excessive laxity. But the disordered ruler who, through indiscreet zeal, shows himself a tyrant to the monks, or who, through lax compassion, is silent and insensible before the gravest crimes, does not know the moderation of just governance. He does not experience in himself the fervor of fraternal charity; while he always esteems himself above the monks, he does not know how to be a humble father and companion. What is fiercer than this rule? What is more wicked than a power where neither God, nor reason, nor understanding, but a beast holds command? For where God and understanding govern authority, the judgments of those who preside do not depart from the uprightness of the law of nature. But the disordered and anxious ruler is bestial and infected with various passions; he always suspects evil of the monks, and, while he perversely directs the burden of governance, he is always anxious to lose the kingdom to which he clings like Herod.

Fifth, a shepherd of cloistered men is called disordered toward his monks if, in dispensing the goods of the monastery, he is found either excessive or obstinate. He is to be called excessive if he is wasteful in distributing, or poured out in indiscreet generosity. But he is called obstinate if he denies what ought fittingly to be given.

Obstinatus etiam dicendus est qui timorem dini proijicit: qui suo sensui numiũ confidit: qui in agendis quibuslibet nulla sapientiũ consilia admittit. Et quidã inter pastores animarũ coplures hacegrutudine mentis inordinati sunt: qui res monasteriũ aut numis improvidě erogant: aut nia mila tenacitate conservat. Coniua suis adulatoribus lau tissima preparant: alis vero quibus sunt auersi etiam mi numa negant. In domo hospitũ vel in abbacia sua pasto res inordinata conversatione depravativisq ad crapulam aliũi comedunt: de vino semp optimo bibunt: sed paupe ribus monachis qui vigilando cantando pondus po tant diei et sust vix tenuiter necessaria concedit. Sexto prelatus monacho valde inordinatus ostent ditur: si contra deum audax iudicia eius paruipendendo in superbiam elevatur. Eniiero cui pastor a subditis cor rigi no poscit, p sanctũ patre benedictũ ad iudiciũ del rea muititur: sicu in multis locis regulẽ habetur. Rouerit in quit abbasse de omnibus iudiciũ suis deo redderaratio nem. Et ite. Ordinatus autem abbas cogitet semper quale onus suscepit: cui villicationis fueredditurus est rationem. Et rursum dicit: Mox vt oriri via caeperine cui charitate illa amputet: non cui tyrannide. Et in alio lo co premonet dicens. Ipe tamen abbas cum timore del et obseruãtie sancte regule omnia faciat: sciens se procula dubio de omnibus iudiciũ suis eqssimo iudici deo ratio nem reddeturũ. Sed inordinatus rector monachorum hanc sanctissimi legislatoris cõminationem exaudire ven luc aspis obturatis auribus despicit: dei longanimitas tis patientiam contemnit: nihil de futuro examine cogin tat: donec sibi tandem iratus iudex in faciem dicat. Hec fecisti et tacui. Nunc itaõ redde rationem villicationis tue: resigna mihi oues hereditatis mee: mihiqz animas tibi quondam in corpore commissas fine mora restituez numerum earum integrum repone: quarum si vel vna te negligente interçt: faciem meam tua anima ineternum B uij non videbit. Quid tuc respodebis summo pastori rector inuicilis, vbi nō solu a te pcreuencii sanguis exigit: sed etiā ratio minus, pficientii postulaet. Ecce nunc in securitate peffima spreto dei examinu ambulas: ioia tibi liccre q plan cêt in corpe putas: t cuiis ratione daturus de omnibus aliqñ nō cogitas. Lico veniet dn̄s omnii cui te ministrũ infidelẽ nō times ostcādere: cuius tibi honoreni nō metuis arrogare. Aisi interea penitẽiā egeris: nui vitā in melius emédaueris: cu demonibus in inferno sine fine ardebis. Septimo contingit inordinatum erga subditos esse pastore. Si neglecta vtilitate comuni propriũ comodum vi ciola intentione quesierit: si presidens in monasterio non Deo sed suis vtilitatibus seruuit: dum se ppter carnis perniciosas libertates consequẽdas gaudet esse prelatũ: sibiis fraudulẽnter exrebus monasterii prouidet in futuq. Hec autc inordinatio in illis maxime qui cedunt officio qualibet occasione conspicitur: quibus pro mercede villicatio nis sue ac si fuissent episcopi annua penlio de rebus mos nasterij assignat. Nō est modus iste querentiũ dũm: non est via hec vetex monachoq. Dum cedis officio pastora li ppter deũ cede simpliciter: noli pter victum et vestitum quicũs exigere: si nō vis cum prietarijs peccare. Dona chus es: monachus priulũ fiercs abbas fuisti: monachus post officiũ permanebis. Cur ergo pensionem exi gas: quite monachũ non ignoras?
