has not given, or who grudgingly spends what is necessary on his subjects.

He too must be called obstinate who casts aside the fear of God, who trusts too much in his own judgment, and who in any business admits no counsels of the wise. And among shepherds of souls there are many who are disordered by this sickness of mind: they either spend the goods of monasteries or money improvidently, or preserve them with excessive stinginess. They prepare the most lavish banquets for their flatterers, but to others from whom they are estranged they deny even the smallest things. In the guesthouse or in their abbey, shepherds corrupted by disorderly conduct eat to excess and drink always the best wine; but to the poor monks, who by keeping watch and singing bear the burden and heat of the day, they scarcely grant even meager necessities.

Sixth, a prelate who is a monk is shown to be very disordered if, bold against God, he is lifted up in pride by making light of God’s judgments. For indeed, when a shepherd cannot be corrected by his subjects, he is sent on by the holy father Benedict to the judgment of God, as is found in many places in the Rule. “Let the abbot know,” he says, “that for all his judgments he must render an account to God.” And again: “Let the abbot who has been ordained always consider what a burden he has undertaken, and to whom he will have to render an account of his stewardship.” And again he says: “As soon as vices begin to arise, let him cut them off with charity, not with tyranny.” And in another place he warns, saying: “Let the abbot himself do all things with the fear of God and observance of the holy Rule, knowing beyond doubt that for all his judgments he will render an account to God, the most just judge.”

But the disordered ruler of monks, like a deaf asp stopping its ears, despises this warning of the most holy lawgiver; he scorns the patience of God’s long-suffering; he thinks nothing of the examination to come, until at last the judge, angered against him, says to his face: “These things you have done, and I was silent. Now therefore render an account of your stewardship. Give back to me the sheep of my inheritance, and restore to me without delay the souls once entrusted to you in the body. Return their number whole; for if even one of them has perished through your negligence, your soul shall never see my face for eternity.”

What then will you answer the supreme shepherd, invincible ruler, when not only the blood of those who have perished is demanded from you, but also an account of those who have made too little progress? Behold, now you walk in the worst security, despising God’s examination; you think that everything plainly permitted to you in the body is lawful for you, and you do not consider that one day you will give an account of all these things. But soon the Lord of all will come, before whom you do not fear to show yourself an unfaithful servant, whose honor you do not fear to claim for yourself. Unless in the meantime you do penance, unless you amend your life for the better, you will burn without end in hell with the demons.

Seventh, a shepherd happens to be disordered toward his subjects if, neglecting the common advantage, he seeks his own profit with a corrupt intention; if, presiding in a monastery, he serves not God but his own interests, while he rejoices that he is prelate in order to obtain the destructive liberties of the flesh, and fraudulently provides for himself, from the goods of the monastery, for the future. This disorder is especially seen in those who resign their office on some pretext, to whom, as the reward of their stewardship, as if they had been bishops, an annual pension is assigned from the goods of the monastery. This is not the manner of those who seek God; this is not the way of the old monks. When you resign the pastoral office for God’s sake, resign it simply. Do not demand anything for food and clothing, if you do not wish to sin with proprietors. You are a monk; you were a monk before you became abbot; after your office you will remain a monk. Why then do you demand a pension, since you know that you are a monk? Just as one commits the vice of simony by buying prelacies, so one sins against the Rule by demanding a pension for the resignation of an abbacy.

What then? Do we condemn those who, resigning the office of pastoral care without fault, have received annual pensions from the goods of the monastery? By no means. We do not forbid necessities; we deny superfluities. But he who is a true monk and lover of God is content, even after an abbacy, with the provision allowed by the Rule.

How monks are citizens of the lowest region, bound to one another by turns.

Article Four.

15
O Pues infime regionis monachiet boies carnales multis et varijs modis sunt inordinati adinuicem: qui q̄ passionibus aialibus more bestiarum concitati semetipos ad rectu iudicium rationis non dirigit: murandu no est si fraterne cōversationis ordinem puertunt. Semp em presumit seuae. pturbata cōscientia: et mala mens nunç gaudia pacis habet: sed cōtinuo via clop merore concutitur: sempiternis ignibus scelerum in tus cruciatur. Itaq monachi cuaes tenebrose regionis malis et inordinatis affectionibus obcecati finem mona stice, pfessionis non considerat: nihil aliud q̄ pṣentis vite cōmodũ amant: salutem propriam negligent: ad eterni tatis amorem non assurgunt. C Primo igit ad inuicem valde inordinatis sunt. du intel lectualem respectu in fratres habendũ abisciit: du imagi nem deï in homine no aduertũ: dum cōmunionem gran tie 7 glorte hoibus infuse 7 in futuro condonade non cogi tant: nec fraterne confederationis dilectionem sibi mutuo exhibere curat. Vtuit inuicem sicut equus et mulus cor porali sceinate concordes: qui q̄cqd sensualitati gratũ et diligũt: quicqd rationi cōuenit non admicũt. Diligie alter ab altero non q̄ homo est: sed q̄ dilectori suo in affe ctione sensualitatis simulis est. Homo emi carnis amat in hoie no virtutes. no religione. no denig ipam naturũ: sed carnũ. sed sanguine. sed corporis qualitatem. Lu ergo amor carniũ sit carnalis: extacili est occasione mutabũ lis. Cuaes emi hui? infime regionis mores venerant consi nules: 7 monachos monachi semp affectione cōplectunq caeles. Quae de? ab eterno dilexit inordiatus cenobita pse quif: quẽ ille pter demerita spernit iste vt sanctũ venerat. C Secundo sunt inordinati claustrales ad inuicerauione dissimilitudinis: du vel seniores austeritate et supbia con citati suos iuniores despicũt: vel iuniores se suis senioris bus cōtumaciter oponũt. Et hec inordinatio sancteren gũle valde probatur contraria: que senioribus mandat iuniores ex paterna affectione diligere: 7 iunioribus prea incipit suis senioribus et pter deum humiliter obedire. Sed cui seniores huius infime regionis civis paternu affectu junioribus subtrahit: in graue odii minores inardescuit: et quse contemni iuvenes ab illis inuuste considerat: eo mores improbos quotidie accusant. Discut ergo infirmi iuvenes mores no rectos senior: et in puerbio dicit suo cui canere maiores considerat: sic quos minores saltat. Tercio male adiuicé ordinantur monachi qui zelus boni et mutua obedientiā abjecti: qui malu et a regula prohibiti zelandi genus assumunt. Verbis et factis sibi inuicē varias comittit inuarias: alter alteru emulandi studio in malu observuare nititur: ad contumeliā inferendam alter ab altero prouocaet. Infirmitates suas mutuo sibi impropertat: ad vindictā semp anhelant. Regularis discipline zelus delspicit: indignationis et amaritudinis passio dominatur. Aversis vultibus sibi inuicē obuiant: quātū lateat in pectore odio apertis indicis manifestant. Non sic impī non sic: quī quisquis odio fratris sui persequitur: homicida et regno dei indignus comprobaet. O misera semper carnaliī monachis conditio: quē tanto inferno est prima: quāto a timore dei fuerit aliena. Imitant eim non angelos sed demones: quīcūs p zelus malu in schola pacis delectantur esse discordes. Anuero sicut animal brus tum nature sue ferita tem non desert: sic monachos bestiā lis a zelo pessimo non recedit. Quaeadimodũ monachi civis infime regionis ad seipos inordinatis sunt. Articulus v. Iues infime regionis moachi carnales ad nihil magis inordinati sunt: qu ad semetipos. Omne em consideratione suiius abjecti: in quem sine fine creati no attendit: qu dum se unusquis serdibus via cio et polluit: a conditionis sue originali rectitudine mens improba recedit. Nec mirandũ si ad alios inordinatus foris cultor infime regionis efficitur: qui p varias passion

Carnal monks and carnal men of the lowest region are disordered among themselves in many different ways. Since, stirred up by animal passions in the manner of beasts, they do not direct themselves by the right judgment of reason, it is no wonder if they overturn the order of brotherly life. For a troubled conscience is always presumptuous and fierce, and an evil mind never has the joys of peace, but is continually shaken by the grief of vices and inwardly tormented by the everlasting fires of crimes. Therefore the monks, citizens of the dark region, blinded by evil and disordered affections, do not consider the end of the monastic profession; they love nothing but the advantage of this present life; they neglect their own salvation; they do not rise up to the love of eternity.

First, then, they are greatly disordered toward one another, when they cast aside the intellectual regard that should be had for brothers; when they do not perceive the image of God in man; when they do not think of the communion of grace and glory infused into human beings and to be bestowed in the future; nor do they take care to show one another the love of brotherly fellowship. They live with one another like horse and mule, concordant in bodily society: whatever is pleasing to sensuality they love, but whatever accords with reason they do not admit. One is loved by another not because he is a man, but because he is like his lover in the affection of sensuality. For the man of flesh loves in a man not virtues, not religion, not even nature itself, but flesh, blood, and bodily quality. Since, therefore, the love of flesh is carnal, it is easily changeable when occasion arises. For the citizens of this lowest region venerate manners like their own, and carnal monks always embrace carnal monks with affection. The man whom God has loved from eternity the disordered cenobite persecutes; the man whom God despises for his demerits, this monk venerates as holy.

Second, cloistered men are disordered toward one another by reason of dissimilarity, when either the seniors, stirred up by harshness and pride, despise their juniors, or the juniors stubbornly oppose their seniors. And this disorder is proved to be very contrary to the holy Rule, which commands seniors to love juniors with fatherly affection, and instructs juniors to obey their seniors humbly and for God’s sake. But since the seniors, citizens of this lowest region, withhold fatherly affection from the juniors, the lesser men burn with a heavy hatred; and because the young men consider that they are unjustly despised by them, they daily accuse their corrupt morals. Thus the weak young men learn the crooked morals of the seniors, and in his proverb he says, considering those greater than himself to sing: as the greater sing, so the lesser dance.

Third, monks are badly ordered toward one another when, casting away zeal for the good and mutual obedience, they take up an evil kind of zeal forbidden by the Rule. In words and deeds they commit various injuries against one another; one strives, out of rivalry, to watch another for evil; one is provoked by another to inflict insult. They reproach one another with their weaknesses; they are always panting for vengeance. Zeal for regular discipline is despised; the passion of indignation and bitterness holds sway. They meet one another with faces turned away, and by open signs they reveal how much hatred lies hidden in the breast. Not so, impious men, not so: for whoever persecutes his brother with hatred is proved to be a murderer and unworthy of the kingdom of God. O wretched condition always of carnal monks, which is nearer to hell the more it has been estranged from the fear of God. For they imitate not angels but demons, who by evil zeal delight to be discordant in the school of peace. Indeed, just as a brute animal does not abandon the savagery of its nature, so a beastly monk does not withdraw from the worst zeal.

In what way the monks, citizens of the lowest region, are disordered toward themselves.

Article Five.

The carnal monks, citizens of the lowest region, are disordered toward nothing more than toward themselves. For, having cast aside every consideration of themselves, they do not attend to the purpose for which they were created without end; and while each one pollutes himself with the filth of vice, the wicked mind recedes from the original uprightness of its condition. Nor is it surprising if the inhabitant of the lowest region becomes outwardly disordered toward others, since through various passions [unclear].

16
nes carnis a semetipso cōfusus interius dissipat. Dicit est scriptura. Qui sibi malus est, cui bonus erit: Rectus hu mane cōditionis ordo carnē spiritui subjiciendā instituit: ipūs iubest subjectus illi a quo sestendi formā accept. Sed apud carnales mentes ordo rationis puertit: du caro spiritui dominat: et ratio q̄ scōm insitā sibi vim intel lectus omni gubernare debuerat: carnis voluptatibus suffocara ad rectitudinē iudicij p simperiū nō festinat. Sunt igni ad seipos monachi carnales inordinati p curiolistatīs viciũ: q̄m singrendo vitā alienā curiose siuis dicat: et propriā omnibus inquinata viciũ nō emendāt. Magnā in seipis scelera corrigere nesciunt: q tamēin mīa numis delinquētes alios supbe rephēdūt. Festuca in ocu lo frātrīs diligenter considerant: et trabem suis herentem oculis tanq sihi sit exculant. Q̄es affectiones suas seno qualitati subjiciunt: pretoq̄ recte rationis iudicio carnali ter sicut bestie viuīt: quos frequēter ad trā passio sōcitat: invidie furor sōtra primū inflāmat. Vindictā in frātrīs anxio semp animo expostulāt: quā sepe nimio furore obce cati nō sine siçmodo priro reportāt. Sed diu latērēn occulto ciues inordinati nequeunt: q suāto sibi p elationē mēris manēt incogniti: tanto p cecīi iudiciũ alīs siūt ma nifesti. Omnīs em supbus s inordinatus primū semetipsm ignorare dicit: q̄m si veraciter seipm cognosceret: nullare nus supbiret. Cum vero suīpīus inordinatio de supbia lumat suīgine: nō possumus banc peste melius describē re: q̄i radices eius p gradus descendentēs ad inferos cu remus aperire. Astīcutvite spūalis summa in duodecim gradibus suilitatis sūcludit: ita tocius inordinationis monastice scaturīgo in bisenīs supbia gradibus sōrīnet. Primus ita s gradus superbie curiolistatīs dicitur: qua male ordinati ad seipos monachi, vitā et mores p prios negligūt: ct aliq̄ vel facta vel dicta iugiter inqrūt. Omni te frātrī negligentias arguīt: vitā pastoris rephendūt: q suāto curiosius aliena foris scire a spetuit: tāto a semetip pis sōgius recedūt. Monachis auc vicium curiolistatīs perniciosissimoe est: quoe metem sua semel inuaserit: omnibus virtutibus spolioes, vicio et domicilioe facit. Verissimoe infirmitatis signoes est alioe factoe discutere: poeter rationoe officioe in alienis se culpoes occupare. Donachus em qui secundoe nosoe sui doefinitionoe seipoem soloe curare poecipitur: non sine salutis sue manifestoe periculo alioe factoe perscrutat. Quicoes aut se vicio curiositatis suboecioet: in secundoe moroe gradoe supoebie descendoet. Senip em vnus disponit ad alioe: nulloes soloe dominoe elatis monachoes peccatoe.

The pleasures of the flesh confuse him and inwardly scatter him away from himself. Scripture says: “He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?” The right order of the human condition was established by making the flesh subject to the spirit; and the spirit itself is subject to him from whom it received the form of its existence.

But in carnal minds the order of reason is overturned, when the flesh rules over the spirit, and reason, which according to the power of understanding implanted in it ought to govern all things, is choked by the pleasures of the flesh and does not hasten, by its authority, toward upright judgment.

Carnal monks are disordered toward themselves through the vice of curiosity: they pry curiously into another’s life, words, and deeds, while they do not correct their own life, stained with every vice. They do not know how to correct great crimes in themselves, yet they proudly rebuke others who offend in the smallest matters. They carefully consider the speck in a brother’s eye, and excuse the beam lodged in their own eyes as though it were nothing to them.

They subject their affections to sensuality, and, setting aside the judgment of right reason, live carnally like beasts. Passion often stirs them to anger; the fury of envy inflames them against their neighbor. With an anxious heart they are always demanding vengeance on their brothers, and often, blinded by excessive fury, they do not obtain it without [unclear].

But the disordered cannot remain hidden long in secret: the more they remain unknown to themselves through pride of mind, the more manifest they become to others through the blindness of their judgment. For every proud man is disordered and is said first to be ignorant of himself, because if he truly knew himself, he would in no way be proud.

Since, then, disorder of oneself takes its origin from the root of pride, we cannot describe this plague better than by attempting to disclose its roots as they descend by degrees toward hell. Just as the summit of spiritual life is comprised in twelve degrees of humility, so the source of all monastic disorder is contained in twelve degrees of pride.

The first degree of pride is called curiosity. By it monks who are badly ordered toward themselves neglect their own life and conduct, and continually inquire into the deeds or words of others. They accuse every negligence of a brother; they rebuke the life of the pastor; and the more curiously they desire to know outwardly what belongs to others, the farther they withdraw from themselves.

The vice of curiosity is most pernicious for monks: once it has invaded the mind, it strips it of all virtues and makes it a dwelling place of vice. It is a very sure sign of sickness to examine the deeds of others, and, neglecting the office of reason, to occupy oneself with others’ faults. For a monk, who according to the true definition of his name is commanded to attend to himself alone, does not investigate the deeds of others without manifest danger to his salvation. Whoever subjects himself to the vice of curiosity descends to the second degree of pride in conduct. For one thing always disposes a person toward another; no sin rules alone in proud monks.

17
Secundoe ergoe supoebie gradoe mentis leoeitas est: et vagoe cordis instabiloes occupatio. The second degree of pride, therefore, is levity of mind and the restless preoccupation of a wandering, unstable heart. In this degree of disordered conduct, carnal monks fall into various passions, which they have contracted in a sensual way from the vice of curiosity. But it is fitting for a true cenobite [unclear].

18
ceperis mor in contrariũ se erigunt: multa in illũ viciosa dicunt: quia dum se solos laudabiles ostendere cupiunt: nullum laudari coram se alium pmittunt. Quintus gradus sngbie singularitas accipitur: qui de lactantie tumore generatur. In bunc gradũ superbi clau strales coaeruũt: qui se vel merito vel scientia pminere alius p lactantia plumpserũt. Unde neceteris p coeversationem a paraecant similes: ex sola lesupbia in omnibus exhibenc singulares. Sed singularitas ista in cenobio rephendit: vbi viuere in comuni omnes secundũ regulã iubent. Su perbi aut monachi divo testante bernardo. dum se alius virtutibus et sapientia pferunt: in tantã arrogantia teme ritatís cadût: vt plus sibi de vno ieiunio blandiantur co medentibus ceteris: q̄ si alius septem diebus ieiunassent: penicis cõmodior illis videtur vna oratiuncula singula ris: q̄ psalmodia tota vnius noctis. Inter prandendum oculos p mensam sepe circũferunt: et si quẽ minus come dere viderint ingemiscũt: secũ dolere victos incipit: sub trahentes sibi crudeliter q̄ necessario victui puiderunt. Di superbi claustrales ad singularia sua sunt strẽnuũ: ad comuniã pigri. In lecto vigilant: in choro et in lectione regulari dormitant. Sertus superbie gradus de quinto sumit erordium: qui dicitur arrogantia superbo. Et muero cu inordinati claustrales p singularitatis studiũ alius apparere foris ino cipiant: in maiorem arrogantie velaniam inardescunt: et quodcuũs in eo laudem ab hoũbus dicitur: verum fatui arbitratur. O miserada superbo stulticia: qui cu in omnis bus rebus alius nulli plus credant q̄ sibi: de se solum sibi minus credit q̄ alteri. Quicũd de selaudatu ab imperio tis audiũt: no ignorante vel bentuolentie laudatoris. sed suis meritis ascribunt. Sed qũng humanis laudibus delectabiliter pascitur: omni virtute vacuus. et arrogans tia plenus coram diu habetur. Seprimus gradus superbie pcedente nascitur: qui superbo. plumprio a pellatur. Di conines arrogantes incipit qui se esse aliquid magni singulariter credunt. De quibus dicit bernardus. Qui se alios pcedere existimat: quomodo plus de se et de alijs non plumat. Primus in convivu residet: in consilii primus respondet: non vocatvs accedit: non iussus se incromittit: reordinat ordinat et refutat ab alijs facta. Quicquid ipse non fecerit aut et dinauerit. non recte factum: nec pulchre existimat ordinatum. Judicat iudicantes: preludicat iudicaturis. Qui enim deus in corde non sufficit: frustra in exterioribus solacium querit. Octauus gradus supple peccator et defenso dicitur: & de presumptione semper generatur. Donachus em presumptuosus se omnibus meliore semper existimat: peccatii quod comiserit. aut peinaciter negat: aut si convictus fuerit multipliciter excusat. Nuomodo nāq culpā sua cōfite ri humiliter poterit: qui se reum nō agnoscit? Huc talem li. p d elictis suis castigare volueris: semp deteriorē facis. Quicūqs ergo p qualibet re correctus in verba malicie dedinauerit: quonos arguenti se excusationes peccatorū oponit: in huc mortis descensum quico humilitatis gra dui oppositi cadit. Clarīs auct modis peccatum sui presumptuosus excusare ntititur: q in hunc superbe gradum corruisse inuenitur. Aut em dicit. non feci: aut feci quidē sed benefeci: aut si male. non multum male: aut si multum male. non mala intentione. Et si convictus de malicia fuerit: mox in sui excusatione alieni consilium assumit. Sed qui procaciter etiā aperta et manifesta negare vel defenso dere nō metuit: nunq occulta scōm regulā abbati suo rea nelabit. Cum vero ad confessionē venerit: veritate simula to animo palliabit: q ve ipse confusionem possit euaderē: alioq studet in meditu negligentias proferre. Intus male ordinatus supbus et presumptuosus culpas in confessione palliat prias: consitek alienas. Semp inquietus apud se aliuj facta examinat: omnes vna sententia damnat: neminem recte in cenobio vivere conqueritur: nulla m esse inter fratres charicatē arbitratur. &ō si vana presumptio

When you have begun, they at once rise up in opposition; they say many vicious things against him, because, while they desire to show themselves alone worthy of praise, they do not allow any other man to be praised in their presence.

The fifth degree of pride is called singularity, which is born from the swelling of boastfulness. Proud cloisterers are gathered into this degree: those who, out of boastfulness, have presumed that they excel others either in merit or in knowledge. Hence they do not appear like the rest in their way of life, but from pride alone show themselves singular in everything. But this singularity is reprehensible in a monastery, where all are ordered by the rule to live in common. Proud monks, as blessed Bernard testifies, while they prefer themselves to others in virtues and wisdom, fall into such arrogant rashness that they flatter themselves more for a single fast while the rest are eating than if others had fasted for seven days; one little private prayer seems to them far more profitable than the whole psalmody of a night. During meals they often carry their eyes around the table, and if they see anyone eating less, they groan; they begin to grieve within themselves that they have been outdone, cruelly withdrawing from themselves what was provided for necessary sustenance. Proud cloisterers are eager for their singular practices, sluggish for common ones. They lie awake in bed; in choir and at the regular reading they doze.

The sixth degree of pride takes its beginning from the fifth; it is called the arrogance of the proud. For when disordered cloisterers, through zeal for singularity, begin to appear outwardly before others, they burn into a greater madness of arrogance, and whatever is said by men in their praise, the fools consider true. O pitiable folly of the proud: although in all other matters they trust no one more than themselves, about themselves alone they trust themselves less than another. Whatever praise of themselves they hear from the ignorant, they ascribe not to the ignorance or good will of the one praising them, but to their own merits. But whoever is delightfully fed on human praises is regarded before God as empty of every virtue and full of arrogance.

The seventh degree of pride is born from the preceding one and is called presumption. From this begin those who singularly believe themselves to be something great. Of them Bernard says: He who thinks he surpasses others, how should he not presume more about himself and about others? He sits first at the banquet; in council he answers first; uncalled he approaches; unbidden he intrudes; he rearranges what has been arranged and rejects what has been done by others. Whatever he himself has not done or ordered, he does not think rightly done or properly arranged. He judges those who judge; he prejudges those who are about to judge. For one to whom God is not enough in the heart seeks consolation in outward things in vain.

The eighth degree of pride is called the excuse and defense of sin, and it is always born from presumption. For a presumptuous monk always considers himself better than everyone else; the sin he has committed he either stubbornly denies, or, if he has been convicted, he excuses in many ways. For how will he be able to confess his fault humbly, when he does not acknowledge himself guilty? If you wish to chastise such a man for his offenses, you always make him worse. Therefore whoever, when corrected for any matter, has turned aside into words of malice, because he opposes excuses for sins to the one reproving him, falls into this descent of death, which is opposed to the eighth degree of humility. The presumptuous man who is found to have fallen into this degree of pride tries to excuse his sin in four ways. For he says either, “I did not do it,” or, “I did it indeed, but I did well,” or, “If badly, not very badly,” or, “If very badly, not with a bad intention.” And if he has been convicted of malice, he immediately pleads another’s advice in excuse of himself. But he who does not fear brazenly to deny or defend even open and manifest things will never reveal hidden things to his abbot according to the rule. When he comes to confession, he will cloak the truth with a feigned mind, so that he himself may escape shame; otherwise he strives to bring the negligences of others into the open. Inwardly disordered, proud, and presumptuous, he conceals his own faults in confession and confesses others’. Always restless within himself, he examines the deeds of others, condemns all with one sentence, complains that no one lives rightly in the monastery, and thinks there is no charity among the brothers. And if vain presumption

Undecimū superbe gradum qui est libertas peccandi consequēter monachi rebellis incidit: qui nō solū fratriī sed etiam plato et correptiones et bortamenta contemnēt. Amōre du rebellio contra pceptorem assumitur: audacia peccandi generatur: qui correptionis auctoritātē despiciēt: iam quasi licenter omnia scelerā committit. Amor dei bonos cenobitas a peccatis voluntarie cohībet: eccia mor infirmos cohercet. Ubi vero nec amor dei nec mens correptionis monachū penetrat: iam mens per rebellionem et consuetudinem peccandi inferno a propinquat. Dicit em scriptura. Impius cūvenērit in profundū malorum contemnit. Quid cōtemnit: Deum cōtemnit: hoies spernit: desperatus animēsue salutem querere nescit. Duodecimū ergo superbe gradū incidit: qui p audacia peccandi in malā consuetudinē currīt. Hic est primus de scensus ad inferos: hec semita inferni: hoc iter velox ad regionem opertā mortis caligine. Quicūs hūc gradū consuetudinis peccandi semel incidentī: non nisi in manu miserationis dei valida resurgit: quia duī consuetudini nō resistitur: necessitas peccandi generat. Semper in peius maliciā proficit: et semper ruens, profundius cadit. Ecce istī sunt superbe gradus duodecimi quos ad in fernum descenditur: quos quuncī cupit cuadere: semper se studeat in humilitatis observatiā custodire. In his duos decimi malis omnis indignitas vicio, cenobitā obnubilat: ad se inordinatū monachū causat: moribus hominē in bestiam ferocissimā commutat. Finis hoc interitus est: ec nīs ante morte carnis penitentieremediū intercueniat: p greffus malō graduum arturum sine fine monachum:

if it has been detected by the diligence of his confessor, he soon seeks another confessor. And if the abbot tries to oppose him, the monk, lifted up into the ninth degree of pride, falls through restlessness of mind.

The ninth degree of pride is described as murmuring or impatience, which for the most part rules carnal monks. But the man whose confession is feigned, when touched by one slight insult or penance, soon rises up into open pride. The deceit that was pretending humility is revealed; the false mind can no longer hide itself for long, but is compelled to bring into public view whatever lies hidden within. From then on, having lost control of himself, the proud cenobite murmurs at everything; he bitterly accuses the judgment of his pastor, however just it may be; he gnashes his teeth, is stirred up and grows angry; without reason, like a madman, he throws everything into confusion. But the proud monk, given over to murmuring, having despised the fourth degree of humility, falls into the tenth descent of pride, through which he runs toward hell.

The tenth degree of pride follows murmuring, and is called rebellion. Proud and carnal monks fall into this, who, still dwelling in the lowest region, devote themselves to murmurings. Hence Bernard says: unless divine mercy looks upon the murmurer, so that at last, being converted, which is very difficult for such people, he silently acquiesces in the judgments of others, he soon becomes brazen and shameless, and falls all the worse into this degree, the more desperately he fails to restrain the movement of his mind. He always advances toward worse things; and he who before had arrogantly despised his brothers in secret now, what is more serious, openly shows that he despises his master as well. But the chastisement of divine judgment does not allow this degree of pride to pass long unpunished, since monks who rebel against their pastors are often quickly consumed by a miserable death. For some, departing from the order, become apostates; others, because of grave crimes, foul the prisons; some, expelled from monasteries, wander in wretched exile; many, horribly struck by the Lord, hasten in despair to hell. For it is written: Whoever resists authority opposes God’s ordinance. And again the Lord says to the prelates of the faithful: Whoever despises you despises me.

What will you still say, rebellious monks? Will you cite laws to me, by which you corrupt the truth? But I dare to say what I wish you were ashamed to hear. Rebellious monk, in the strict judgment of God no presumption of law will save you, who now proudly despise the obedience of subjection. Law commands obedience; it requires humble subjection in the order.

Consequently the rebellious monk falls into the eleventh degree of pride, which is freedom to sin, when he despises not only his brothers but even his prelate, and corrections and exhortations. When rebellion against the preceptor is taken up, boldness in sinning is born; and one who despises the authority of correction now commits every crime as if lawfully. The love of God voluntarily restrains good cenobites from sins; fear of correction restrains the weak. But where neither the love of God nor fear of correction pierces the monk, the mind, through rebellion and the habit of sinning, is already drawing near to hell. For Scripture says: When the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises. What does he despise? He despises God, spurns men, and, despairing, does not know how to seek the salvation of his soul.

Therefore he falls into the twelfth degree of pride, who through boldness in sinning runs into evil custom. This is the first descent to hell; this is the path of hell; this is the swift road to the region covered with the darkness of death. Whoever once falls into this degree of the custom of sinning rises again only by the strong hand of God’s mercy, because when custom is not resisted, it produces a necessity of sinning. He always advances in malice toward the worse, and, always falling, he falls more deeply.

Behold, these are the twelve degrees of pride by which one descends to hell. Whoever desires to avoid them must always strive to keep himself in the observance of humility. In these twelve evils every unworthiness of vice darkens the cenobite, makes the monk disordered within himself, and by his conduct changes the man into a most savage beast. The end of this is destruction; and unless the remedy of penitence intervenes before the death of the flesh, through the steps of the evil degrees it drives the monk endlessly to Tartarus.

condemns. But whoever, being disordered in himself, has once fallen into the first degree of pride, unless he strives to rise again as quickly as possible through penance, soon casts himself down into the second and then, in order, into all the rest. In these degrees of elation, then, the sum of the disorder of carnal monks in themselves is expressed; through them the disordered citizens of the lowest region are shown. And what we have said about disordered and proud monks must also be understood of the prelates of the lowest region.

How the citizens of the lowest region, the disordered carnal monks, are disposed toward the monastery’s goods.

Article Six

Whoever, being placed in a monastery, neglects to order his inward affections toward the purity of a holy purpose, often also exceeds grievously in outward things. Monks disordered toward God are, consequently, declared disordered toward their duties. For just as a good cenobite, united by love to the divine will, considers all things with a simple eye according to the right order of reason, so one who is turned away from God through disordered affections sins even in the good things that he uses badly. Therefore the carnal monks who inhabit the lowest region are badly disordered not only with respect to their souls, but also with respect to the monastery’s temporal property. For an outward disturbance of the body follows the inward confusion of the mind, and the one is shown by the other.

First, then, the citizens of the lowest region are badly ordered toward the monastery’s goods when they demand that these be granted to them in an improper order, or in any way usurp more than the usage of regular observance permits. For the Rule, which commands that all necessary things be given to monks, utterly forbids superfluous things.

Second, those use the monastery’s goods badly who, against the prohibition of the master, do not fear to give and receive, or who faithlessly commit deceit and fraud in what has been entrusted to them. For a monk who, at his own pleasure, without reasonable cause, against the Rule and without permission, in any way squanders the monastery’s goods, sins under the Rule like an unfaithful dependent and a falsifier.

Third, monks or abbots show themselves disordered toward the monastery’s goods when they devote them to unlawful uses. Theft and sacrilege are committed together when the monastery’s goods are turned to illicit uses. For the monastery’s property, dedicated to God, is commanded to be guarded like the vessels of the holy altar, lest it be squandered in any way through negligence. But one who forbids cloistered persons to spend goods uselessly must by no means allow them to be granted and paid out for sinful purposes. What will the monks and rulers of the lowest region answer to the lawgiver in the strict examination, when they have not feared to squander the monastery’s goods on parents, relatives, mimes, actors, and shameful people, as an occasion and reward of sin?

Fourth, abbots and carnal monks sin gravely in regard to the monastery’s goods when they heap them up too greedily, to the detriment of divine charity and their own salvation. For, inflamed by the torches of avarice, they think of nothing but profits and money; they violate and do not observe all feast days; they always desire to increase temporal goods; they do not notice the losses of charity. They grieve more over a beast dying than over a sinner perishing. Indeed all disordered cloistered persons are so blind that they consider avarice to be prudence and think riches to be reform. They join field to field, call gain piety, and where they see temporal goods abound, there they say the best discipline is observed. They refuse to spend even a little for the common good of the order, because they have lost the inward order of true charity. They raise useless, curious, and damnable buildings on high; they buy costly garments and ornaments less necessary for divine services; they clothe sacred things with gold and leave Christ’s poor naked. This greedy curiosity does not befit monks, since we are commanded to imitate the saints of old and are ordered to sell [unclear] for the support of the poor. But a covetous monk and an avaricious abbot are as far from the purpose of holy religion as the devil is from heaven.

Fifth, carnal monks sin in regard to the monastery’s goods when they do not repay them with prayers. Alms [unclear].

When things are offered, all receive them cheerfully; but few repay the givers with the support of prayer. Among these are many citizens of the lowest region who, when they have come to the order, serve not God but their belly. They desire to have more food, drink, and clothing given to them than necessity requires; and those who in the world could scarcely have had bread and vegetables for food, now, having become monks, refuse eggs and little fish. They importunately demand that large, varied, different, and delicate fish be given them; murmuring through the concupiscence of the flesh with the children of Israel in the desert, they cry out against their leader. They say that they cannot eat eggs and peas; they always desire more delicate things.

How the citizens of the lowest region are ill-ordered toward contempt of the world.

Article Seven.

The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it. Therefore whoever desires to enter the heavenly kingdom through the weapons of holy obedience, whoever chooses to live for God under regular discipline, must do violence to the pleasures of the flesh and strongly contemn the world with all its vanities. But carnal monks, citizens of the lowest region, who are so badly ordered toward God and toward themselves, are also badly ordered toward contempt of the world.

First, they are infected by the concupiscence of the flesh, for they are always burning with the fire of pleasure. In food and drink they are found excessive; in beds and baths they are delicate against the rules; they prefer the desires of the flesh to the salvation of the soul; they do not seek the sweetness of inward conversation. They nourish their flesh too delicately, and because of this they are continually inflamed with various desires. For no one can truly contemn the world who neglects to restrain the appetite of the flesh even in the smallest things. If you eat to satiety, you do not truly contemn the world. The first great commandment imposed on those who contemn the world is founded on abstinence. But if you fill your belly even once to satiety with food, you immediately fall either into lust or into heavy sloth. Therefore the concupiscence of the flesh draws back the mind of the disordered cenobite, so that he cannot contemn the world.

Second, they are disordered with respect to contemning the world because of the vain concupiscence of the eyes. For the monk who forgets the true honors of faithful souls takes delight in worldly displays and utterly curious ornaments. And truly, what each person is inwardly, hidden within himself, his outward apparel makes manifest. To carry rings on the fingers, corals on the rosaries, scent-vessels in the hands, and pleats in the cowls does not show a monk but a soldier; it displays not a humble cenobite but a proud worldling. Such adornment in monks can please none but the reprobate, and it is often found to have displeased even the proud. Woe to you, disordered cloisterers, who descend to hell through the double concupiscence of the eyes: while you desire to see in others what is not fitting, and while you present yourselves to be seen by others otherwise than is proper. What have the trinkets of the world to do with you, or the curiosities of the world? Beauty of clothing, as Bernard testifies, quickly makes a masculine soul effeminate; the honorable fashions of outward attire quickly weaken a manly disposition. These men are like children in little rags who, because of one red thread fastened to a torn sleeve, think themselves very beautiful and handsome, and insolently mock others standing before them in the best garments as if they were naked. These pompous cloisterers see others walking in humble clothing, contemning the world in the spirit of poverty, and for that reason pleasing both God and men; they see themselves despised by the wise and by princes, and sometimes not even admitted to conversation. Seeing these things, the proud are deeply grieved, as if by an injury; yet they utterly refuse to lay aside their arrogance.

Third, the citizen of the lowest region is badly ordered toward contempt of the world because of the pride of life: for they are not only infected with the vain pleasures of the flesh, but are also proud through the swelling of the mind. For all who follow the desires of the flesh vainly raise themselves above themselves; they contemn others, however much better they may be; they do not know how to endure equals; they do not accept superiors. They take delight in having a great retinue of servants stand by them in [unclear].

22
consilii primi contendunt residere: vidéri hominibus gloriis a petuit: pomposa et publica incedunt. Inflatiusque spiritu monasteria se gloriant ex fundatione posidere insignia: rebus temporalibus opulentis: clenodis structuris et privilegiis curtosa. Pauperes monachos vel abates exilium cenobio et elato corde despiciunt: se perire melioribus non crubescunt: qui quato gloria in rebus exterioribus venari cupiunt: tanto a vera gloria cum fatis virginibus recedunt. Quaeadmodi civis huius in- firmae regionis sint inor- dinati ad penitentiam. Articulus vii. Unus homo natus de muliere breui viuens temo- pore multis repletus miseris in eodem statu pa- manere diu non valeat: necesse est ut se omni studio quotidie reformado ad finem debitu coevertat: qui diu quis viuere in hoc modo mittitur: in virtuae parte muta- bilis phibeat. Quisquis ergo in hac mutabilitate consti- cutus venire ad immutabilitatis gaudia desiderat: suam fragilitatem humiliter agnoscat: semper post lapsum pec- cati ad penitentie remedia coefugiat: et iacere in scelere etiam ad momenti primum escat. Vita enim monachis semper in peni- tentia salutaris debet consistere: et adventu iudicis cum timo- res sancto iugiter expectare. Dicit enim Hieronymus. Amonachus non docentis sed plangentis habet officium: qui vel scugeat vel mundum: et dini pauidus prestoletur aduentum. Sed infirmae regionis inordinati claustrales hoc remedium salutare despiciunt: tempus acceptabile in vanitate coesumunt: et quod oia male ordinari non metuunt: etiam ad agendae penitentia valde se inordinatos ostendunt. Primo quidem male ad penitentia ordinati et mentis incuria: dum quantu displiceat omnipotenti deo peccatum intelligere negligunt: cui praevae voluntatis arbitrio contradicere non primum escut. Sic ut noctetra diei oppositae sic peccator divinae bonitati auersus et aduersarius habet. Sed monachi carnales dei honoris despiciunt etideo contumelia peccati non aduertunt. Emendare venialia negligent: qui quasi licenter mortalia committunt. Dicitem scriptura. they strive to sit in the first place of counsel; they desire to seem glorious to men; they go about in pomp and public display. With a more swollen spirit they boast that by foundation they possess distinguished monasteries, rich in temporal goods, costly in treasures, buildings, and privileges. With proud and haughty heart they despise poor monks or abbots of a poor monastery, and they are not ashamed to prefer themselves to better men; for the more they desire to hunt for glory in outward things, the more they withdraw, with the foolish virgins, from true glory.

How the citizens of this inferior region are disordered toward penitence.

Article VII.

Man, born of woman, living for a short time and filled with many miseries, cannot long remain in the same state. It is necessary that, by reforming himself daily with all zeal, he turn himself toward his due end; for as long as anyone is sent to live in this world, he proves changeable in the matter of virtue. Therefore whoever, placed amid this changeability, desires to come to the joys of immutability must humbly acknowledge his own frailty, must always after the fall of sin flee to the remedies of penitence, and must dread lying in wickedness even for a single moment.

For the life of monks must always consist in saving penitence, and must continually await the coming of the Judge with holy fear. For Jerome says: “A monk has the office not of teaching but of weeping,” one who should mourn either himself or the world, and wait in dread for the divine coming. But the disordered cloisterers of the inferior region despise this saving remedy; they waste the acceptable time in vanity; and because they do not fear to order everything badly, they show themselves very disordered even for doing penitence.

First, indeed, they are badly ordered toward penitence through negligence of mind, when they neglect to understand how greatly sin displeases almighty God, whom it is not lawful to contradict by the choice of a perverse will. Just as night is opposed to day, so the sinner is turned away from divine goodness and stands as its adversary. What a putrid corpse is accustomed to do in the sight of men, sin does in its own way, incomparably more, in the sight of the angels. But carnal monks despise the honor of God, and therefore they do not notice the insult of sin. They neglect to amend venial sins, as though they might lawfully commit mortal ones. For Scripture says: “He who neglects the least things falls little by little.” Hence Bernard warns us with his judgment, saying: “Let no one, brothers, say in his heart: These are slight matters; I do not care to correct them; it is no great thing to remain in these smallest venial sins. This, brothers, is impenitence; this is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which is unforgivable. No one can avoid falling into greater sins if he despises amending the lesser.” Nothing is worse than this negligence of mind.

Second, carnal monks, lovers of the lowest region, are exceedingly disordered toward penitence because they do not notice the contagion of sin. For just as a healthy man is very often infected by a contagious disease, so from one sin a man is inclined toward another. One sin is always said to dispose toward another, unless it is amended as quickly as possible through contrition. For the prophet says: “Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become unstable.” And elsewhere: “He who is in filth, let him be filthy still.” We have shown this contagion of disease sufficiently in the degrees of pride: just as one is always said to arise from another, so we perceive that through negligence a man becomes liable to slip from one sin into another.

Third, carnal monks, disordered toward penitence, contract through the sickness of sin and the habit of sin a harmful blindness of mind. Every vice, often committed, is treated lightly, and through habit is judged less serious. Just as grace illumines the mind, so the frequency of sin blinds reason. It is written: “Blind the heart of this people and make their ears heavy, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand, lest they be converted and I heal them,” says the Lord. For when the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises them. No sin is so great that it does not seem light and small through habit.

Fourth, disordered cloisterers, through the habit of evil...

Inde autem cam

The blinded do not come to the grace of true compunction. They approach confession superficially, from habit alone. They have not abandoned their depraved will. They do not truly take up a resolution of amendment. Such people, buried in the habit of sin, do not fear the censure of strict examination; they do not withdraw from blindness of mind through the remedy of contrition. As they now despise the long-suffering goodness of God, so in that terrible hour they undergo the sentence of eternal death. What can confession of the mouth avail where there is no true contrition of heart? Without contrition, confession is not saving; nor can contrition exist without a resolution of amendment. The sign of contrition is the will to sin no more.

Fifth, the disordered citizens of the lowest region, made despisers of almighty God through the habit of sinning, continually fall into graver dangers of soul, because they always approach the most holy sacred mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood in an evil manner. They make a superficial confession from habit; they allow the great beasts of vices to run through their senses. And thereafter, being in league with hell, they do not fear God; they despise the paths of amendment of life; they think themselves well ordered; they do not care with how many vices they are inwardly filled. Sometimes, sensibly moved by a fanciful devotion, they suppose that the Holy Spirit is now present; they affirm that they are beloved by God and holy. They impudently thrust themselves into the divine mysteries; not discerning the Lord’s body and blood, they receive them to judgment and condemnation.

Such people, communicating unworthily, are gravely hardened; they think themselves very secure and living well, and they do not duly care to cleanse their conscience from vices. Thus Judas the apostate did not fear boldly and shamelessly to complete the evil of betrayal which at first, as someone says, he feared to carry out against the Savior, after the morsel entered and the devil entered into him. O how many citizens of this lowest region there are: carnal monks, puffed up, proud, envious, murmurers, and entangled in various sins, whose conscience is rarely or never made clean by true contrition, and who nevertheless do not fear to approach the most holy altars almost every day.

Behold the evil company of all who dwell in this lowest region, whose end is destruction, for whom, after bodily death, a descent into hell is prepared. This is the far country of beastliness and unlikeness, into which that prodigal son went away, and squandered the portion of his inheritance luxuriously with harlots. In this region carnal citizens dwell, of whom the holy Apostle says: “The animal man does not perceive the things that are of God.” In this dark region, covered with the gloom of the dead, no spiritual good dwells; in it there is not peace, but beastly discord reigns, the prophet saying: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.”

Concerning Those Who, Being Near This Lowest Region, Often Fall Back [unclear] Through Inconstancy of Mind

Although between the first region, which is evil, and the second, which is good, there is properly no middle, nevertheless there are some who often move between the two: at one time, from weakness, they are lukewarm; at another, from contrition of mind, they seem to be devout. These are weak people. Though they are not submerged in the lowest region, nevertheless through negligence they are very near it, and frequently indeed they fall into that evil habit, because they do not withdraw, as far as they can, from the affections of the flesh. Of these Bernard says in a certain sermon: “Pernicious lukewarmness, how dangerous it is, how troublesome and full of misery and grief, and plainly nearest to hell! It is rightly judged the shadow of death. Indeed, one finds people faint-hearted and slack, failing beneath the burden, needing rod and spurs; their joy is slack, their sadness faint-hearted, their compunction brief and rare; their thought is animal, their conduct lukewarm, their obedience without devotion, their speech without circumspection, their prayer without intention of heart, their reading without edification. Finally, as we see, fear of Gehenna scarcely restrains them, shame scarcely holds them back, reason scarcely bridles them, discipline scarcely keeps them in check. But if such people remain long under the burden, either they are crushed and succumb, or in a certain way they are in hell, so that they never fully breathe again into the light of the Lord’s mercies, nor into the freedom of the Spirit, which alone makes the yoke sweet and the burden light.” From there, however, [text breaks off]

In inferno omnes sunt mali: et in regione infima nusquà reperiitur boni. Quicũg au tem ad infernũ corrũt: de regione infima fuerũt. Semp em cives suos infima regio mittit ad inferos: nisi peniten tia ducti viuentes operibus mortuis renunciare curaues rint. Secunda mansio purgatorium dicitur: et hec regio nilecunder rationali comparatur. Quemadmodum em purgatorii animas purgat et perficit: purgatasque ad re gnum celo: transmittit: ita secũda hec regio cives suos feuerantes in se p continuũ exercicũ a sordibus peccato abluit: et ad conscensum regionis tercie que spũs dicitur disponit. In hac mansione omnes sunt boni: sed tamem vt meliores fiant purgandi: et in regione secunda nusqu sunt mali: sed tamem vt meliores efficiantur semper exerci tandi. Hec regio cives suos morientes in se mittit ad pur gatorium: quantam et si omnes sunt boni: nonũ tamem ad regnũ sine purgatione temporanea videntur idonei. Anuero qui banc regionẽ mediam inhabitant: quãutũ supreme videantur esse proximi: non tamem a puluere in ferioris adhucpenitus sunt remoti. Tercia vero anima separata: mansio regnum celo: dicitur: et hec supreme regioni spũs comparatur. Sicut em in illa celesti patria requies summa et pa:habetur eterna: ita in regione spũs tranquillitas est mentis contiuua. Explicit regio prima.

Vicious lukewarmness flows from the fact that the will has not yet been purified; they do not will the good as they know it, being drawn away and enticed by evil desire. For they love earthly little consolations in their flesh, whether in word, or in signs, or in deeds, or in something else; and even if this sometimes interrupts these things, it does not entirely break them off. Hence it is that they rarely direct their affections toward God, and their compunction is not continuous, but only for an hour.

But a soul that lies under these distractions cannot be filled with divine visitations; and the more it is emptied of the former, the more fully it will be filled with the latter. If much, much; if little, little. Or perhaps, if you prefer it put more strongly: these things will never be able to be mixed with those for eternity. For spirit and flesh do not dwell together, nor fire and lukewarmness in one dwelling, especially since lukewarmness itself is accustomed to provoke vomiting in the Lord.

Therefore whoever desires to flee from the midst of Babylon, whoever longs to come to the region of the spirit, should always take care to repel from himself the sluggishness of mind, and in holy purpose to burn continually with the fire of divine love. Nothing harms those who wish to serve God so much as lukewarmness of mind. It always arises at first from some small negligence, but unless it is cured at once, it grows wonderfully by degrees.

One who is placed near the lowest region always slips down into it, because the dregs of his former carnal way of life still subtly occupy his will, and on an easy occasion disturb his weak fervor of devotion. But no one can rise from the depth of hell with a lukewarm will; no one can overcome habit without a contrary habit, because unless some violence intervenes, the habit of sinning will always strengthen vice.

Rightly, then, this lowest region is called hell, since by a certain likeness of disturbance and aversion it is compared to hell. Now after this life there are three dwelling places of souls, which receive their citizens departing from the three regions and from this world.

The first dwelling place is called hell, and this is compared to the lowest region. For just as in hell no order, but perpetual horror, dwells, so in this lowest region all things are disturbed by the fury of a mind blinded by carnal affections. In hell all are evil, and in the lowest region nowhere are the good found. All who fall into hell have belonged to the lowest region. The lowest region always sends its citizens to the lower world, unless, led by penitence, while still living they have taken care to renounce dead works.

The second dwelling place is called purgatory, and this is compared to the second, rational region. For just as purgatory cleanses and perfects souls, and sends them, once purified, to the kingdom of heaven, so this second region washes its citizens, persevering within it through continual exercise, from the stains of sins, and disposes them for ascent to the third region, which is called spirit. In this dwelling place all are good, but still they must be purified so that they may become better; and in the second region nowhere are there evil people, but still they must always be exercised so that they may become better. This region sends its citizens who die within it to purgatory, because, even though all are good, they do not yet seem fit for the kingdom without temporal purification. For those who inhabit this middle region, however near they may seem to be to the highest, are still not yet entirely removed from the dust of the lower one.

The third dwelling place of the separated soul is called the kingdom of heaven, and this is compared to the highest region of the spirit. For just as in that heavenly homeland there is supreme rest and eternal peace, so in the region of the spirit there is continual tranquility of mind.

Here ends the first region.

Dicit em in euangelio dũs. Regnum celorũ vim patitur: et violenti rapiunt illud. In ista regione belo lum certaminis dco fernituris indicitur: sic vir sapiens re- statur. Fili inquit accedens ad servitutem del ŋtã in timo re: et prepara animam tua ad tentationem. Quante ŋinc in hac media regionetentationee per exercitiũ spiritualis difficultatem quotidiie discimus: dum variũ modis imo pulsi manere dum in feruõris spũ non valemus. Jam nos a pficiendi studio infirmitas carnis revocat: nunc hostis antiqui tentatio verat:iam ŋprimũ conviuctus ŋspedit: nunc mundi fallacia seducit, Volentibus igitur in hac re glone laboris proficere, maxima fortitudine opus est: q̄ nemo tentationibus suis potest vsis in finem relistere: n̄ si vim sibi quotidiie studeat inferre. Quicunq autem ad hanc regione se puennisse existimat: de suis viribus n̄ plu mat: q̄m licet gratia dei vt bonũ in nobis operetur volũ catis nostre arbitriũ exigit: ita volũtas gratiã necessario requirit. Nemo em sanctus viribus suis. Nemo igitur de se audeat plumer: sed quistat videat necadat. Dilicia est vita bois sup terra: q̄m p multas tribulationes venī ad regnum: laboribusq̄z virtutũ arduis acquirit celum. Euntes inquit, pheta ibant et flebant mittentes semina sua: vententes aut venient cu exultatione portantes ma/ nipulos suos; Eniuer o qui seminat in lacbrymis: in gau dio metent; Si q̄s aut defecerit in semine: certe non gau debit in melle. Cu ergo p cotinuos exercitũ spualis labo res mens a puluere prime regionis purganda sit: nolũ in hac media regione octum querere: nolũ quietem negligen cie amare: quia nemo hic stare sufficit: nũ qui se ad labo/ rem continuum fortiter accingit, Qũsquis in hac region ne media non semper ad meliora psic: mor in negligenn tias priores vite cadit: ibis incidit deficiendi periculum! ubi amisit proficiendi a petitum. Hic locus est continui certaminis: in quo pugnare qui negligit: vincendus retro cedic; Explicit prefatio, Incipit secunda regio anim que rationalis dicitur: in qua sub multis laboribus hom mines versantur. Secunda igitur anim regio rationalis di/ citur: in qua mens pro inquisitione summe veritatis labore continuo exercetur: que quanto se ab infima longius segregat: tana to supre me magis appropinquat. Et hec regio certis modis celo ethereo assimilando proponitur: in quo situs astrorum et motus continuus habetur.

Preface to the second tract of the first part, concerning the middle region, namely the rational region of cloistered persons.

But now let us at last leave the dark region of the carnal, in which the whirlwind of wickedness abides and the continual storm of vices. We have granted enough to it, and have lingered over it longer than our purpose had set. Let us therefore leave the dead to bury their dead; let us yield to the darkness; let us seek the light of the spiritual life. We must go out from the Egypt of the dark region; we must hasten diligently, through the middle way of reason, to the highest summit of the spirit. Let us therefore now at last approach the middle region of the soul, through which one comes gradually to the highest. This region of the soul is quite fittingly called rational, for in it there is continual labor in seeking the highest truth. The fervor of the mind in this middle region always strives to raise itself to higher things; but the weakness of the flesh, through the motion of the storm that follows, runs together with it to draw it back to lower things. From this comes continual labor; from this arise sighs and groans, because the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks on many things. This is the narrow way that leads to life, and few walk by it. In this region force is applied against the desires of the flesh until the will is subjected to the spirit at its nod. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” In this region the war of contest is declared for those who are to serve God; so the wise man bears witness: “Son,” he says, “when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation.” How great the temptations are in this middle region we learn daily through the difficulty of spiritual exercise, while, driven in various ways, we cannot remain long in fervor of spirit. Now the weakness of the flesh calls us back from the pursuit of progress; now the temptation of the ancient enemy troubles us; now the company of our neighbor hinders us; now the deceitfulness of the world seduces us. Therefore those who wish to make progress in this region of labor need the greatest fortitude, because no one can withstand his temptations to the end unless he studies daily to do violence to himself. But whoever thinks that he has come to this region must not presume on his own strength; for although the grace of God, in order to work good in us, requires the free choice of our will, so too the will necessarily requires grace. For no one is holy by his own strength. Therefore let no one dare to presume on himself, but let him who stands see that he does not fall. The life of the good upon the earth is warfare, for through many tribulations they come to the kingdom, and by the arduous labors of the virtues heaven is acquired. “Going,” says the prophet, “they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.” For whoever sows in tears shall reap in joy. But if anyone has failed in sowing, certainly he will not rejoice in the harvest. Since, therefore, through the continual labors of spiritual exercises the mind must be cleansed from the dust of the first region, let us not seek leisure in this middle region; let us not love the rest of negligence, because no one here is able to stand unless he girds himself strongly for continual labor. Whoever in this middle region does not always press on to better things soon falls back through negligence into the former habits of life; there he incurs the danger of failing where he has lost the appetite for making progress. This is the place of continual conflict; whoever neglects to fight in it retreats in order to be conquered.

The preface ends.

The second region of the soul begins, which is called rational, in which human beings are occupied amid many labors.

The second region of the soul, then, is called rational; in it the mind is exercised with continual labor in the search for the highest truth, and the farther it separates itself from the lowest region, the nearer it approaches the highest. And this region is set forth as resembling in certain ways the ethereal heaven, in which there is the position of the stars and continual motion.

For just as motion itself is always disposed in heaven by the order of the first mover as cause, so continual labor is exercised in the middle region, so that each intellectual power may be perfected in its own object and in no way depart from the order naturally implanted in it. There are three powers of this sort: memory, intellect, and will.

Of these, memory gathers the likenesses of things and their images, and extends itself toward what is arduous. The intellect, by discerning these images themselves, considers them, and here investigates the true. The will embraces what has been approved and ordered by the intellect, and it is occupied with the known good. When these three powers of the soul rightly keep their order, they lead the spirit by faith toward heavenly things.

The second region of life is compared to the ethereal heaven: for as in that heaven there is continual motion and the fixed position of the stars, so in this middle region there is motion and continual labor against the contests of vices. And as the motion of the stars fulfills the office appointed to it by nature in due order, so also in this region the equity of uprightness is required, so that each power of the soul, while subjected to its own object, may be perfected toward the end appointed for it, so far as this can happen to wayfarers.

But no power itself can be brought simply to fullness in this region, since no one in this pilgrimage is so perfect that he cannot become more perfect in his own order. For even if memory, in its own object, which is the arduous, could behold the gathered likenesses and images of all creatures, it would not be satisfied unless it could apprehend their principle, which is God. But this is altogether impossible in this region, in which we can form no images or likenesses of God. The intellect also, the counselor, so to speak, of the blind will, is extended toward the true; but however much it considers its own object, it is not satisfied until it can apprehend all truth and arrive, without the opinion of imaginative speculation, at knowledge of the eternal, highest, and unfailing truth. But that perfection is possible to none of the wayfarers so long as he remains in the body of mortality. The will too, although it is directed to its own object, which is the good, will not be able to be satisfied and truly gladdened unless it comes to that unchangeable and highest good, which no instability of change overshadows.

The highest truth and unchangeable good is God, who says to Moses: “Man shall not see me and live.” And the disciple of the highest truth says: “No one has ever seen God.” And the prophet, addressing the Lord, says: “Truly you are a hidden God.” But although the aforesaid three powers of the soul cannot perfectly comprehend their objects in this life, none of them ought to cease from its office, lest it incur the danger of failing in the very place where the task of striving has been appointed.

Therefore the citizens of this middle region mortify evil affections in themselves, adorn themselves with continual virtues, direct all their works by right intention, and in no way withdraw from the office of reason.

The citizens of this region are scholastic, contemplative, and active men, [unclear], devoted to honorable arts: they subject the sensual or carnal powers to reason; they keep these three powers of the soul clean from all unlawful objects; they always raise their intention toward the end of honorable goodness; and they reform the will, in act or in habit, toward its due end. Therefore the cenobite who loves this cleansing and desires to ascend to the third region of the spirit ought to consider and keep the following principal articles in the middle region.

The summary of the truth of this middle region is expressed in seven principal articles. Whoever desires to make progress in this middle region according to the vow of his profession should diligently take care to observe the following articles. If he neglects to keep them, he shows that he has not yet become a citizen of the middle region. For, as we said above, no one can remain in this middle region without a continual effort to advance; here not to make progress is to fall away, and not to have ascended is to descend. Therefore the monk who, having overcome the dark region, has at last, with God’s help, been able to reach this middle one...

cauendum sibi moverit, ne conatum, pfaciendi vel ad mon dicum deserat: sed semp ad ulteriora se extendat: memi- neritq admonitionis viri sapientis qui dicit: "Ausite con stanter in timore dini teneas: cito subvertet domus tua- id est conscientia: Impossibile nacq est queplam in sancta conuersatione pfacere: qui conatum pfaciendi p timorem dini quotidie neglexerit innouare: Effectus aute innoua- tions buius tunc ordinatus ostenditur: cu veritas artis culoy regionis medie debite obseruatur: Primus ergo articulus est diligēs cenobitici finis intentio: secūdus est debita viri sensualium restrictio: tercius potentia y fide lis einündatio: quartus opey infimeregionis attentare reformatio: quintus ordinata veri cenobitici pfectus insti tutio: sextus ad ingressum tercleregionis potentia y ada aptatio: et septimus predicto y omnium exemplaris vel experimentalis certitudo; De cotinua et diligente finis cenobitice puersa Articulus primus. Deus inquit Ioannes charitas est: et qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet: et Deus in eo. Omnis autem qui in Deo manet, non peccat. Finis autem iste dispositivus ad ultimum quantu ad cenobitas ptinet secundus Ioannem Cassianum in collacontibus patru. est omnes curas mudi a se penitus abijcere: suas voluntates mortificare: omnemque dispositionem sui et cum prudenti committere: et nihil de crastino cogitare. Oportet enim cenobita in hac regione media plicere voluntatem penitus sui pliis abnegatione assumere: ac deinde se totaliter in manus sui prudentis resignare: quaten? apud semetipm intus sic muddus ab omni pre voluntatis pulsare: et foris ad serviendo dno liber ab omni seculari occupatione. Eniuero nisi ad hunc finem cenobita nostre puene rit nequaes verus est monachus: quonia adhuc in carne corruptibili corruptione seminat: et virtute sue professio nis minime observat. Decente prius voluntatis monastice abnegatio principaliiter in tribus videtur consistere: sine quibus nemo se veraciter dicendus est abnegasse. Et primo quidem voluntatis mortificatio requirit in monacho eradicatione prius iudicii: quonia quicquid suo iudicio vel consilio innitiatur: humiliter subesse alteri de dignatur. Decet enim cenobita aliis no potius imperio prius vivere: si ad vitâ eternâ pobe dientie meriti desiderat punire. he should beware lest he abandon the effort of advancing even a little, but always stretch toward further things; and he should remember the warning of the wise man, who says: “If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown,” that is, your conscience. For it is impossible for anyone to advance in holy conduct if he daily neglects to renew the effort of advancing through fear of the Lord. The ordered effect of this renewal is shown when the truth of the articles of the middle region is duly observed.

The first article, then, is the diligent intention of the cenobitic end; the second is the due restraint of the sensual powers; the third is the faithful cleansing of the powers; the fourth is the attentive reformation of the work of the lower region; the fifth is the ordered instruction in the progress of the true cenobite; the sixth is the adaptation of the powers for entry into the third region; and the seventh is the exemplary or experimental certainty of the aforesaid and of all things.

On the continual and diligent pursuit of the cenobitic end.

The first article.

Since the end is first in the intention of the wise man, and everything in its own kind is judged the more perfect the more closely it approaches its end, the monk who cultivates this middle region should always consider why he entered religion. If he finds his intention ordered, he should strive to continue it; but if he finds it corrupt, he should not fail to reform it according to the rectitude of the due end.

But note that in spiritual exercises the end is described as twofold, by which the virtue of monastic life is increased in merits. The first is charity, which is called the principal and ultimate end, to which all monastic exercises are ordered as to their first cause. Whatever good we do must always and principally be ordered to this end, because no work of virtue perfects merit unless charity always establishes the due foundation.

“God,” says John, “is charity; and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him.” And everyone who abides in God does not sin. The second end is dispositive toward the first and principal end, and is directed to it as a kind of intermediate fittingness; this is called secondary, or less principal. The monk must always attend to this too, and order his exercises through it to the ultimate end. For no one can lightly reach the end of principal charity if he neglects to observe the intermediate end.

This dispositive end toward the ultimate, so far as it pertains to cenobites, according to John Cassian in the Conferences of the Fathers, is to cast away from oneself entirely all the cares of the world, to mortify one’s own wills, to entrust every disposition of oneself to a prudent superior, and to take no thought for tomorrow. For in this middle region the cenobite must utterly reject his own will by taking up the denial of himself, and then resign himself totally into the hands of his prudent superior, so that within himself he may be clean from every impulse of his own will, and outwardly free from every secular occupation for serving the Lord. Indeed, unless the cenobite has come to this end, he is by no means a true monk, because he still sows corruption in corruptible flesh and in no way observes the virtue of his profession.

Next, the monastic denial of one’s own will seems principally to consist in three things, without which no one can truly be said to have denied himself. First, the mortification of the will requires in the monk the prior uprooting of his own judgment, because whoever relies on his own judgment or counsel disdains being humbly subject to another. For the root from which the defense of one’s own will first arises is called adherence to one’s own counsel or judgment. But whoever, while established in a monastery, desires to cling to his own judgment sins gravely in the Rule by usurping his own will. For it is fitting that the cenobite live by the command of others rather than by his own, if he desires to attain eternal life by the merit of obedience. Indeed, love of one’s own judgment is the greatest leprosy of the soul; according to Bernard, it is the more dangerous the more hidden it is, and the more [unclear].

Quemadmodu prudentis viator mansionem quo tendit delectabiliter procedendo considerat: sic bonus ce nobita in omnibus que facit semp cu feruente desiderio ad finem su qui deus est principaliter anhelat. Conatus aut bonus est nihil co que deus mandauit obmittere: pastori p dei amore in omnibus humiliter obedient: semp affectu a terrenis elongatu ad memoria superno erigere: et p continuu exercitiu spiri tualis couverstationis sanctu politu quotidie innuare. Quicquid boni facit cenobita denotus semp omnipoten ti deo fidel attenione offerat: omia terrena forti animo cõemnmat: soli deo placere cõocupiscat.
