Whatever visible thing is now seen will shortly decay. Take full consideration of things past, and see that what has passed away does not exist, and that what now seems to exist will, after a little while, no longer be.

Where are the kings of the nations, where the princes, where the leaders, where the rich, where those once powerful in the world? Where are all the lovers of the world, where the men who despised the steep path of heaven? Finally, where are all those once known to you in the world, whom death has meanwhile carried off while you have been in the cloister? Behold, from the beginning of the world, both those who lived for many years and those who lived for few have all died in their own generation; and according to the diversity of their merits, at the dictation of justice, they have also received different rewards.

The lovers of God, joined to the Creator of all, receive everlasting bright dwellings filled with inestimable joys; and the worshipers of the world, despising the commandments of God, once swollen here with honors, puffed up with knowledge, immersed in riches, given over to pleasures and vices, have gone down to hell to be tormented without end. What harm, I ask, does the once laborious contempt of the world, contrary to the flesh, now do to the saints in heaven, for which they now enjoy the glad vision of God forever? What profit now to the impious, buried in hell, is the consolation of the flesh once possessed, for which they now receive the torments of eternal damnation? Think on these things while it is profitable; meditate on these things while the opportunity for taking care is present.

Again, climbing higher, try with all your strength to fix the gaze of your mind in the abyss of infinite depth, and to consider how long that is which is eternal. Eternal is time that is enclosed by no end, bounded by no space. The saints of God will exult forever in blessed glory; sinners will burn forever in hell in misery. O eternity, name terrible without end: who will be able to think of you or speak of you without fear? Truly, he who thinks of you never sins eternally. Eternity has no end.

Hear a comparison, and though it will not be sufficient for eternity, receive fear from it. If a heap of sand were set up in the size of Mount Olympus, stretching to the sky, and from it after ten thousand years one little bird carried away only one grain, that mountain would by no means be said to last forever, but would be subject to an end; and although after innumerable years, nevertheless it would sometime cease to be. Yet all that time in which anything of the mountain remained, however very long it might be, would still seem as nothing in relation to eternity. For what is eternal receives no end even in imagination, nor does it admit hope of completion or limit.

Therefore the man is foolish, senseless, and mad who casts away this consideration of eternity, and uselessly spends the acceptable time granted him for deserving eternal goods. The hour will come, and is already hastening near, in which, no longer able to do better, he will learn what eternity is. But you, my monk, who desire to be faithful, cast from yourself every anxiety of the world; set all your care upon the love of God. Do nothing, say nothing, think nothing except what you know can lead you to the love of the Creator, or what pertains to the edification of others or to the pure necessity of the body.

Separate yourself, I pray, from low things, so that you may be able to delight in eternal goods. Let no anxiety of the flesh move you away from the inner tranquility of the mind; let no pleasure corrupt you. Strive to be always intent on prayers, as much as you can, with devotion, and again to lift yourself up more often through the affection of love.

On always having zeal for God.

The seventh root of the fear of God is called zeal, in which the monk is commanded to exercise himself no little. For no one who truly loves his lord tolerates calmly the injuries done to him. Therefore you, monk, who desire to be a faithful servant of Jesus Christ, do not neglect his zeal within yourself. Do not pretend not to see an injury to God when you see one, because whoever does not at once resist those who disparage his Lord is proved to love him too little. Let men know you as such a lover of God and enemy of vices that they do not dare to speak evil in your presence, nor to do any evil when they suspect you are watching.

te non presumant. Esto rectitudine animi conspicuus: vite merito clarus: zelo reverendus. Te recti velut dei famulû diligent: vultum tuum reprobi ut indicem pri/ mescant. Nemo in cõspectu tuo quicq̄ alienum a bonis moribus plumat agere: quippe cui te omnes nouerint dei iniuriam non posse tolerare. Sic phinees sacerdos tuum sempiternũ promeruit: quado iram dñi legem zeo lando fortiter placavit. Nuri te oppone fortiter p domo domini: exerce quantũ prenales zelum dei: destrue cõsilia malis gnantiũ: temeritati obsiste superborum. Te monachis et abbatis qui dei zelũ tã audacter abiciuit: qui familiaritates hominũ divino imperio an teponũt: qui vicia subdito:ũ stulta cõmiferatione diffi mulũt:qui traditioũs sancte regule nec in se nec in aliũ obseruũt. Fedus inter se ami cicte carnalis. sub noie charitatis duo vel plures cõtra bũt: infirimi suos morbos aie infirmioubus cõfidũt: et del amicicla p puritate mentis maxime requirit. Unus quisq meliorem ceteris suum socii existimat: alterus al teru no spiritualiter sed carnaliter deceptus amat: quip pe qui affectus suos in deu non elevant: nihil aliud q solacia carnis amat. Sed monachum quae videris ina firmo y fratri amiciclam querere: no dei seruũ sed amatorum carnis debes estimare. Qui enim cor suum in de amor et veraciter occupat: nihil de amicicia humana curat. Amor ieu sibi ad omnia sufficit: extra quem nihil amplius requirit. Qui antē in exterioribus mentis lolaciti questerit: qo deum extoto corde no diligat ope re ostendit. Amor dei solitudinem diligit: tumulcvs bos minu odit: amicoru colloquia non requirit. O bone ieu dulcis est amor tuus quoniam cor amantis te penetrat: te videns videre desiderat: te habens amplecti animus ecopetat. Anuero qui te amat suũpium obliniscitur: nihil aliud q dulcissima placentiam cui meditatur. Nihil est in mundo qo amanti te placeat: nihil vsquã reperitur qo pter te animas concupiscat. O quot suspirijs amore vul nerata mens angicit: qy vberrimis lachrymis in secreto facies irrigatur: quia quotiens dilecti faciem in cco psidentis cogitat: toties se in terris desolata plorat. In terea lepe tentat aliquid de suo ieu amantifimo mens languens amore dicere: in eius amorem conatur etiam alios prouocare: sed mox vt nomen ieu dulcissimu pfer re ceperit: pre amoris magnitudine nolens obmutescit. Amor eni ieu nullis verbis exprimif: sed in secreto men tis cu dulcedine sentitur. Scio qui dicebat. Amor meus crucifixus est. Quis est amor tuus o famule dei? Cur plo ras: Quare ingemiscis: Ignacius. Amor meus est cru cilicus: et ego no lugeã: Dns meus est mortuus: et ego cobibere lachrymas potero: Noli flere o fidelis anima: nam csi amor tuus mortuus est vt te a morte redimeret: sed iam resurrexit a mortuis vt te in ccelo coronaret. Esto fidelis vsq ad morte: et dabit tibi coronã vite.

Let them not presume against you. Be conspicuous for uprightness of soul, renowned for the merit of your life, worthy of reverence for your zeal. Let the upright love you as a servant of God; let the wicked dread your face as that of a judge. Let no one in your sight presume to do anything alien to good morals, since all should know that you cannot tolerate injury done to God.

Thus Phinehas the priest merited an everlasting covenant, when, by zealously defending the Lord’s law, he bravely appeased his anger. If you see order perishing in the monastery, if your brothers have begun in any way to corrupt regular observance, do not, if you are God’s servant, keep silence about their vices. Now set yourself bravely on behalf of the house of the Lord; exercise zeal for God as much as you can; destroy the counsels of the malicious; withstand the rashness of the proud. If you are a true lover of God, by your face alone you will scatter wicked gatherings. For no one will lay bare his plan before you if he suspects your zeal to be opposed to it. But if the wicked do not fear your presence when they are doing evil, they certainly recognize no zeal for God in you.

Therefore, to show yourself a true servant of Christ, you ought, for love of God, gladly to forgive injuries inflicted on yourself, and to pray to God for those who injure you. But injuries against the Lord, which it is not yours to forgive without his will, you should rather avenge out of zeal for righteousness. Let love of blood-kin cease in these matters; let the bond of friendship withdraw far away; zeal for God must rightly be preferred to all things. For friendship with a man must be maintained in such a way that it is never preferred to zeal for God.

Woe to monks and abbots who so boldly cast away the zeal of God, who place human familiarities before the divine command, who through foolish compassion conceal the vices of their subjects, who observe the traditions of the holy Rule neither in themselves nor in others. And what shall I say? We discern among cloistered monks that obedience to commands is despised, zeal for righteousness is scorned, observance of the Rule is contemned. Two or more contract among themselves a covenant of carnal friendship under the name of charity; the weak entrust the sicknesses of their souls to those weaker than themselves, though the friendship of God especially requires purity of mind.

Each one thinks his own companion better than the rest; one loves another, deceived not spiritually but carnally, because, since they do not raise their affections to God, they love nothing but the consolations of the flesh. But when you see a monk seeking friendship with a weak brother, you ought to judge him not a servant of God but a lover of the flesh. For he who truly occupies his heart in the love of God cares nothing for human friendship. The love of Jesus is enough for him in all things; outside it he seeks nothing further. But he who seeks the consolations of his mind in outward things shows by his deeds that he does not love God with his whole heart.

The love of God loves solitude, hates the tumult of men, and does not require the conversations of friends. O good Jesus, sweet is your love, because it pierces the heart of the one who loves you; seeing you, it desires to see you; having you, the soul longs to embrace you. Truly, he who loves you forgets himself; he meditates on nothing but the sweetest pleasure of you. There is nothing in the world that pleases one who loves you; nothing is found anywhere that the soul desires except for your sake.

O with how many sighs the mind wounded by love is distressed; with what abundant tears the face is drenched in secret, because as often as it thinks of the beloved’s face enthroned in heaven, so often it weeps that it is desolate on earth. Meanwhile the mind, languishing with love, often attempts to say something about its most beloved Jesus; it tries also to rouse others to his love. But as soon as it begins to utter the sweetest name of Jesus, unwillingly, from the greatness of love, it falls silent. For the love of Jesus is expressed by no words, but is felt with sweetness in the secret of the mind.

I know who said, “My love is crucified.” Who is your love, O servant of God? Why do you weep? Why do you groan? Ignatius: “My love is crucified, and shall I not mourn? My Lord is dead, and shall I be able to hold back my tears?” Do not weep, O faithful soul, for although your love died to redeem you from death, yet now he has risen from the dead to crown you in heaven. Be faithful unto death, and he will give you the crown of life.

Sed hāc sanctissimā occupationē me tis circa passionē dũi in secūda pre huius operis princi pali oportune tractabimus: vbi modũ spūalis exercitī latius exponemus. Quantũ vero ad rationē dictoru in hoc loco ptinet. tres modos amandi dei inuenio: quos breuiter secundũ ordinē explicabo. Deus em totũ cũ sit. cor totũ solus possidere amātis desiderat: a displis lecogi tacōnibus elongat. Ergo si amare vís dulciter: amia to caliter. Aut totũ em aut nihil dei pficit amor. Meditān tio passionis iesu christi saluatořis nostri te totũ possi deat: donec amor in te dulciter cōualescat. O porzet te totũ quod in carne blanditur cōtemnere: si ad amorem dei desideras quenire. Ao em potest aliquis dei in hac vita dulciter diligere: c̄diu aliq̄id in mundo cōuincio tur amare. Amor sīquidem mūdi penitus est divino cō trarius: quonā vbi alter ad penetralta cordis admictein tur: alter adesse prohibetur. Quantam vero dulcedinem quantam suauitātē quantāc mentis leticiā amor dei in corde amantis generet nemo proflus intelligit: nisi qui spretis omnibus rebus et eventibus mūdi deū solū muls to tempore amavit. Cor deū amātis nihil eoet que sunc in mūdo diligit: divicias honores et fauores seculi cona temnic: nulla subire aduersa p amore dñi sui primescit. Amor dei nunquā est ociolus: semp venire ad suī prin ciptum desiderat: nullos in hoc mūdo labores perpet recusat. Ergo qui non vult fieri desidiosus amet. Proxi mus quoet propter deū dulciter amiandus est: et nulla ratione contra deū vel iusticiā offendendus. Fratri suo vnusquisq verbis et factis talem se semp exhibeat: qua les ad se allos expectat. Veraciter enim proximũ suum diligit: qui pro eo res corpus et animam exponit. Hoc christus docuit.hoc pro nobis dei filius fecit. Eniuero qui dicit se in christum veraciter credere: debet sicut ille ambulauit et ipe ambulare. Christũ veraciter non vlla git: qui eius mandata non custodit. Ait enim. Hoc est pceptum meum ut diligaris inuicem: sicut dilepi vos. Membra sumus vnius capitis ielu christi: in quētunc credimus: cui eius pceptum de dilectione in deuni et ad proximũ obseruamus.Diligamus ergo proximũ nostrũ quia membrũ in christo nobiscũ est: vt quēadmodũ vnũ membrũ in corpore alteri compatititur: ita frater a fratre pro amore christi humiliter adiuvetur. Secundus modus tibi mādat vt sapicenter diligas: nihilq in divino amore aluud quā deū queras. Extende affectum tuum in illud verbum quod erat in principio apud deũ: mentem tuā eleua supra omne quod est crea cum: quoniam nisi teipm et omnia que sunt in mūdo des leras: venire ad eum non poteris quem amas. Denicũ si deum sapienter cupis diligere: noli te aliud estimare: quoniam vbi se aliquid esse homo existimat: iam insi pienter amat. Tercius modus precipit vt fortiter diligas: et expon nere corpus 7 animā pro dei amore nunquā primescas. Non est dei amato fortis: qui subire morte pro eo per timescit. Fortis cest enim ut mors dilectio. Proximus sa pienter diligitur: si non homo sed viciu oditur. Fortiter autem diligitur: si omnis iniuria ex animo benefacien o di eadem remittatur. Explicit regio secunda. [unclear]

On the mode and degrees of divine love: a collected conclusion of this second region.

Since no one suddenly becomes perfect, nor can anyone by his own strength suddenly ascend to that supreme summit of divine love, I now think it useful briefly to note certain modes or degrees of loving God. Therefore, for moving the human heart to divine love, the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is, in my judgment, more effective than all other things, if it is considered in a person’s mind purely, sweetly, fervently, perseveringly, and diligently. For truly, whoever often recalls to memory the life, Passion, and death of our Savior, with compassion and thanksgiving, according to their chief and principal articles, prepares a swift ascent of the heart to divine love. But we shall deal fittingly with this most holy occupation of the mind concerning the Lord’s Passion in the second principal part of this work, where we shall set out more fully the manner of spiritual exercise. As far as the meaning of what has been said in this place is concerned, I find three modes of loving God, which I shall briefly explain in order.

The first mode commands that you love sweetly him who loves you, and that you join your whole self to him sweetly, so that your heart loves nothing outside God and seeks nothing from elsewhere. For since God is the whole good, he alone desires to possess the whole heart of the one who loves him; he drives it far from displeasing thoughts. Therefore, if you wish to love sweetly, love totally. For either the whole of divine love perfects, or nothing does. Let meditation on the Passion of Jesus Christ our Savior possess you wholly, until love grows sweetly strong in you. You must despise everything that flatters in the flesh, if you desire to come to the love of God. For no one can sweetly love God in this life so long as he is convicted of loving anything in the world. Indeed, love of the world is utterly contrary to divine love, because where one is admitted to the inner chambers of the heart, the other is forbidden to be present.

But how much sweetness, how much delight, how much joy of mind the love of God produces in the heart of the lover, no one fully understands except one who, having despised all the things and events of the world, has loved God alone for a long time. The heart of one who loves God loves nothing that is in the world; it despises riches, honors, and the favor of the age; it does not fear to undergo any adversities for the love of its Lord. The love of God is never idle; it always desires to come to its own source; it refuses no labors to be endured in this world. Therefore let him who does not wish to become slothful love.

One’s neighbor also must be loved sweetly for God’s sake, and must in no way be offended against God or justice. Each person should always show himself to his brother, in words and deeds, such as he expects others to be toward himself. For he truly loves his neighbor who exposes his goods, his body, and his soul for him. This Christ taught; this the Son of God did for us. Indeed, whoever says that he truly believes in Christ ought himself to walk just as Christ walked. He does not truly love Christ who does not keep his commandments. For he says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you.” We are members of one head, Jesus Christ; and then we believe in him when we observe his commandment concerning love toward God and toward neighbor. Therefore let us love our neighbor, because he is a member in Christ together with us, so that just as one member in the body suffers with another, so a brother may humbly be helped by a brother for the love of Christ.

The second mode commands you to love wisely, and to seek nothing in divine love except God. Stretch out your affection toward that Word which was in the beginning with God; lift up your mind above everything that is created, because unless you leave behind yourself and all things that are in the world, you will not be able to come to him whom you love. Finally, if you desire to love God wisely, do not think yourself to be anything else; for where a person thinks himself to be something, he already loves foolishly.

The third mode commands that you love strongly, and that you never fear to expose body and soul for the love of God. He is not a strong lover of God who is afraid to undergo death for him. For love is strong as death. One’s neighbor is loved wisely if it is not the person but the vice that is hated. But he is loved strongly if every injury is forgiven from the heart, by doing good, on the same day.

The second region ends.

Preface to the third treatise of the first part, which describes the supreme region of the spirit of cloistered persons.

At last, with the Lord’s help, as I am about to write of that supreme region of the spirit, I am shaken by fear and shame together: for, small as I am, I fear to speak of the greatest things, and I greatly blush to teach what I have not sufficiently experienced. For what mind of any man, however much exercised, could recognize the state of a mind resting sweetly in God? Or what [unclear], even of the most eloquent orator, could explain the sweetness of inward contemplation? Indeed, the exercise of this third region surpasses human understanding for the greater part. In it the mind of a purified man, through the fervor of divine love, is carried above itself and, while its natural essence remains, is lulled and absorbed with wonderful sweetness in the abyss of divine contemplation. It is oppressed by so great a sweetness of inward majesty that it seems able neither to understand nor to express its own state. Once the operation of sense has plainly been left behind, it wholly surpasses even the intellect; and, as though leaving itself still further, without imagination, reasoning, or understanding, it is raised by affection above itself to that supreme summit of divine darkness.

But when it has utterly failed away from itself, it does not act but rests; nor, when returned to itself, can it understand what it has undergone, or reveal to anyone the manner of its elevation. For this elevation of the mind into God is so pure and so sublime that not only can one who has not experienced it not understand it, but even one who has experienced it cannot fully explain in words what it is like. But what shall I be able to say about the mountain of divine darkness, which I have not yet deserved to penetrate? For the well of inward contemplation is deep, and I am weak: I have brought neither a bucket fit for these waters, nor have I prepared steps suitable for climbing to the heights. Polished words do not befit a fool; nor ought an inexperienced and cold man to speak of the secrets of divine contemplation, when he still stands with the weak in the valleys. For only he speaks fruitfully of profound matters who is illumined by the ray of the twofold spirit.

Yet since I am a man placed under obedience to the annual chapter, I am compelled to accept the command of that synod and, according to my strength, to complete the work set before me. Therefore I enter the third region of cloistered persons under the guidance of the venerable father, lord Johannes of Bursfelde, a devout abbot, so that what he described in learned and truthful speech, I may seem to reduce, as far as I can, to my own manner of speaking, in obedience to the chapter.

Here begins the third region of the soul, which is called spiritual, in which the highest tranquility of the mind is found.

The third, or supreme, region of the soul is called spiritual; in it the highest rest and tranquility of the mind abide. And this region is compared to the empyrean heaven, in which there is the true rest of all and the true happiness of souls. The spirit dwelling in this region leaves behind what is beneath reason and, raised by love into God, ascends wondrously. For whatever it does in this most holy region is judged wholly divine. Here the human spirit, rapt above itself, receives the divine inpouring and, lulled in the darkness of divine contemplation, withdrawn from all creatures, sweetly rests. In this region almighty God directs the spirit of the one contemplating him; he perfects the simplified intellectual powers of the soul, recalled from every phantasm into the inner chamber, according to the objects of their own tendencies; and he leads the mind, stripped of every multiplicity, to himself, the one principle, making it one with himself, not by nature, but by gracious participation. The inhabitants of this supreme region are truly spiritual men, who, having despised all the things and affections of the world, love nothing in this world except God, desire nothing inordinately, but through inward affection absorbed by [unclear].

divino spiritu, deum ipsum vehementer sitiit: in eius amo rem inestabilis desiderio inardescit. Tanto enim amoris feruore aguntur in deo, ut sup semetipos eleuat. omnes plerus operacones intellectuales deserant: et in divino cotemplationis abyssum rapti nihil pentus pter deum admittat: ibi existentes insensibiliter p gratia amoris: vnus cui deo fiant salua naturarũ prietate, munere part cipaconis. Dicit eni sanctus lefu christi apostolus. Qui adheret domino: vnus spiritus est. Et icerũ dicit. Qui spiritu dei aguntur: hi filii dei sunt. Huius quocq san ctissime regionis civem se idem apostolus indicat: qui philippensibus clamat: Nostra aute conversatio in celis est. Quadiu enim sumus in corpore peregrinamur a do mino: sed quasi per somniũ ad patriam nostrã suauiter ducimur: quado mente et spiritu in celestibus conversam mur. Per somniũ dixerim no propriae: sed remota cõpan racõne. In somniũ nãq imaginibus rerũ nobis intell gibũũ. reservatis speciebus in phantasía egressimur: in cotemplatione pter omnẽ imaginationẽ purũ ad deum mẽre et spiritu eleuamur. Et idco bec suprema regio ant me spiritualis dicitur: a qua omnes religiosi nomen spi ritualitatis sortiuntur. Ue nobis. Spirituales ab hac regione fellcissima dicimur: religiosi dei amatores nũcu pamur: qui camen montis huius verticem p cotempla cõnis altitudinem nũ ascendimus: sed cui infirmis semp infirmi in lectulo desideriorum carnalium lacemus. Ad quid nomen sanctum gerimus: qui sancti non sumus Euremus ergo totis viribus per continuum medie rea gionis exercicium ad hanc supemi verticis celitudine ascendere: si nomen spiritualis conversationis veraciter cupimus obtinere. In hac regione charitas tenet im perium: sapientia consolatum: in qua nihil preter deũ diligitur: nihil inordinatẽ perpetratur. Hec autem sanctissima regio ad celum empyreum pertinet: quo niam quos in ciues spiritualiter suscipit: ad celi gaudia 2 ii sine medio trāsnicet. Hā sicuit infima regio carnis clivis suos morientes mittit ad infernum: et media racōnis ad purgatorium: sic ista pfectos cultores suos decedentestrasa mittit ad celum. Huic autē tercē ac supreme regionis dignitas multis progratiuis exprimit: et in septē articulis maxime cōmendatur: sicut p ordinē dicetur. Quod hec suprema regio spiri ricus claustraliũ sic grata cōparatione. H primo quidem hec tercia regio anime grata cōparatione dicitur: q̄m supremo celo empyreo cōparatur. Nam sicut in celo empyreo trāquilla sunt omnia: sic in isto supreme regionis vertice mens ho minis ctemplantis deũ. nullis est turbacōnibus agitata. Hic quies sumnia ctemplantis est anime: hic nulla vi ciox turba inhabitat: amaritudo mentis nulla proṣus a propinquat. In celo fiquidem empyreo maiestas dei a sanctis spiritibus ineffabili munere cernitur: hic in cali gine p desideriũ amoris supra intelligentiā videtur. Ibi deus est omnia in omnibus: hic pter deũ nihil placet ex omnibus. Ibi sanctis cōceditur a labouribus sinefine quiũ escere: hic mens interne dulcedinis indicibile fuauitate pmittitur quiescendo pgustare. Hō est maior ōs in celo fen licitas: et nō est in miúdo tāsuavis ōs in ista regione tran quillitas. Beati nimirũ qui hũc monte divine ctempla cōnis meruerũ ascendere: q nihil penitus in hoc miúdo diligũt: nil alind ōs semp deo adherere cōcupiscũt. O ō secura est isto ō civiũ conscientia: ōs cōversatio leta: vbi nihil mali cōmittitur:nihil alind ōs summũ illud incōmu tabile bonũ desideratur. Dens em purificata p divinũ amorẽ que hanc regionẽ veraciter et pleuerāter ascende rit: nihil carnale nihil inordinatũ concupiscũt: se totā in cōtemiplationẽ summe maiestatis per desideriũ ergiũ: in solo deo dulciter quiescit. by the divine Spirit, thirsts intensely for God himself; he burns with an unceasing desire for love of him. For they are driven in God by so great a fervor of love that he raises them above themselves; they generally leave behind all intellectual operations, and, carried into the abyss of divine contemplation, admit nothing at all except God. There, existing insensibly through the grace of love, they become one with God, while the property of their natures remains intact, by the gift of participation. For the holy apostle of Jesus Christ says: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit.” And again he says: “Those who are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God.” The same apostle also shows himself to be a citizen of this most holy region when he cries out to the Philippians: “Our conversation is in heaven.”

For as long as we are in the body we are exiled from the Lord; but as though through sleep we are sweetly led to our homeland when in mind and spirit we have our conversation in heavenly things. I say “through sleep” not properly, but by a remote comparison. For in sleep we go forth among images of things intelligible to us, the forms being preserved in the imagination; but in contemplation, beyond every imagination, we are raised by pure mind and spirit to God. And therefore this supreme region of the soul is called spiritual, from which all religious receive the name of spirituality.

Woe to us. We are called spiritual from this most blessed region; we are named religious, lovers of God; and yet we never climb the summit of this mountain by the height of contemplation, but, weak with the weak, always lie sick upon the bed of carnal desires. Why do we bear a holy name, who are not holy? Let us strive, then, with all our strength, through the continual exercise of the middle region, to ascend to the height of this supreme summit, if we truly desire to obtain the name of a spiritual way of life. In this region charity holds command, wisdom the consulship; in it nothing is loved except God, nothing disorderly is committed.

This most holy region belongs to the empyrean heaven, because those whom it spiritually receives as citizens it sends straight to the joys of heaven. For just as the lowest region of the flesh sends its dying clients to hell, and the middle region of reason sends its own to purgatory, so this region sends its perfect worshipers, when they depart, to heaven. The dignity of this third and supreme region is expressed by many prerogatives and is especially commended in seven articles, as will be said in order.

That this supreme region of the spirit of the cloistered is shown by a pleasing comparison.

First, then, this third region of the soul is described by a pleasing comparison, because it is compared to the highest, empyrean heaven. For just as all things are tranquil in the empyrean heaven, so on this summit of the supreme region the mind of the person contemplating God is disturbed by no agitations. Here is the highest rest of the contemplating soul; here no crowd of vices dwells; no bitterness of mind approaches at all. In the empyrean heaven, indeed, the majesty of God is seen by the holy spirits with an ineffable gift; here, in darkness, through the desire of love, he is seen above understanding. There God is all things in all; here nothing among all things is pleasing except God. There it is granted to the saints to rest endlessly from their labors; here the mind is permitted, in resting, to taste beforehand the unspeakable sweetness of inward delight.

There is no greater happiness in heaven, and there is not in the world so sweet a tranquility as in this region. Blessed indeed are those who have merited to ascend this mountain of divine contemplation, who love nothing at all in this world and always desire nothing other than to cleave to God. How secure is the conscience of these citizens, how joyful their conversation, where no evil is committed and nothing is desired except that supreme, unchangeable good. For the mind purified by divine love, which has truly and perseveringly ascended this region, desires nothing carnal, nothing disorderly, but, wholly raised by desire into contemplation of the highest majesty, rests sweetly in God alone. O who can [unclear] the inward sweetness

In hac suprema regione diuine cōtemplantionis spiritus rationalis vircs et potentiās suas in suā cōclauē reuocat: in quo etīpe liber ab omni phantasmāte vacat: se supra se in diuine caliginis densum erigit: in quo soporatus p amōre extaticũ suaviter requiescit. Nulla versatur hic cogitationũ importuna cōfusio: nulla phantasmārum imaginatio: sed nuda mens sursum erigitur: sine cogitatione vel imaginacōne qualibet cōtemplatur. Eninero quādo mens ipa cōgitacōibus aditū referat: rursus ad media regionē que rationis est descendere se manifestat. Sed cū mens hominis nō valeat semp in vertice cōtem plationis diuine immota pāstere: necessārũ est ea sepius ad secunde regionis rationale exercitiũ redire. Si vero in passiones sensuāles prolapṣa fuerit: iam rursus ad regionē infimā descendit. O ḍ bonũ est adherere dno: ḍ dulce est so li intendere deo: vt mens dũm ielum pre omibus sitiat: et eũ cōplecti semp ignitis desideriũs cōcupiscat. could truly express the lover of God: where the mind recalls the powers and capacities of the soul from the dispersion of multiplicity into one, and, fired by burning affections, lifts them into the chamber of the spirit; and directs its gaze by love toward that supreme, unchangeable Good, utterly rejecting from itself every created and creatable multitude; the spirit gathers itself into one, so that, united within itself, it may seek to rise without the impediment of multiplicity to its own principle, by which it is one. To the one principle of all things, clearly, unity alone can attain, because unity flees multiplicity and seeks the one. For the more you yield to multiplicity, the more you withdraw from unity. Therefore the mind, in this supreme region of the spirit in which man dwells, when it seeks to ascend by contemplation to its principle through love, is accustomed to cast away from itself every multiplicity clinging to imagination or understanding, so that, gathered in its own unity, it may be able to direct itself ardently toward that one with the simple affection of love, whom it knows to be above every position.

That this supreme region of the spirit is sweet and lovable by reason of its nearness.

Article two.

Secondly, this supreme region of the spirit is sweet and most pleasant by likeness and singular nearness. For the citizen of this most holy region is separated from the citizens above by only one clay wall, so to speak, since as long as the spirit inhabits the flesh, it cries out to heaven as though through a wall. But the clay wall of flesh is the prison from which the spirit, when set free and about to migrate to heaven, goes forth when it is separated from the body by death. But the spirit wounded by sins, which cannot lift itself to this region through the pure affection of love, is still said to stand farther away from the empyrean heaven. Those, however, who dwell in this most quiet region are nearest to the empyrean heaven, because, weighed down by no stains of sins, they despise all earthly and carnal things, and always long to live in mind and spirit among heavenly things.

Indeed, those who inhabit the empyrean heaven and those who dwell in the third region have one and the same delight. But this is the difference: these contemplate God in a mirror and enigma, while those contemplate him in clear vision. The sweetness of those contemplating is on both sides; here it is great, there it is greatest; here it is in the fierce desire of love, there in possession of the most blessed vision.

In this supreme region of divine contemplation the rational spirit recalls its powers and capacities into its own chamber; and there, free from every phantasm, it is empty of them, raises itself above itself into the dense darkness of the divine, and, lulled to sleep by ecstatic love, rests sweetly. Here no troublesome confusion of thoughts moves about, no imagining of phantasms, but the bare mind is lifted upward and contemplates without any thought or any imagination. For whenever the mind itself opens access to thoughts, it shows that it is descending again to the middle region, which belongs to reason. But since the mind of man cannot always remain unmoved on the summit of divine contemplation, it must often return to the rational exercise of the second region. If, however, it has slipped down into sensual passions, then it has again descended to the lowest region. But the spirit of the true lover of God, although because of the frailty of the flesh it cannot always remain in the pleasantness of contemplation, nevertheless strives more often, through the affections of fire, to lift itself to that region, so that it may fulfill the exercise of reason in such a way that it does not entirely lose the sweetness of inward delight. O how good it is to cling to the Lord; how sweet it is to attend to God alone, so that the mind may thirst for him above all things and always long to embrace him with burning desires. Indeed, the one who stands in this region is nearest to the empyrean heaven, and therefore is inflamed toward it with the greatest desires of love. O how many groans and tears the mind fervent with love is accustomed to send forth; how ardently it sighs for heavenly things, since the nearer it is to the empyrean heaven through the secret of contemplation while standing in this supreme region, the more ardent its desire to go forth from the prison of the body is known to be. Thus

Sed considerandum nobis est, quae mystica theologia p exercicium affectus purificati acquirit: p amoris incendium doceit. Enivero nisi affectus ab omni coecupiscencia inordinata purgatus fuerit: ad sublimi tatem huius sacratissime sapientie non ascendit. Si autem passiones sensuales abiecerit: si voluntas hominis divina voluntati conformata fuerit: mens per ignitum amoré sursum erigitur: et in diviine caliginis immensitātā tem anagogicis motibus elevat. Sed mens in secretũ huius mystice sapien tie nō admittitur: nisi post omninodũ purgationẽ affe ctus ab omi creatura excurat: atzseipam sibimet vniat: et ab omni racõne vel imaginacõne rerũ cogitabiliũ lona gins recedat. Ausi em ab omi creatura recesserit: ad crea torem qui est sup omnia nō accedit. In hac igitur schola diviina eruditione spũ sanctus psidere discentibus creu ditur: qui docet hominẽ nihil in hoc mudo diligere: et dei se voluntati in omnibus cõformare. Felix qui huiũ ma gistrũ discipulus esse meruit: felix qui hanc scholũ pamo ris desideriũ intrauit: quonũ in mystico silencio miran da pcipit: que deus nō amāribus abscondit. Quod hec suprema regio spir ritus fundata sic simplicitate. Quarto hec sanctissima regio spiritus fundata simplicitate dicitur: in qua mens nō p̄ essentiā

The third article: this supreme region of the soul is called divine instruction.

This supreme region of the soul is called divine instruction, in which the mind, burning with divine love, is taught not by man but by the Holy Spirit. For Christ said to his lovers in the holy Gospel: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” And again, that word of the prophet: “And they shall all be taught by God.” The Holy Spirit of eternity dwells in the heart of the one who loves [unclear], and illumines it by his invisible teaching.

In this region the spirit chooses true wisdom, the best part of Mary, in silent tranquillity; mystical theology is taught in secret, in the ineffable sweetness of the divine darkness; the mind, disposed toward its beloved by the fervor of most holy love, speaks in secret with him and continually raises itself to him through desire. This wisdom, or mystical theology, can indeed be commended by man, but it cannot be taught except in divine instruction. For it is the work of the Holy Spirit when the mind is illumined in true contemplation.

But we must consider that mystical theology is acquired through the exercise of a purified affection and is taught through the fire of love. Speculative theology, which we call scholastic, is learned through the exercise of the intellect, while the mind devotes itself continually to study. For the acquisition of mystical theology, the purification of the affection from every entanglement is required, so that the will, depraved through aversion, may be reformed toward its beginning through the quest of inward love. For unless the affection has been purified from every disordered concupiscence, it does not ascend to the height of this most sacred wisdom. But if it has cast off sensual passions, if the human will has been conformed to the divine will, the mind is raised upward through fiery love and is lifted by anagogical movements into the immensity of the divine darkness.

No one understands the certainty of this theology unless he receives it; no one receives it unless he seeks it alone above all things through the sighs of love. The psalmist sought this when he prayed to the Lord: “O that my ways may be directed to keep your statutes at all times.” For by such movements of desire the holy man was borne upward to obedience to the divine will, so that in that same Psalm 118 he said almost no verse in which he did not place some word equivalent to the divine judgments. The exercise of this purification is begun in the second region and is completed in this one. For no small labor is undertaken, that the affection may be purified from the concupiscences of the world. But once the exercise of spiritual reformation has been taken up, the mind gradually advances in love, desires to ascend to this region by sure steps, hastens through desire to the invisible school of this theology, and, sighing with continual groans, knocks at the door of divine compassion.

But the mind is not admitted into the secret of this mystical wisdom unless, after complete purification of the affection, it is freed from every creature and unites itself to itself, and withdraws far from every reason or imagination of thinkable things. For unless it withdraws from every creature, it does not approach the Creator, who is above all things. Therefore in this school of divine instruction the Holy Spirit is believed to preside over those who learn: he teaches a person to love nothing in this world and to conform himself in all things to the will of God. Happy is he who has deserved to be the disciple of this master; happy is he who has entered this school through the desire of love, for in mystical silence he receives wonderful things that God has hidden from those who do not love him.

That this supreme region of the spirit is founded in simplicity.

Fourth, this most holy region of the spirit is called founded in simplicity, in which the mind, not through essence [unclear].

Virtute enim ipiūs vnius solū fit vnio: qūī nō alia racōne facilius vnī ri similiora inuicē dicimus: qūī vnū esse in qualitate vi demus. Animus ergo cu summō rerū principio vno tūc demū posse vniri creditur: cu exutus omnē multitudinē. sibi q metiī vnitus, amore fervētissimo in deū eleuacur. Sicut inter diversa qualitate nō fit vnio: sic inter deū r animū insemerīpo divisū non potest esse adheio. Unius em ad vnu similitudine qualitatis fit vnio: et mētis sim/ plificare et exute ab omībus p amatorū affectū erit cum deo adhesio. Simplicitate iraqz fundata est suprema re gio spiritus: in qua mens purificati hominis in deū fer/ uentissimo amoris desiderio erigīt: et suī principiū inco mutabili p grānā vnīcur. Intellectus et affectus duo sūr oculi animi: quiprimus quidem intellectus ad cognoscendum dei erigitur: sed venire ad montem divini caliginis non sufficit: quoniam oneratus phantasmatibus rerum sensibilium incedit. Affectus igitur animae simplicior oculus montem caliginosum sine imaginibus quibuscunque ingreditur: deum et amoris contemplatur: ab omnibus creaturis segregatus nihil sensibile cogitat: quiescens in mystico silencio nudus vacat. Iste est oculus simplex qui totum corpus lucidum efficit: igitur de quo sponsus in canticis gloriatur. Vulnerasti cor meum soror sponsa: vulnerasti cor meum: in uno oculo tuo. Affectus enim feruum rem amoris ad divinam contemplationis secretum sine ductu intellectus solus ingreditur: et ergo in uno et in ambo bus oculis sponsus vulneratur. Quisquis autem exercitii devotionis et puritatis ad haec unionis et simplificaconis regionem Christo largiente puenire meruit: discat omni tpe in profunda humilitate prudenter colistere: neque superbia amittat donum quod se gaudet obtinere. Dicit enim profundus et cautissimus divinorum contemplator bernardus. Oportet profundare humilitate et de se humiliter sentire nitentem ad altiora: ne dum supra se vane extollitur: cadat ab alto quo ascendisse videbatur. Consistens igitur in hac regione ad gradus humilitatis in secunda descriptos, prudenter aliquando redeat: manere in profunda resignatione sui ipsius humiliter discat: quia morut abnegatione sui animus colerit: de altissimo monte in immane papicu ruat. Multi enim iubilo sensualis devotionis sue colidentes decepti sunt: qui in monte hunc altissimum sine fundamento humilitatis ascenderunt. Alii capitibus lesis sensibus destructis stulti facti sunt: quoniam nodum moraticatis passionibus suis caliginem mystici silencii ingredi plumperunt. Alii in superbia elati dum adhuc sensuali tati fuerunt dediti: et voluntatis proprii vicium descende runt in profundum inferni! Dicit enim de ascensu huius

but through the love of adhesion it is united to its immutable one principle. For, as we have said above, that highest good, God, is one; and our soul cannot draw near to it unless, stripped of all multiplicity, which it receives by attraction, imagination, and understanding, it strives to present itself wholly one to itself. For the soul naturally desires to reach the highest good; but the more it is divided in its operation through multiplicity, the less fit it is found to come to it. For multiplicity is opposed to unity, and the more the mind turns itself toward many things, the more it withdraws from unity. One, two, three, four are ten. You withdraw from the one when you are multiplied in number. Return to the one if you desire to have the beginning. For the one is the beginning of all things; if you add anything to it in your mind, you at once withdraw from it. When you say “one,” you say “beginning.” If you say “two,” you have already abandoned the beginning. Therefore, so that you may always be able to contemplate your beginning, take care at every time, stripped of all multiplicity, to make yourself one.

For since all good things are from the first good, and every love, toward whatever good it is borne, is naturally kindled by that same good, our love cannot be touched by any goods or rest in any final end unless, naked and pure, it strives at last to return to its own beginning. For union comes about only by the power of the one itself; and for no other reason do we more readily say that things more alike are united with one another than because we see that they are one in quality. Therefore the soul is believed to be able to be united with the one highest principle of things only when, stripped of all multiplicity and united even to itself, it is lifted up to God by most fervent love. Just as there is no union between things different in quality, so between God and a soul divided in itself there can be no adhesion. For the union of one thing with one thing comes about by likeness of quality; and the adhesion of a mind simplified and stripped of all things through the affection of love will be with God.

Therefore the supreme region of the spirit is founded on simplicity; in it the mind of the purified person is raised up to God by a most fervent desire of love and is united by grace to its immutable beginning. Intellect and affection are the two eyes of the soul. The first of these, the intellect, is indeed raised up to know God, but it is not sufficient to come to the mountain of divine darkness, because it proceeds burdened with images of sensible things. Therefore affection, the simpler eye of the soul, enters the dark mountain without any images whatever; separated from all creatures, it contemplates God in love, thinks nothing sensible, and, resting naked in mystical silence, is free. This is the simple eye that makes the whole body full of light, the eye of which the bridegroom boasts in the Canticle: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart in one of your eyes.” For the fervor of loving affection enters alone, without the guidance of the intellect, into the secret of divine contemplation; and therefore the bridegroom is wounded in one eye.

But whoever, by the exercise of devotion and purity, has deserved through Christ’s gift to arrive at this region of union and simplification should learn at every time to stand prudently in deep humility, and not through pride lose the gift he rejoices to possess. For Bernard, that profound and most cautious contemplator of divine things, says: “One who strives for higher things must be deepened in humility and think humbly of himself, lest, while he is vainly lifted up above himself, he fall from the height to which he seemed to have ascended.” Therefore, standing in this region, let him prudently return sometimes to the degrees of humility described in the second part; let him humbly learn to remain in profound resignation of himself, lest, if the soul [unclear] by denial of self, it fall from the highest mountain into a dreadful precipice.

For many, trusting in the jubilation of their sensual devotion, have been deceived, who climbed this highest mountain without the foundation of humility. Others, their heads injured and their senses destroyed, have become foolish, because, without having mortified their passions, they presumed to enter the darkness of mystical silence. Others, lifted up in pride while they were still devoted to sensuality, and through the vice of their own will, descended into the depth of hell. For he says concerning the ascent of this…

Articulus V. et peregrinos quasi ad paternam habitationem sedulo vocat. Quid esto anima. & in terra inimico et es et Inueterasti in terra aliena: coin et quinata es cu mortuis: deputata es cum descend et tribus et in infernu. Demento quoni et om et potens et Deus exnihilo et te condidit: cogita q et te ad imaginem et similitudinem et sua formauit: memor esto unde excideris: vide vbi pro et fecta inter porcos imm et dar et affection et pedibus et co et cul et caris. Te condit et tuus in suprema hanc region et spirit et tus ab in et cio posuit: tibi amor et sui naturale exercic et commisit: vite quo et semp et mansure spem contulit. Tu et aut et dereliquisti fontem sapientie: egressa es in inf et am et regionem dissimilitudinis: dissipasti bona promissa her et reditatis. Sed reuertere vel sero tandem ad exercicium et penit et di regionis medie: donec purgata ab om et in et qu et atibus tuis re et dic et mercaris ad amenic et at et regioni&

The Scripture says concerning the summit: “The beast that touches the mountain shall be overwhelmed with stones.” A beast is said to touch the mountain when a man, not yet purified by the exercise of the second region, tries to ascend to the third. For as long as his affection has not been cleansed from the passions of his sensuality, the beast still lives in him. But if the mind of man permits itself, with its beastliness, to approach the mountain of God, it will be overwhelmed by as many stones as there are movements of the passions by which it is wounded.

For the wise man says: “The sluggard is stoned with a muddy stone, and all will speak in contempt of him.” By the muddy stone carnal affection is meant, because man is compared to mud. For it is written in Job: “Remember, I pray, that you made me like clay, and you will bring me back to dust.” And again he says: “I am compared to mud, and I am likened to ashes and dust.” Thus the sluggard is overwhelmed with a muddy stone when the mind, still unclean with carnal and sensual passions, attempts to ascend to the mountain of contemplation; there, as unworthy, it is forced to suffer repulse and ruin by the hard stones set against it. For no one will be able to reach this most tranquil region of the spirit who has not first cleansed himself by long exercise in the furnace of the middle region. Whoever, still given over to carnal passions, tries to approach this highest region of the spirit is striving, as it were, to draw water in a sieve. For this region does not admit carnal minds into itself, since it is prepared for hearts purified from every affection.

That this supreme region of the spirit is magnificent in restoration.

Article V.

It diligently calls strangers and pilgrims as if to their father’s dwelling. In this region, returning like the prodigal son, he receives us mercifully; he rushes with love into our embrace; he clothes us with the first robe; he grants the garment of charity to those who love. Why, then, do we neglect to return as quickly as possible to the most indulgent Father, whom we see ready for our embrace even after our contempt? We wretched ones have withdrawn by our own will and by our deserts; we squander the portion of our inheritance with the prostitutes of carnal affection; we have been shamefully stripped of all beauty and paternal adornment. Why do we not return to the Father, whom we know to be ineffably merciful? Let us return at least, I beg, after our fault, since we have scorned to avoid ruin.

Return, return, wretched soul; return, you who are grievously captive in your affections; return, you who are mortified in sorrows. Why do you delay? Why do you tarry? Return, faithful soul, to the leader of your youth; return to your former husband; go back to your most loving Father, who awaits you with love and desire. For behold, with patience he awaits you, and through Isaiah the prophet he cries to you: “Return to me, for I have redeemed you. I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist.”

Why, soul, are you in the land of the enemy? You have grown old in a foreign land; you are defiled with the dead; you are counted among those who descend into hell. Remember that almighty God created you from nothing; consider that he formed you to his image and likeness; remember from where you have fallen; see where you have gone, among swine, and are trampled under the feet of filthy affections. Your Creator placed you from the beginning in this supreme region of the spirit; he entrusted to you the natural exercise of love for him; he bestowed on you the hope of life that will endure forever. But you have abandoned the fountain of wisdom; you have gone out into the lowest region of unlikeness; you have squandered the promised goods of your inheritance. But return, even late at last, to the exercise and repentance of the middle region, until, purified from all your iniquities, you deserve to be brought back to the pleasantness of the region [unclear].

Ibi te pater indulgentissimus letereuerententem fusciptet: stolā tibi innocentie primā recuperatā induet: dabitq̄ tibi annulū sanctissime cōfederationis in manis bus: calciamenta veremorificāonis malarī affectiōnū in pedibus: quatenus his ornamentiis decorata tānq̄ sponsa fidelis uigiter illi adhercas: et ab eius amore dea incept nullatenuis recedas. Denicg in escā saginatu tibi occidet vitulū: dapifer cric ipe simul et cōuiuui: preamo ris magnitudine carnē sua dabit in edulum: et propriū sanguinē in potū. Ibi spiritus dñi sanctus aderit: suis te donis mysticis implebit. Tunc exultans in dño cana tabis. Fructus iesu dulcis est gurturi meo:quia spiritus cius super mel dulcis. Est icaq̄ bec suprema regio spiritus reductione ma gnifica: q̄m ciues suos quos in suāhabitationē fuscipt: ad amenitātē celestis patrie reduct. Ciues autē huius sancissime regionis ex fructibus spūs infallibiliter co gnoscimus: de quibus diisse sanctū apostolū scimus. Fructus autē spiritus est charitas, gaudiū, pac, patiēna cia, benignitas, bonitas, longanimitas, māluctudo, fides modestia, cōtinentia, castitas. Hos fructus ciues huius tercie regionis proferūt: quoniā deo pleni et vniī, semp leti in dño et charitate feruentissimi incedūt. Quicq̄d eni lusto viro in hoc monte amoris habitanti acciderit: nō eum cōtristabit. Semp namq̄ pacatus et tranquillus in dei amore animus: nullis prosperitatibus erigitur: nullis adueritatibus pturbatur. Quod hec suprema regio spi ritus sit thesaurizacōne iocunda atq̄ verissima. Articulus vi. Ecco hec pulcherrima regio spiritus thesauri zatione iocunda dicitur atq̄ verissima: quoniā quicquid p̄ exerciciū boni operis acquiritur: in simplicitate spūs possidet. Animi thesaurus dei amor cuius fervore dum mens purificata incenditur: ad hanc regione quasi ad apothecā amoris ipria elevatur. Dicit em in sacro euangelio dn̄s. Ubi thesaurus tuus est: ibi et cor tuũ erit. Hic est thesaurus in agro scriptus rarũ absconditus: quũ qui inuenerit homo abscondit: et vadens omnia vendit: vt agrũ cu thesauro emere possit. Ager est suprema hec regio spiritus: thesaurus est amor divinus: quũ homo inueniens cetera omnia debet ptene: re: vt agrũ cu thesauro iocunde valeat possidere. Hũ est in mundo iocundior amore divino possidio: non est in hac vita amplior pulchritudo: quonũ quisquis hũc the saurum amoris habuerit: nihil amplius requirit. Et si cuit ignis naturaliter sursum agitur: sic amor in hũc rea gionẽ spiritus quasi ad suũ domicilũ propriũ elenatur. Aũens nãũ divino amore succensa ignitis affectibus in deũ semp sustollitur: et supra omne cogitationẽ mirabili in suũ principũ dulcedine mouetur. In exercicio enim secũde regionis purificata se ad ascensũ huũs terciũ amatorũ affectũ ŕparat: venire ad cu quũ diligite quũto cũs anhelat: nihil aliud quũ iẽsum cordũ sui thesaurũ cogitat: illum pre amoris magnitudine ignitis suspirũ adorat. Expleto autẽ suauissimo cõtemplacũnis officio. Subito dilectus elabitur: ad secũde regionis exercicium mens amore languida reuocatur: in quo dei verus ama tor corpu quũdẽ cõmorari inter hoũs cernũ: sed affectu et desideriũ cu suo amãctissimo iẽsu cõversatur. Et licet anagogica istũ spũs creati actio fiat impulsa spiritus deũ: oportet tamẽt mens p exercicũ secunde regionis purgata selũam ad ascensũ proueçat: et diũ uno spiritũ p affectũ ferventissimu disposita cõcurrat. Eniuero deũs omnipotens qui nobũs arbitriũ libertate cõtulũ: nemine ad hũc supremũ cõtemplationis sue reu gionem non volentẽ eleuabũ. Volũtas igitur nostra ad propriũ salutẽ requiritur: amor ad ascensũ postulat. Si vis ad hũc divine caligini supremũ verticũ ascensũ

There the most indulgent Father will receive you as you return with joy; he will clothe you with the first robe of innocence recovered; he will give you the ring of most holy covenant on your hands, and shoes of true mortification of evil affections on your feet, so that, adorned with these ornaments, like a faithful bride you may cling to him continually and never thereafter withdraw from his love. Finally, for your food he will kill the fatted calf for you; he himself will be at once the server and the feast: because of the greatness of his love he will give his flesh as food and his own blood as drink. There the Spirit of the holy Lord will be present and will fill you with his mystical gifts. Then, exulting in the Lord, you will sing: The fruit of Jesus is sweet to my throat, for his spirit is sweeter than honey.

Therefore this supreme region is magnificent in the spirit’s return, because it leads back to the pleasantness of the heavenly fatherland those citizens whom it receives into its dwelling. And we unfailingly recognize the citizens of this most holy region by the fruits of the Spirit, of whom we know the holy apostle spoke. Now the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity. These fruits the citizens of this third region bring forth, because, filled with God and united to him, always joyful in the Lord and most fervent in charity, they walk onward. For whatever happens to a just man dwelling on this mountain of love will not sadden him. For the soul always peaceful and tranquil in the love of God is not lifted up by any prosperity and is not disturbed by any adversity.

That this supreme region of the spirit is joyful and most true in its treasuring up.

Article Six.

Behold, this most beautiful region of the spirit is called joyful and most true in its treasuring up, because whatever is acquired through the exercise of good work it possesses in simplicity of spirit. The soul’s treasure is the love of God; when the purified mind is kindled by its fervor, it is raised to this region as to the very storehouse of love. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Where your treasure is, there also your heart will be. This is the rare treasure hidden in the field of Scripture; when a man has found it, he hides it, and going away sells everything, so that he may be able to buy the field with the treasure. The field is this supreme region of the spirit; the treasure is divine love. When a man finds it, he ought to count all other things as worthless, so that he may joyfully possess the field with the treasure. There is no possession in the world more delightful than divine love; there is no greater beauty in this life, for whoever has this treasure of love seeks nothing more. And as fire is naturally borne upward, so love is raised into this region of the spirit as to its own proper dwelling.

For the soul, kindled by divine love, is always lifted up to God with fiery affections, and beyond every thought is moved with wondrous sweetness toward its own beginning. For, purified in the exercise of the second region, it prepares itself for the ascent of this third affection of lovers; it pants with all its strength to come to him whom it loves; it thinks of nothing but Jesus, the treasure of its heart; in the greatness of its love it adores him with burning sighs. But when the most sweet office of contemplation has been completed, suddenly the beloved slips away; the mind, languishing with love, is called back to the exercise of the second region. In this exercise the true lover of God sees that his body indeed dwells among men, but in affection and desire he lives with his most beloved Jesus.

And although this anagogic action of the created spirit comes about by the impulse of the Spirit of God, still the mind, cleansed through the exercise of the second region, must advance itself toward the ascent, and, disposed by a most fervent affection, concur with the divine Spirit. For almighty God, who has bestowed on us freedom of choice, will raise no one unwilling to this supreme region of his contemplation. Therefore our will is required for our own salvation; love demands the ascent. If you wish to ascend to this supreme summit of divine darkness,

Ista libertal animi p dini amoris feruorẽ acquirit:qr cos amantis dei supremus sanctus inhabitat: qui vera liber taté amáribus donat. In hac sanctissima libertate divina sapientia discitur: suavitas divinae bonitatis inestimá bui dulcedine gustatur: mens liberrima effecta supra se rapit: in silencio divinae caliginis quiescēs soporatur. Et hec mystica sapientia in mére elevata et in dei pu rificata cōsistere dicit: que nullo obstaculo cuiuscūs rel a suo effectuali pgressu impeditur. Ascendens in hac re gionē mens amore succensa cogitacōnes et imagines pe nitus deserit: sola nuda et liberrima evadit: quia cogita cōnes pter officiū memoriae in media regione coguntur plisterē: nec suprema regionē spūs que sup omnē intelli gentiā est bois nullatenus poterunt a propriare. Sola enim affectu et desiderio huc p amorē ascenditur: procul hinc phantasimata cogitationū repellitur. Nam mox ve ascendere p cogitacōnes mens incipit: in regionē media repulsa cadit. Verūcamen p intellectus operationē ascen sus ipē incipitur: quo mox deficiente p affectū cōlsumat. Intellectus eni in amorē summi boni desideriū excitat: quantū potest eius pulchritudinē cōmendat: sed cui affe ctus excitatus p amorē ascendere ad cōtemplationētāte pulchritudinis ceperit: intellectus pre stupore deficiens obmutescit. Mens autē comutatū intellectus nō sufferēs sola et nuda. ab omnīs cogitacōnis imagine liberrima montē caliginosum sup splendentē ingrediēt: dilectū non quidē facie ad faciem sed in enygmate cōtemplatī: p ma gnitudine amoris deficit: rapta in silencio quiescit. Quondā israhelitici pili dux moyses vocatus a deo montē caliginosum solus ascēdisse legit: plebē phibusse ab accessu montis sub interminacōne mortis memorat: in caligine dūs a paruit: legem populo p ipim moysen dedit. Si eni in exodo scribit. Totus autē nions synai fumabat: eo qō descendisset dūs sup cu in igne: et ascen deret fumus exeo quasi de fornace. Eratqō mis mons terribilis:7 sonitus buccine paulatim crescebat in maius:

[unclear], you will have to love exceedingly. The will, purified by love, receives; love, when very fiery, produces ecstasy. Therefore, if you desire to fly to the mountain of contemplation, you must, by loving God most fervently, wholly exceed yourself. But if you truly love God, you will despise both yourself and all things for the sake of him alone. For he is truly the treasure of the soul; if anyone has obtained him through love, he will always think upon that treasure. This treasure is acquired by loving; no one understands its usefulness who has not received it through love. Whoever desires to have this inestimable treasure should continually fix his heart in the love of most sweet Jesus. For truly, he who loves has; he who has, loves. The mind that has deserved to possess this treasure of the love of Jesus remains continually with him in affection, in this highest region.

That this third and highest region of the soul rejoices in the greatest freedom of spirit.

Seventh, this most holy region of the soul overflows with great freedom of spirit; in it the mind, free from the passions of the flesh, reigns with God alone through love. For the holy Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” And again: “Whoever is led by the Spirit of God, they are the children of God.” For truly, the spirit abiding in this region is made free from every defilement of flesh and blood; stripped of every phantom of thought, naked and alone, it is lifted up into the darkness of divine contemplation. This is the true freedom of the soul: to rest in the fervor of divine love and to love none of the consolations of this world.

Therefore let a person consider himself, and diligently examine his love; and if he finds himself devoutly affected, often raised up to divine love by fiery desires even without prior thought, let him trust that he can rightly be counted among the citizens of this region. For the Spirit of God bears witness to our spirit, and when he raises the mind into the ray of divine love, he also makes it know the condition of its own state. This freedom of soul is acquired through the fervor of divine love, because the supreme Holy Spirit inhabits the heart of one who loves God, and grants true freedom to those who love.

In this most holy freedom divine wisdom is learned; the sweetness of divine goodness is tasted with inestimable delight; the mind, made most free, is carried above itself; resting in the silence of divine darkness, it is lulled to sleep. And this mystical wisdom is said to consist in a mind raised up and purified in God, which is hindered by no obstacle whatever from its effective advance. Ascending in this region, the mind kindled by love wholly abandons thoughts and images; it escapes alone, naked, and most free, because thoughts, on account of the office of memory, are compelled to remain in the middle region, and can in no way appropriate to themselves the highest region of the spirit, which is above all understanding. For one ascends here by love through affection and desire alone; far from here the phantasms of thoughts are driven away. For as soon as the mind begins to ascend by thoughts, it is thrust back and falls into the middle region.

Nevertheless, the ascent itself is begun through the operation of the intellect; when that soon fails, it is completed through affection. For the intellect stirs up desire into love of the highest good and, as far as it can, commends its beauty. But when affection, stirred by love, has begun to ascend to the contemplation of so great a beauty, the intellect, failing in amazement, falls silent. But the mind, not enduring the commotion of the intellect, alone and naked, most free from every image of thought, enters the dark mountain that shines above; contemplating the beloved, not face to face indeed but in a riddle, it fails because of the greatness of love, and, carried away, rests in silence.

We read that Moses, once the leader of the children of Israel, called by God, ascended alone into the dark mountain; and it is recorded that he kept the people back from approaching the mountain under threat of death. The Lord appeared in the darkness and gave the law to the people through Moses himself. For so it is written in Exodus: “The whole of Mount Sinai was smoking, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire; and its smoke went up as from a furnace. And the mountain was very terrible, and the sound of the trumpet gradually grew louder.”

et prolislus tendebatur. Cũctus autẽ populus videbat lápades montẽ fumantẽs: et pterriti ac pauore cõcussi steretit procul dicentes moys. and was drawn out at length. Then all the people saw the torches and the smoking mountain; terrified and shaken with fear, they stood far off, saying to Moses: “Speak to us yourself and we will listen; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.”

All these things are full of mysteries; if they are examined with careful consideration, they will splendidly commend this supreme region of the spirit. For Mount Sinai signifies the height of this region; the smoking cloud represents the object of contemplation; Moses expresses the affection burning in love; the people show the crowd of thoughts and phantasms. Moses alone, the leader of the people, is permitted to ascend the mountain and enter the cloud, because the affection inflamed with divine love alone is raised to the summit of the light of contemplation. But the people are forbidden, under threat of death, to approach the mountain, because no intellect, no thought, no imagination or reasoning can in any way penetrate the secret of the divine majesty. The common crowd stands far from the mountain, stricken with fear, because when the mind alone enters the abyss of contemplation through the affection of love, the whole crowd of thoughts, failing utterly, is thrown into confusion. The intellect does not dare to approach its own affection as it ascends, but, standing far off and shaken with fear within itself, is forced to remain behind. Therefore, yielding in wonder before majesty, it says with the prophet to the Lord: “Truly you are a hidden God.” But Moses, standing on the summit of the mountain, is wrapped in the cloud: he does not grasp God by the light of the intellect, but passes into contemplation of him only through love and desire. Moses, and not the Lord, speaks to the fearful people, because the purified affection enters the dwelling-place of love, through which the powers of the spirit are enlightened.

By what modes or degrees one must ascend to this supreme summit of this region.

Although in several preceding places of this little work I have briefly handed down the manner of ascending to this supreme region of the spirit, nevertheless, as I think, it will not be useless to repeat blessed things more often, so that we may be able to retain them more firmly. For it seems to me of little profit to describe the beauty of contemplation unless we also know how to show those who desire it the way of coming to it. Therefore, whoever wishes to ascend through the desire of love to the pleasantness of this upper region should strive to exercise himself diligently in the labors of the middle region, because unless in that region he has been purged from sensual passions through the practice of holy compunction, he approaches this one not without danger. For undertaking this exercise, let him often recall to memory the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; let him weep from delight in divine love; and let him learn to run through the text of that Passion frequently in attentive meditation, and to stir himself to compassion for the Savior.

And because the body, which is corrupt, weighs down the soul, so that the mind cannot vigorously direct itself in this meditation on the Lord’s Passion, let him strive, if need be, to present to his thoughts images that are truly perceptible to the senses. Therefore, withdrawing from crowds into silence, let him begin to turn over in memory the order of the Passion; let him see himself with the eyes of the mind as present at each event with the suffering Lord; let him hear Jesus speaking in his imagination; let him go with him through all the places of the Passion. Then at each article let him bring his affections out of a desire for compassion; let him gaze with faithful eyes upon Jesus suffering, set before him; flowing with anguish of heart, let him grow accustomed in spirit to address him as though bodily present, and to embrace him, wounded at the pillar and on the cross, through the desire of love. For the mind can easily be kindled in love of the Lord Jesus if it truly grows accustomed to suffer with him through the tears of meditation. But I remember having written elsewhere more fully on the most effective exercise of the Lord’s Passion; therefore I have touched on it briefly here. For it is enough to have given beginners the first principles of meditation, since those who are experienced have higher things.

Therefore, when the affection has been purged from every passion and hindering concupiscence, the mind, with the help of the intellect, begins to think somewhat upon the goodness and beauty of the highest good; then it desires to behold the immutable good. But when, with the intellect lifting it up, it raises itself through admiration toward knowledge of that good, at once the operation of the intellect grows faint; nor can reason follow the affection any farther, since it sees that it can be raised only in another way, and only when wholly and completely stripped bare of all things. But so long as the mind has not been lawfully purified, the affection does not reach the true cloud of this mountain.

Contemplation, however, sometimes comes through the enlargement of the mind: when the soul stretches itself more vigorously by its own effort in holy meditation, meditation is changed into contemplation. And this mode of contemplation is accustomed to rise up through three degrees: teaching, by which we learn what we must do; exercise, by which we carry out what we have learned; and attention, by which we fulfill the task.

Sometimes contemplation raises the elevation of the mind toward God: when the mind has been divinely irradiated above human effort, it draws it, as though carried beyond itself, into the contemplation of divine things. This mode also lifts it up into the height of contemplation by three degrees. For sometimes understanding, divinely inspired for the good, receives something that wholly surpasses the mode of foreknowledge. The second degree raises the mind above effort, when, divinely enlightened, it receives something to which no human effort attains. In the third degree the mind is raised on high, when it is divinely illumined in contemplation above the limits of human nature and effort.

Sometimes, too, contemplation directs itself by alienation of mind toward the mountain of divine darkness, when, the memory of present things being lulled to sleep, the soul is drawn into an unknown state beyond human knowledge by the illumination of divine operation. And this mode belongs especially to this highest region of the spirit, in which the mind of the true lover of God, kindled with so great a fervor of love, perceives that it is often proved to be estranged from itself. For sometimes, by the greatness of devotion, it is rapt outside itself; sometimes, by exceeding wonder, it is lifted above itself. Sometimes, because of immense exultation, it leaves itself behind, and through the ray of love passes into the highest elevation of contemplation. But mortal man does not understand the loveliness of this most high and supreme region if he has not ascended to it, purified through experience of love.

Here ends the third region of cloistered persons.

The beginning of happiness.

[unclear]

Preface to the second part of the principal exercise of cloistered persons. It happily begins.

Since, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have recently completed the little work on the threefold region of cloistered persons, set forth for us by chapters, it remains now that, undertaking according to our strength the second principal part of the work, we describe the mode and form of daily spiritual exercise.

For there are many among cloistered persons who are weak and feeble; and of these, some perhaps would gladly ascend to the contemplation of divine love if they had a mode suited to beginners. For all who are established in holy religion must take the greatest care that the mind not grow sluggish in idleness, since whoever has failed in the continual labor of spiritual exercise gradually falls into the depth of the body. For just as this visible fire of ours cannot continue in its operation without fuel suited to it, so the love of inward compunction cannot remain in a person’s mind without the continual exercise of devotion. For when the labor of spiritual study has died through inward negligence, all compunction of devotion gradually vanishes. No one placed in a holy state can remain steadfast and firm if his mind does not strive each day to be renewed by some exercise. For when the fuel of divine love is withdrawn, devotion is changed into torpor. Scripture says: “In desires is every idle man.” Therefore, lest the mind gradually flow away through sloth from the holy fervor of the spirit, it must learn to renew itself daily by some spiritual exercise, so that, while the fuel of singular love is supplied day by day, the desire for greater progress may be more fully kindled. Thus we read that the most holy fathers once advanced in the order; thus we know that they remained in devotion, because they knew very well the instability of the human mind, and therefore [unclear] to stir themselves to new [unclear].
