Another, through the practice of bending in prayer, used to stir his mind to the compunction of devotion; another, through meditation on the Lord’s Passion, kindled himself; another, by continual attention to his holy purpose, set before his inner eyes each day the image of death close at hand; another, by a fixed manner in his prayers, daily offered himself to the Lord with tears. None among them is believed to have been without a daily spiritual exercise of the mind; none is found to have been given to idleness, because the kingdom of God is promised to those who labor in the vineyard of the Lord, but denied to the idle.

Considering this, the devout fathers of the annual chapter unanimously resolved to adopt the present exercise and to offer it for practice to their subjects who have nothing better. And although so great a multitude of monks subject to the aforesaid chapter neither can nor ought to be restricted to the pattern of a single exercise, still it is proposed to all in common, so that those who do not have a better exercise may use this one. It is especially fitting that one newly converted to the order should exercise himself in the manner set down below, until, grounded in humility, he grows through compunction to better things. But whoever thinks that for a long time now he has been dwelling, by accustomed devotion, in higher things, let him at least permit these things to the little ones without envy. For I do not doubt that there are many living in the order who are devoted to better modes of spiritual exercise, and who have learned by long practice to remain in the highest region of the spirit through the ray of divine love. We in no way force our childish things upon them, for we know that they are higher than the steps of the present exercise. For we, imperfect men, write for beginners who are starting to make progress, not to teach the perfect. Rather, we are humbly ready to listen to them as teachers.

Here begins the second principal part of the little work on the threefold region of cloistered persons, which contains the manner and form of the daily exercise of monks.

Therefore, one who is to serve as a soldier for the king, our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the monastic rule, should first of all strive humbly and perseveringly to take up the strongest weapons of holy obedience; then he should accustom himself to be continually exercised in holy works, to persist in prayers without ceasing and with devotion, and to love God above all things. Whatever he does, let him set before himself the honor of God alone; whatever he begins, let him always send prayer before him to the Lord. For he truly speaks with the Lord God who is always occupied in devout prayers.

So that a good cenobite may always have ready at hand a manner of praying with elevation of mind, let him not neglect to read the present little work frequently and attentively. For in it we have arranged, for the individual hours of the seven offices, certain brief little prayers, by which the mind is more often raised to the love of heavenly things and the fervor of holy purpose is frequently renewed.

At Matins.

Awakened, the devout cenobite rises at once for Matins and shakes off from himself all sluggishness of sleepiness. He should believe that he has been called to fight for his Lord, to whom he has been professed. Therefore let him strive to meet his king with cheerfulness, and to prepare himself humbly, with fervor of spirit, for his immortal service. And so at once let him rise with the greatest dignity, and, sitting on his bed and fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, let him say:

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Blessed be the name of the Lord, from this time forth and forever.

Then, getting down from his bed, with knees bent let him say:

I give thanks to you, almighty God, who have deigned to guard me, an unworthy sinner, this night. I ask you, by your mercy, to direct me through this day and at all times in your praise, to keep me clean from sin, and sweetly to kindle me in your most holy love.

Ut autẽ cor tuũ lemp libere posis in oracõe ad dũm deu erigere: disce nihil in hoc mũdo singulariter amare: qũĩ q ad nullã rem penitus afficit: rarius euagaũ. Nibil em sic exonerat cor liberũqz reddit. nihil tã liberaliter sine angustia corã dũo cõversari facit. nihilqz tã cito et leuiter post varios tumultus externos hoiem ad interioara recol ligt: qũĩ in omnibus rebus et casibus nullo priuato affectu ad aliqũd affici: sed deũ t superioribũ suis resignatũ in oũa bus hũlilcer cõversari. Ad bec quicqũd p gla dei et cõserũ natione regularis discipline iniũctũ taliter disposito fuen rit: hoc totũ cenobita cui humili obedientia. Sue cõmos dosum sit sue molestũ synceriter assumit. Et bec animũ soliditas tã pspera qũ aduersũ ptemnẽs mentẽmirabiliter

O adorable Trinity, O venerable Unity, through you we have been created, true eternity; through you we have been redeemed, you highest charity. Protect, save, free, rescue, and cleanse all your people. We adore you, almighty one; to you we sing; to you be praise and glory for endless ages of ages. Amen.

Then, turning to the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, let him say:

Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb, Jesus Christ. Amen.

Show yourself to be a mother; may he who, born for us, consented to be yours receive prayer through you. Mary, mother of grace, mother of mercy, protect us from the enemy, and receive us at the hour of death. Glory be to you, Lord, who were born of the Virgin, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for endless ages. Amen.

At the first signal, the monk should go to the secret place of his inner cell; cleansing his conscience, he should examine it diligently, and in the three things that follow he should compose himself in preparation for prayer.

First, he should strive to draw his mind back from outward things, vain and perishable and contrary to the spirit, to inward things, and to think absolutely nothing about worldly or temporal affairs. Just as Abraham is read to have stood firm and driven the birds away from the sacrifice, so it seems necessary for us to act against worldly thoughts that fly importunately around us during divine things. The monk can more easily bring his mind to this forgetfulness of passing things if he often wishes to recall to memory the sixth root, set above in the second region, concerning the vanity of present things.

Second, with humility he should direct the eyes of his mind to knowledge of himself, knowing that by his own strength he cannot persist in holy fervor of spirit unless divine mercy deigns to help him. Finally, let the humble monk understand that he is not worthy to praise his Creator, and therefore let him ask help from the Lord and worthy merit for praise. But if he desires to know more about knowledge of himself, let the devout monk read the fourth root.

Third, for one who wishes devoutly to stand before the Lord God in prayers, it is necessary to lift the mind with fervor of spirit to heavenly things. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: God is spirit, and those who adore him must adore in spirit and truth. The most devout suppliant of God, Bernard, also says: The little novice must be taught in his prayer to lift his heart upward, to pray spiritually, to withdraw from images of bodily things, and to think nothing bodily.

But because it is not given to all to be able to raise the mind to God, invisible and beyond understanding, provision must also be made for the weak in an easier manner of raising themselves to God. Hence he also says: For a weak person meditating or praying, an image of the Lord’s nativity, humanity, passion, or resurrection is more safely set before him; in it the mind may be stirred to tears of compunction, so that the weak soul, because it has known only bodily things, may have means by which, according to the measure of its capacity, it may be moved toward divine things. For while through faith in the form of the mediator it does not divide God from man, it attains to God himself in man. For our Savior, the mediator of God and men, Jesus Christ, is God and man.

Therefore let the devout monk often turn over the first root of divine knowledge, so that he may be able to lift himself higher through love. For the more perfectly he knows God, the more ardently he loves; and the more he loves the Lord, the better he praises him. For praise is the first work of lovers.

But so that you may always be able to raise your heart freely to the Lord God in prayer, learn to love nothing in this world in a private way; for one who is affected by no thing at all wanders less often. For nothing so unloads the heart and makes it free, nothing makes it converse before the Lord so generously and without constraint, and nothing so quickly and lightly gathers a person back to inward things after various outward disturbances, as to be attached to nothing in all things and circumstances by any private affection, but to live humbly in all things resigned to God and to one’s superiors. In addition, whatever has been enjoined on one so disposed for the glory of God and the preservation of regular discipline, the monk undertakes all this with humble obedience, whether it is advantageous to him or troublesome. And this firmness of soul, despising prosperity as much as adversity, wonderfully [unclear].

Ante omnes horas. Ouoniā virtus omice incarnacónis 7 passionis oim sanctoy merita incóparabiliter exsuperat: idcirco amator dei antefingulas horas ad deú patré hac oratio ne cui mécis attentione cor de velo re dicat.

[unclear] in a certain enjoyment of most chaste love transformed.

At the second signal.

When the second signal sounds, the monk, now sufficiently recollected within, should leave his cell with composure, always blessing the Lord in his heart. With the prudent virgins let him hasten to meet the bridegroom; let him consider that he hears the signal of the great king. On leaving his cell, let him say:

Protect, Lord, your people by the sign of the holy cross from all snares of every enemy, that we may render you pleasing service, and that our sacrifice may become acceptable to you. Direct us, Lord, in the way of peace, to the everlasting glory of your name.

On entering the church, let him say:

Blessed are they who dwell in your house, Lord; they shall praise you forever and ever. Cleanse me, Lord, from every defilement of mind and body, that I may be worthy to praise and bless you in your house forever.

Passing before the crucifix, let him say:

I beseech you, most loving Lord Jesus, by all the bitterness of your most holy Passion which you endured for me, and especially when your most noble soul went forth from your body: have mercy on my soul at its departure. Amen.

At the holy water:

Take away from me, Lord, all my iniquities, that with a pure mind I may be worthy to enter into the holy of holies. You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and so forth.

Before the image of the blessed Virgin Mary:

O blooming rose, beautiful mother of the Lord. O gentle virgin. O most fruitful vine, brighter than the dawn, pray for us continually.

Passing before the altar, let him say:

Glory to you, Lord, who were born of the Virgin, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto everlasting ages.

Or:

You, the unbegotten Father, you, the only-begotten Son, you, the Holy Spirit, the holy and undivided Trinity, I praise, bless, and adore without end. O highest unity, beginning of all things, have mercy on me for your own sake.

Before the venerable sacrament:

Hail, living host, truth and life, in whom the ancient sacrifices are ended. Through you the glory of the homeland is given without end. Through you the Church stands ever fortified. Grant me rewards in eternal life. Amen. Hail, saving host.

Praying in his place in choir.

When he has come to his customary place of standing in choir, if there is time, let him consider what our holy father Benedict said in the Rule about reverence in prayer and psalmody. Looking carefully at the matter of the psalms to be sung, let him strive to subject his intention to them, and diligently foresee to what he wishes to refer each thing. If the morning office is being sung for some saint, let the psalmody be said before the Lord in memory of that saint. But if the subject matter of the psalms fits the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, it should be referred to his memory. Yet if the spirit of compunction is present to the singer, it will teach all things through love. For a mind fervent in the love of God knows very well how to direct its intention to the praise of the Creator, and how, according to the nature of the psalmody, to vary it suddenly in individual verses. For according to the subject of what is being sung, it exercises itself on whatever it wishes: now it embraces the humanity of Christ, now suddenly in another verse it is raised up to his divinity. Nevertheless, if it pleases him, our faithful monk may, while the same signal lasts, bring back to mind the fervor of the saints and angels praising God without ceasing, and conform himself to them by desire, according to his powers.

Before all the hours.

Since the power of the Incarnation and Passion surpasses beyond compare the merits of all the saints, therefore before each of the hours the lover of God should say to God the Father, with due attention of mind and heart, this prayer [unclear].

Cum potens sempiterne Deus et nos cu no essemus de nihilo creasti, cu perissimus misericorditer redemisti: rogo te p incōmutabile majestatē tua: suscipe bas laudes et oracōnes quas tibi nūc et omni tpedicturus sum: in ulla vnione charitatis et dilectionis qua vnigenitū filiū tuī misisti in vterū beatiffime virginis marie: et in qua cu pa/ tientē et morientē p nobis in cruce suscepisti. On putes hūc orandi modū esse frivolu: nechūa/ na curiositate adinuentū: q̄ si deũ anticos suos p reuelationē multa docere cōlueuisse credideris: nihil huic forme sanctissime cōtradicis. Cenobita deuotus magnā diligentiā adhibeat: ne mens imagines vel cogitacōnes de rebus trāsitoriūs ad- mittat: q̄m nīs mor in principio vane cogitacōnes ren pulse fuerint: p totū officiū intentionē cordis pturbabūt. Idcirco fidelis orator se totū in serēcolligat: et nihil dīo uino famulatūi uerta regulā preponat. Inter psallendū materiā ip am psalmo et ad ɔgruentē intencōnis sue aciem referat: sensū oronis prudēter respio ciat: vbā distincte 7 ordinate pferat: mēte sursū tendat. Post singulos vero psalmos vel lectiones femerīp Oelligenter considerando examinet: et si adhuc compunctio deuoconis in mente ferueat exploret. Si adhuc feruore adesse inuenerit: sanctis cui desiderijs amplius studeat accendere: et semetipm ad altiora puocare. Si vero te puisse affectu vel p cogitacones distractu senserit: mor re prehendes semetipm hec vel similia dicat. Ue mihi mi fero: qui deũ meũ tã negligenter laudo. Ecce dũs meus amariffime, p me tota nocte passus nulla requie habuit: et ego una hora vigilare cui eo nõ potui: Adiuua me dũs deus meus: vt tibi prudenter psallere possum. Deniqs sub quolibet psalmo semetipm oportune per aliqua ardentia verba ad cõpunctione feruoris excitet: quatenus p mentalē exhortationē affectu amplius inflā met. Utinā inquiens dũs deus ex toto corde sup omia te possim diligere: et tibi soli iugiter adherere. O bone de incende cor meũ in tuo sanctiffimo amore. Amor meus crucifixus est: et ego quid facio sup terra: O ielu dulcis amor meus: posside cor meũ:quia thesaurus cordis mei cs: rex meus et deus meus. Post Matutinas. Ompleto matucinali officio, confessionibus factis vel auditis, cõfestim hora de sancta cruce legere nõ negligat: qua cõpleta banc oraciunculam subdat. Oration Blecro dulciffime dũs ielu, p dolorẽ vulnerũ tuo per sanctiffimi sanguinis tui effusionẽ: ac inno centiffimi mortis tue virtutẽm: miserere mei nũcetin ho ra mortis mee Amen. Bein de dicat. Ancete et indluidue trinitati: ielu christi dũi nostrũ crucifixe huaniicati: beatiffime marie semp virgint: et sancte anne eius venerabili genitrici: cui omnib sanctis sit sempiterna laus et gla: p infinita secula Amen.

Since, almighty eternal God, you created us from nothing when we did not exist, and mercifully redeemed us when we had perished, I beseech you by your unchangeable majesty: receive these praises and prayers which I am about to say to you now and at all times, in that union of charity and love in which you sent your only-begotten Son into the womb of the most blessed Virgin Mary, and in which you received him as he suffered and died for us on the cross. Amen.

Note on the preceding prayer.

Do not think this manner of praying frivolous, nor devised by human curiosity. For if you believe that God was accustomed to teach his people of old many things by revelation, you will in no way contradict this most holy form. Rather, read the wondrous works of the Lord which he has shown to those who love him, and you will find that he revealed this manner and form of praying to Mechtild and to others. Know this also as something fully assured: that a prayer is most pleasing to almighty God when a devout mind has resolved to offer it to God the Father in union with the Lord’s passion. And this offering can be made, in mind or by mouth, not only before the canonical hours, but also before other prayers, Masses, and any good exercises or works. But if through forgetfulness it has not been made beforehand, it can be inserted during the prayer, or even added after its completion.

How a monk ought to conduct himself in the hours.

From the beginning of the divine praise the devout cenobite should use great diligence, lest his mind admit images or thoughts about transitory things; for unless vain thoughts are driven away at once in the beginning, they will disturb the heart’s attention throughout the whole office.

Therefore the faithful worshiper should gather himself wholly within himself, and set nothing before the divine service and the true rule.

While chanting the psalms, he should refer the very matter of the psalm to the fitting focus of his intention; he should prudently consider the meaning of the prayer, pronounce the words distinctly and in order, and lift his mind upward.

After each psalm or reading, let him diligently examine himself by reflecting, and test whether the compunction of devotion is still fervent in his mind. If he finds that the fervor is still present, let him strive to kindle it further with holy desires, and to summon himself to higher things. But if he feels that he has grown lukewarm in affection or distracted by thoughts, then, reproving himself, let him say these or similar words: Woe to me, wretch that I am, who praise my God so negligently. Behold, my Lord, suffering most bitterly for me through the whole night, had no rest; and I could not watch with him for one hour. Help me, Lord my God, that I may be able to chant psalms to you wisely.

Finally, under each psalm he should suitably stir himself to compunction of fervor by some burning words, so that through inward exhortation he may inflame his affection still more. Let him say: Would that, Lord God, I could love you above all things with my whole heart, and cling to you alone without ceasing. O good Jesus, kindle my heart in your most holy love. My love has been crucified; and what am I doing upon the earth? O Jesus, my sweet love, possess my heart, for you are the treasure of my heart, my king and my God.

After Matins.

When the office of Matins has been completed, and confessions have been made or heard, let him not neglect immediately to read the hour of the Holy Cross. When it is completed, let him add this little prayer.

Prayer.

O sweetest Lord Jesus, by the pain of your wounds, by the pouring out of your most holy blood, and by the power of your most innocent death, have mercy on me now and at the hour of my death. Amen.

Then let him say:

To the holy and undivided Trinity, to the crucified humanity of Jesus Christ our Lord, to the most blessed Mary ever virgin, and to Saint Anne, her venerable mother, with all the saints, be everlasting praise and glory for infinite ages. Amen.

After confession.

It is our custom that those who are to celebrate on a given day should prepare themselves by confession. Therefore the devout monk, after making his confession, at whatever time has been appointed, should at once devoutly carry out the penance enjoined upon him; and he should not approach the altar unless sacramental confession has always first been made, so far as this can be done.

On leaving the church.

When each Hour has been completed in the divine office, or also whenever he begins, he may repeat the order and manner of praying at entering the church described above, and observe the same rite in each of his places. But if, for greater devotion, he wishes to vary this manner, he shall pray the following little prayers, or pray silently.

Before the high altar, bowing:

Blessed be the holy Trinity and the undivided Unity. We shall confess him, because he has shown his mercy to us. O highest majesty, beginning of all things, have mercy on me. Amen.

Then, after returning to the cell.

At each Hour of the day, when the devout lover of Christ has returned to his cell, let him fall on his knees before his bed and humbly give thanks to almighty God, because he has deigned to admit him, an insufficient servant, to his service, and there to number him among his sons. Therefore let him say this or a similar prayer.

Prayer.

I give thanks to you, almighty and eternal God, because you have deigned to call me, an unworthy sinner, to your service, not by any merits of mine, but by the sole condescension of your mercy. I beseech you, by the pain of the wounds of our Lord Jesus Christ, your only-begotten Son, and by the shedding of his most holy blood, and by the power of his most innocent death: receive this sacrifice of my service for the glory of your majesty, for my sins, for your holy Church, and for the souls of all the faithful departed who are placed in the pains of purgatory, in that union of charity in which you received our same Lord Jesus Christ dying for us upon the cross; and grant me, through the merit of his passion, to love you in truth and to remain continually faithful in your service. Amen.

Morning recollection.

Then enter for a little while into the examination of your conscience, and see whether you still have in yourself the marks of a good cloistered monk described in the seven articles of the second region. If you know that anything is lacking, do not neglect to reform it as quickly as possible, lest little by little you vanish away through negligence. For it is written: “He who neglects the least things gradually falls.” And Augustine, the holy lover of God, says: “No sin is so small that it does not grow when neglected.” Therefore, when your conscience has been examined and reformed in holy fervor, turn to the Lord.

Prayer for perseverance.

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, through the merit of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and through the intercession of blessed Mary ever virgin, of all the holy heavenly powers, and of the blessed patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all your elect, perseverance for us in your will, so that we may be able continually to offer you service pleasing to you. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

Approaching the bed, let him fortify himself with the sign of the holy cross; and while going up to his bed, with attentive spirit, let him say:

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ I intend to lay myself down, so that, restored by his divine majesty, I may be able to praise him more fully through the day.

Sitting on the bed:

May the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ, the integrity of blessed Mary ever virgin, the sign of the holy cross, and the virtue of the Lord’s passion, and the intercession of all the saints, guard my mind and spirit. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Signing himself, let him lie down.

The exercise of the monk at Prime.

Consideration I.

When our devout monk has been awakened for Prime, as usual, let him observe the order and manner of recollecting himself and of the prayers set out above before Matins.

and, fortifying himself with the sign of the life-giving cross, let him say: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Then, rising from his bed, fervent in holy purpose, let him again fall to his knees and, with hands joined, say:

Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love; you who, through the diversity of all tongues, gathered the nations together in the unity of faith. Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created. And you shall renew the face of the earth.

O God, to whom every heart lies open, every will speaks, and from whom no secret is hidden, purify the thoughts of our heart by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, that we may deserve to love you perfectly and praise you worthily. Through Christ our Lord. Let him add “O flowering rose,” and, if he wishes, anything else out of devotion.

At the first signal.

Then, at the first signal of any hour of the day, or even at the striking of the clock, if he has not been occupied with higher meditations, let him say: Blessed be the name of the Lord, from this time forth and forever. Let him add some brief little prayer, formed from the fervor of his mind, in this or a similar way.

A little prayer.

Receive me, sweetest Lord Jesus, as your perpetual servant, that I may always have you as my only good.

Another.

I beseech you, most merciful God: grant me to live so innocently in holy religion that I may be able to come to you, the beginning and end of all good things.

Another.

O that my ways may be directed to keeping your statutes at all times.

Another.

Most loving Lord Jesus, I ask you, by the merits of your most holy Passion, teach me to despise all things, that I may continually deserve to find you, the highest good of my soul.

Then let the general preparation for fervor in prayer, set down above before Matins, be observed, and let the conscience be cleansed if anything has been committed against its purity. Yet if the mind has been lifted up in contemplation of divine love and continual desire, it will have less need of this little exercise.

At the second signal.

At the second signal, both for Prime and for the other hours of the day, when it sounds, let the method set down above for Matins be observed, as much as the time allowed for prayer permits each one. But when a monk enters or leaves our church, let him not neglect to show reverence to God before the altars and the crucifix; rather, bowing humbly, let him say the customary fitting prayers. For the modest bowing of the body is regarded as a sign of the inner good disposition of a soul well ordered toward God.

In the chapter house after Prime.

When the devout monk enters the chapter house after Prime, let him remember to give thanks to God for the victory of the saints and martyrs, whom he knows to have fought for the Lord in the greatest fervor of spirit, despising the torture of their bodies through the witness of death. Therefore, when you have heard the holy and mighty deeds of the saints read aloud, pray the Lord that through their merits he may deign to forgive you your sins, and mercifully strengthen you to bear the yoke of monastic discipline, so that you may attain fellowship with them. And this desire is to be taken up by you when, after the reading of their passions, divine help is invoked three times by all. At the beginning also of the day we pray that, strengthened to patience by the examples of the saints, we may fear no adversities throughout the whole day. But when you hear that some martyr stood bravely in the contest of battle, you may pray to him in these or similar words:

Prayer.

Holy soldier of the eternal King, I ask you, by the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, who made you overcome the torments of the flesh and the snares of this world: pray for me, that I may deserve to come to your fellowship.

If the name of a confessor, or of a virgin, or of a saint of any other condition has been recited, the devout lover of God will easily, according to the ardor of his affection, vary his prayer extempore to any saint whatever. For affective prayers are efficacious above all others.

At the reading of the Rule.

When the reader, according to custom, recites one passage from the Rule, let the devout monk say in his heart: Help me, most sweet Lord Jesus Christ, that according to this rule of your religious servant Benedict I may be able to live, and to remain faithfully in your most holy service at all times.

Then let him consider that, just as the Rule is read daily to the good and devout for their progress, so it is recited to the lukewarm, the evil, or the negligent, that they may be inexcusable, to the heaping up of damnation. Finally, let him know that he is bound to a faithful effort at all the things which the Rule contains, just as the tenor of his profession holds. For thus he says in profession: I promise obedience and the conversion of my conduct according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

When the names of the dead are recited.

But when, after the reading of the Rule, the names of the dead have been recited, then for these and for all other faithful, commended to him and not commended, no less out of charity than out of duty, let the monk pray thus:

Prayer.

I beseech you, most sweet Lord Jesus, by the pain of your wounds, and by the shedding of your most holy blood, and by the power of your most innocent death: have mercy on these souls, and on all those commended to me in prayer, and on all the faithful departed, and grant them everlasting rest.

It is indeed a great work of mercy to intercede before the merciful Judge for the souls confined in the prison of purgatory, and to come to their aid out of charity by the remembrance of the Lord's passion. For I firmly believe, and with pious presumption I trust, that the prayer which is poured out for the dead from charity alone will return doubled into the bosom of the one who prays. For the devout man who here, by the fervor of divine love, praying singularly for all the faithful departed, suffers with them in charity, will at his death be honored with an inestimable reward. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

On the chapter of faults.

Since nothing in human actions is perfect in every part, let the devout monk rejoice that he has found a remedy for his imperfection: for whatever is done amiss through human frailty in well-reformed monasteries is amended daily. For the chapter of faults, continued every single day, washes away public offenses; sacramental confession, daily repeated, remits hidden negligences through the grace of contrition. We discern four chapters in the monastery, of which we shall speak in order.

The first chapter is the passive one, when a brother accuses himself or is accused by another.

The first chapter is called the passive one: that in which our devout monk accuses himself of his negligences, or is accused by another. In this chapter the lover of God, who has denied himself to himself, both humbly accuses his own negligences and suffers himself to be accused by others, lest he be judged more harshly by the Lord after this life. For the holy apostle of God says: If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged. And the prophet Nahum says: A double tribulation shall not rise up. Truly indeed, he who here and now is willingly afflicted for his sins for the love of God deserves, as one thus well purged, to be freed from future tribulation through the mercy of the Creator. If only all cloistered persons knew how much it would profit them toward the merit of everlasting life when they willingly endure chapter accusations, they would endure all accusations and injuries for the love of God with inestimable joy. For we merit more when we patiently suffer injuries and adversities for the love of God and fraternal charity than if we apply ourselves to good works.

Standing therefore in judgment, let the devout monk not fear any accusations whatever, but long to be accused by others in memory of the Lord's passion, knowing that the glory of highness is set before him, and is to be conferred in heaven upon humble patience. O brother, why would you not endure the accusations of the brothers — you who ... the fellowship [the sentence breaks off at the page's end and continues in the next chunk].

Do you expect angels? And let all indignation be far from you; let murmuring be absent; let pride withdraw far away. For you have no cause for impatience. Either you are accused justly, or unjustly. If justly, why would you not endure it? It is better to be cleansed here in small matters than after this life in great ones. And whoever sins publicly is to be corrected before all. But if you are accused unjustly, remember that you are a monk, and you will find that you are bound to endure injuries. For when you are accused justly, know that you are to be cleansed by humble patience; when unjustly, you show yourself a true monk and merit more. Therefore, when you are accused, recall to mind the fourth and sixth degrees of humility, and if you are a true monk, pray even for those who accuse you. For a true lover of God loves all the more the one who accuses him, and on that same day always offers him either some prayer or some special service. If you are good and wise, accusation will not be able to displease you; but if you are evil and foolish, you are worthy to be accused at all times. For Scripture says of the wise man: “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.” But of the evil and foolish the prophet says: “They hated the one who rebuked in the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke perfectly.”

The second chapter on action is that in which one accuses another.

We call the second chapter on action that in which we no longer accuse ourselves, but others. For the action of this accusation charity is supremely necessary; compassion too must be applied no less, and discretion. Therefore, when, by reason of charity, you wish to accuse your brother, you should always apply the fear of God; and, mindful of your fellowship in eternal life, at the beginning you should say: “Our beloved brother has committed this or that; I ask that, for the Lord’s sake, he may be willing to amend himself.” Whatever has to be said, let him put it forward in few words and with compassion. Let him state the deed simply; let him not increase the fault of the one accused by making it heavier; let him silently entrust to the president the judgment whether what he did was good or evil. For the man who, alone among many, makes his brother’s fault heavier by passing sentence on it very often brings back the suspicion of bitter zeal and displeasure. Therefore, whoever attempts to accuse another should beware lest he be moved against his brother by the zeal of bitterness; for when the charity of the accuser does not intervene, resentment does not amend the accused. The accusation of one who accuses never bears fruit in the hearing of the offender when love of God and brotherly charity do not commend it. Indeed, since almighty God is supremely good, he will not give the effect of compunction to your accusation in your brother’s heart when he finds that you have been moved to accuse not by charity but by duplicity. For where he has found the root of his charity, he will not deny good fruit. But if you perceive that you have been moved against your brother by some indignation, it is better to put off the accusation for a time than to wound yourself so cruelly with another’s wound.

The third chapter is that of private humiliation.

They call it the third chapter of private humiliation whenever a brother is rebuked by a senior for his own negligences. For our most holy father Benedict commands in the seventy-first chapter of the Rule that a monk, in whatever place or time he has been accused, as soon as he has sensed that the mind of his senior is even slightly moved against him, should prostrate himself at that senior’s feet and lie there humbly until his command. Here he is in no way permitted to excuse himself or to lay the fault on another; rather, the monk is ordered to be silent and humbly acknowledge himself. For whoever is a true monk neither murmurs when justly corrected nor excuses himself when unjustly accused. Likewise in the divine offices and in the other conventual places, as soon as a devout cenobite has offended in anything through negligence, he humbles himself and does according to the custom there, choosing rather to undergo a greater penance in doubtful matters than to harm his conscience with a lesser one, or to cause scandal to others. But whoever still understands this humiliation, to be undergone at every time and place, as burdensome and difficult, does not walk in the spirit but still lives carnally; and unless he subdues this Jebusite and makes him tributary to himself, he will never be a true and devout cenobite.

Quartũ capitulũ est tractatuum et consiliorum. Quartũ capitulũ deliberatiũ dicimus: quando fratres p aliqua ardua causa ad consiliũ vocaũ mus. Quaeadmodũ hoc capitulũ celebrari deo beat: sanctus benedictus de adhibendis ad cõsilũ fratris bus in regula manifestat. Humilis ergo t verus cenobi ta cui ad consiliũ vocatus fuerit: cui reuerentia et verecunda dia humiliter accedit: interrogatus qõ sentiat pauca los quitur: cõtemni suũ consiliũ et aliena pbari minime deo dignatur. Quod eiõ sentit humiliter dicit: sed aliõ y semp consilia suo pferens, et se et sua sententia discutiendã põs denti veraci subiectione cõmucit. Adeo em in humilitas te profunda seipm annihilat: vt semp plus aliõ õ sibi metiõi credat: cõfiditqõ melioribus sebonũ divinitus ina spirari consiliũ: et tanõs vicariũ christi suũ in mente omia bus solet pponere prelatũ. Maxime liquidẽ ad mortificatõnẽ prie volũtatis monachus proficit: qui suã opi nione in cõsilũs dandũs abbati cui hilari huinilitate omi tpe submittit. The fourth chapter is that of discussions and counsels.

We call the fourth chapter deliberative: when we summon the brothers to counsel about some difficult matter. How this chapter ought to be held, Saint Benedict makes clear in the Rule, in the passage about admitting brothers to counsel. Therefore the humble and true cenobite, when he has been called to counsel, approaches humbly, with reverence and modesty; when asked what he thinks, he says little; he is in no way offended if his own counsel is disregarded and another’s is approved. What he thinks he states humbly, but always preferring the counsels of others to his own, and with true submission he entrusts both himself and his judgment to be examined by the one presiding. For in deep humility he so annihilates himself that he always believes others more than himself, and trusts that good counsel is divinely inspired in those better than he; and in his mind he is accustomed to set his prelate before all, as Christ’s vicar. Indeed, the monk makes very great progress toward the mortification of his own will when, in giving counsel, he submits his own opinion to the abbot at all times with cheerful humility. But when the devout cenobite perceives that his counsel has been disregarded or rejected, let him give thanks to almighty God out of true humility, and recognize that an occasion for pride has been taken away from him.

After the daily chapter.

If, after the chapter of faults, one must return to the church for Terce, let the manner of orderly prayer set out above be observed in each particular. But if you have gone from chapter to your cell, then again, with knees bent, as after Matins [unclear], if the hour permits, you will pray again to God. Let him recollect himself a little, and call back to mind the debt of his profession. Afterward let the cenobite pray thus.

Prayer.

Grant me, I ask, good God, in the observance of your commandments, to know the good pleasure of your most holy will, and to fulfill the debt of my profession according to the rule set before me [unclear].

At private Masses.

Since human nature, by its own strength, cannot gain entrance into the kingdom of heaven, it pleased God, the most merciful Father, mercifully to help us through the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, so that we, who because of our weakness cannot approach the invisible majesty, might have a mediator approaching on our behalf, who is both God and man. Truly, the merit of the most holy passion of our mediator has opened to us the entrance of the kingdom of heaven, has given us the food of spiritual life, and, as the branch draws nourishment from the vine, so our mind truly lives in Christ. We receive this spiritual nourishment with special sweetness in the sacrament of the body and blood of this same mediator of ours, whenever we devoutly offer it to God the Father as an odor of sweetness. And this most sacred oblation of the body and blood of the Lord avails not only for the forgiveness of our sins, but also wonderfully assists the souls of the departed who are placed in purgatory. Therefore so noble a sacrifice must be offered with great and continual devotion, since all our good works, which of themselves are too worthless, become most pleasing to God the Father through this most holy oblation. Therefore, so that the devout cenobite may be able fervently to apply himself to the offering of this precious sacrifice, let him be willing to note four things in order.

Concerning the one serving at Mass.

The devout brother who is to serve at Mass ought to come with the greatest cheerfulness and fervor, and prepare himself most diligently to serve the priest. For Saint Hugh says: Serve willingly at Masses, for that office belongs to angels; and when you serve at that sacrifice, you make familiar to yourself those whose fellow-worker you stand as. If, according to the Savior’s promise, one who receives a just man in the name of a just man receives the reward of a just man, who will deny the reward of the celebrant to one who devoutly serves at Mass? For whoever, with the fervor of divine love, has always been accustomed devoutly to assist those celebrating by serving them, divine kindness will also [unclear].

hac vita solet aliqua speciali gratia remunerare: morulentis quos sancti angeli tanq̄ familiariter noto credunt oca currere: et anima mistri iesu ad conspectu eius cu gaudio plentare. Sic nāq̄ ad patrem orat in scō euangelio filius. Uolo pater ut vbi sum ego: illīc sit et mister meus. Ma gna est eni in hoc venerabili sacramento divine pietatis dignatio: q̄m sicut idem hugo dicit. nihil minus videtur deus facere in eo q̄o quotidiē dignat de celo descendere sup altare psaluten nostra: q̄u de celo descendēs huma na naturā homo factus assumpt. Et sicut dnis nostre iesus christus nobis in memoria sue amarissime passio nis hoc venerabile sacramentum ad indiciu maxime dile ctionis cōtuit: sic eos qui se ad fusciendũ illud vel ad ministrandũ sumentibus q̄u humili deuotione et amore disponēt amplius et singulariter diligit: eisq̄ infidele per illud postulantibus in omni necessitate succurrīt. Nec eni durus esse nobis plena fide orantibus iesus poterit in celo psidens: qui tam clemens 7 pius fuit mis ricordia postulatibus in terris ambulās. Quis vnq̄ ac cessit ad pedes eiet et repulsus est. Quis infirmus sanari petit: quē ambulās inter boies nō curavit. Aunq̄ ergo dnis iesus nobis in fide postulatibus misericordia negat reputerit: q̄ adhuc mortalis orantibus se tā misericors fuit. Ait enim. Omnia possibilia sunt credentī. Ministraturus itaq̄ ad missam ante omnia se purga re ab omni mala tentatione et inordinata affectione tua deat: fe quantũ potest ad se p amoris iesu desideriũ redi cat: quaten? purificatus dno possit assistere: et tā p se p tota ecclesia viuis ac mortuis efficaciter orare. Stas igitur sub missa post sacerdotē o portuno tempore his vel similibus verbis oret. Oratio ministrantis. Dulcissime et amātissime dne iesu rogorete pomo ve angustiā sanctissimi cordis tui quā in passio ne tua sustinuisti: rogo p sanctissimi sanguinis tui effusioné: et p innocentissime mortis tue virtuté: rogo p sancto sancti corporis et sanguinis tui mystériu ad cuiet tibi immolationé inutilis minister assisto: miserere mei et pu rifica cor mei ab omni affectione illicita: vt tibi digneva leam ministrare. Da mihi vera omni peccato et meor contritioné et indulgentiá: sancte cōpunctionis gratiá: iugem passionis tue memoria. cordis pura devotioné: la chrymaru fontem. serene cōscientie puritati: et sanctissi mi amoris tui perpetuā feruorem. Da mihi obsecro clea mectissime amator hominii p dolore vulneri tuop firmi in sancto feroore,positi: verú quoq omnii mundiali contempti: continui celestis patrie desideriú: et certi in sancta religione profecti. Concede mihi dulcisissime iesu in adversis constantiá: in tribulacóne patientiá: in moa ribus disciplina: et vera semp et vbicq in mente humilitatem. Fac me precor huius sanctissimi sacrificiú corporis et sanguinis tui participem: quaten? mens mea pene tue dulcediné sentiat: in tuo amore suauiter ardeat: et a te ineteriú nó recedat. Amen. Oret etiá pro suo pastore: oret, p tota cōgregatione: vt illi in sua voluntate d̄s misericorditer dirigat:istam sub regulari obseruantiá custodienś ab omni adversi tate defendat. Insup oret, p vnuerfalí ecclesia: oret, p fidelib̄ et infi delibus: quatenius omnipotens deus credentes in fide custodiat: nó credentes ad fidé catholica cōvertat. Oret etiá, p cōersione vtiliú psonarũ ad ordiné: p quas et suũ monasteriũ in vtroq statu proficiat: et tota obseruantiá ordinis in melius crescat. Non obliniscatur fidelũ ania marũ in penis purgatoriũ misericordiá cōditoris expecta tium: sed orans, p eis nouerit se post paululũ ad eas trā siturũ:vbí oratio nūc fusã in finũ orantis reuertetur. Aveat auté devotus christi minister ne aliqde coq que suo incũbunt officio qualibet occasione negligentine:

In this life he is accustomed to reward with some special grace those at whose death the holy angels, as though meeting one familiarly known to them, are believed to come, and to present the soul of Jesus’ servant before his sight with joy. For thus the Son prays to the Father in the holy Gospel: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be.”

Great indeed in this venerable sacrament is the condescension of divine goodness. For, as the same Hugh says, God seems to do nothing less in it, when daily for our salvation he deigns to descend from heaven upon the altar, than when he descended from heaven and, having taken human nature, was made man. And just as our Lord Jesus Christ established this venerable sacrament for us in memory of his most bitter passion, as a sign of the greatest love, so he loves more fully and especially those who dispose themselves with humble devotion and love to receive it, or to minister it to those receiving it; and through it he helps them in every necessity when they ask faithfully.

For Jesus, reigning in heaven, will not be able to be harsh to us when we pray with full faith, since he was so gentle and kind to those who asked mercy while he walked on earth. Who ever came to his feet and was rejected? What sick person asked to be healed whom he, walking among men, did not cure? Will the Lord Jesus therefore be thought to deny mercy to us when we ask in faith, he who, while still mortal, was so merciful to those who prayed to him? For he says: “All things are possible to one who believes.”

Therefore, one who is about to serve at Mass should before all things take care to purify himself from every evil temptation and disordered affection, and should bring himself, as much as he can, to the desire of Jesus’ love, so that, purified, he may be able to stand before the Lord and pray effectively both for himself and for the whole Church, the living and the dead. Standing, then, during Mass behind the priest, at a suitable time let him pray in these or similar words.

Prayer of the server.

Most sweet and most beloved Lord Jesus, I beseech you by every anguish of your most holy heart which you endured in your passion; I beseech you by the shedding of your most holy blood and by the power of your most innocent death; I beseech you by the sacred mystery of your holy body and blood, at whose offering to you I, a useless servant, assist: have mercy on me and purify my heart from every unlawful affection, so that I may be able to minister worthily to you. Give me true contrition for every sin and forgiveness of my sins, the grace of holy compunction, continual remembrance of your passion, pure devotion of heart, a fountain of tears, purity of serene conscience, and the perpetual fervor of your most holy love. Give me, I beg you, most merciful lover of mankind, by the pain of your wounds, steadfastness in holy fervor [unclear], true contempt for all worldly things, continual desire for the heavenly homeland, and sure progress in holy religion. Grant me, most sweet Jesus, constancy in adversities, patience in tribulation, discipline in conduct, and always and everywhere true humility in mind. Make me, I pray, a partaker of this most holy sacrifice of your body and blood, so that my mind may feel the sweetness of your suffering, may burn sweetly in your love, and may not inwardly depart from you. Amen.

Let him also pray for his pastor; let him pray for the whole congregation, that the Lord may mercifully direct him according to his will, and may guard this congregation under regular observance and defend it from every adversity.

Furthermore let him pray for the universal Church; let him pray for the faithful and the unbelieving, that almighty God may keep believers in the faith and convert unbelievers to the Catholic faith. Let him also pray for the conversion of useful persons to the order, through whom both his monastery may make progress in each state and the whole observance of the order may grow for the better. Let him not forget the souls of the faithful who, in the pains of purgatory, await the mercy of the Creator; but as he prays for them, let him know that after a little while he will pass to them, where the prayer now poured out will return to the benefit of the one who prays.

But let the devout servant of Christ take care not to neglect, under any pretext, any of the things that belong to his office.

or disturb those celebrating in their prayers, or render them distracted by restlessness. When he has leisure, he will be able to meditate or pray in silence; while he is serving, he ought at least to omit verbal prayers and answer the priest diligently in all things as he ministers.

At the elevation of the most holy body of Christ, following the example of blessed Thomas Aquinas, he may say attentively to Christ: “You are the King of glory, O Christ; you are the everlasting Son of the Father,” and so on to the end of that hymn.

After the elevation, let the devout cenobite turn himself to the Lord Jesus, desiring from his inmost heart to have converse with so great a mystery; and let him prepare his affection as if he were about to communicate. For as often as a devout lover of God, from fervent remembrance, desires to receive the body of Christ, he is believed to have received the power of the sacrament. The Lord Jesus said to a soul dear to him: If a man fervent in my love desired, if it were possible, to receive my body a thousand times in one day, so often, before me, through the power of the same my body, he would truly obtain his desire in his soul. Therefore, with this desire conceived in the mind of one who loves Jesus, let the cenobite pray to the Lord in this or a similar manner.

Prayer of the One Ministering

Would that, most loving Lord Jesus, I were so well and fervently disposed that it might be permitted me now to receive your most holy body in this venerable sacrament; would that it might be permitted me to repeat this sacred communion many times in the day. O my sweetness, O only delight of my heart, O my hope, Lord Jesus, you know the ardor of my mind toward you, and before you is all my desire. Therefore I beseech you: by all your goodness, grant me to receive the virtue and grace of this most holy sacrament now and at every time in my soul, so that I may be able to remain continually in you.

The Careful Preparation of the Priest About to Celebrate

When the priest is about to approach to offer this most sacred sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, let him first examine himself diligently and most carefully consider of which region he is a citizen. If he still finds himself to be a cultivator of the first region, he ought not to approach the altar unless, by contrition and confession, with a firm resolve set upon amending himself, he first strives to cleanse himself. But if he finds himself a citizen of the second region, if he perceives that his powers have been reformed and ordered toward the cenobitic end, he can readily dispose himself to celebrate, since by daily increasing his former affection he has learned more frequently to lift himself upward through desire. For divine goodness quickly enters the affection of a person that is stained by no private desire.

Therefore, wishing to perform this most holy priestly office with devotion and fervor of divine love, let him first set forth some ardent prayers by which he may be able to stir himself to greater compunction. For devotion is rarely granted at the altar if the mind has not first been prepared for fervor. For this reason our fathers, desiring each one of us to advance in his own free devotion, did not wish to burden us, in the manner of certain others, with many psalms before approaching the altar: not because anyone ought therefore to approach without recollection, but so that each one might more freely devote himself in secret to exercises or prayers more suited to his own devotion.

Therefore, wishing to commend elevation of mind to the Lord Jesus for those about to celebrate before approaching the altar, we have placed below a prayer from that which is said to be of Saint Ambrose of Milan, which we believe to be sufficiently effective in view of the merit of the Lord’s Passion. Accordingly, the devout cenobite who is about to approach the altar, if he has leisure and freedom, will be able to use the following, or to set before himself a similar prayer, or to prepare himself in whatever ways he wishes.

Prayer Before Approaching

Highest priest and true pontiff, Jesus Christ, who offered yourself to God the Father as a pure, holy, and spotless victim on the altar of the cross for us miserable sinners; who gave us your flesh to eat and your blood to drink; and who established that mystery by the power of the Holy Spirit, saying, “As often as you do these things, you shall do them in memory of me”: I beseech you, through the pain of your wounds and through your most precious [unclear].

by the shedding of your blood and by the power of your most innocent death, and by your very body and blood, the great price of our salvation, I beg you, by that wondrous and unspeakable charity with which you so loved us, wretched and unworthy though we are, as to wash us from our sins in your blood: have mercy on me and forgive me all my sins. Teach me, your unworthy servant, whom among your other gifts you have deigned to call to the priestly office, through no merits of mine but solely by the gracious condescension of your mercy, through your Holy Spirit, to handle this mystery with that reverence and honor, devotion and fear, with which it ought and fittingly should be handled.

Grant me, I beseech you, always to believe, understand, feel, firmly hold, say, and think concerning so great a mystery that which pleases you and is profitable for the salvation of my soul. Let your good Spirit enter into my heart; let him sound there without sound, and without the noise of words speak within me the truth of such great mysteries. For they are exceedingly deep, and covered with a sacred veil.

For the sake of your great mercy, sweetest Lord Jesus, grant me to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass with a pure heart and a clean conscience. I beg you, by the sweetness of your most holy heart, most loving Savior, free my heart from all vain, unclean, harmful, and unlawful thoughts, that it may become a worthy dwelling place of your love, now and without end forever.

I beg you, lover of humankind, sweetest Lord Jesus, by all the power of your most holy passion: drive away from me the spirit of pride and arrogance, vainglory and envy, lust and blasphemy, and fill my soul with the power of charity and innocence. King of virtues, Jesus Christ, lover of holy chastity and integrity, I beg you by the most holy virginity of the most blessed mother of God and undefiled Virgin Mary, and by the body of your most reverend purity: extinguish in me, with the dew of heavenly blessing, the burning heat of lust, so that the brightness of all purity may be and remain in me. Choke in me, I beseech you, the goads of the flesh, and all lustful stirrings and disordered affections; and give me true and perpetual chastity, together with the other good things which truly please you, so that at all times, with an unstained body and a clean heart, I may be able to offer to you the sacrifice of your body and blood.

I know, Lord, and truly know, and I confess this very thing to your goodness, that I am not worthy to approach so great a mystery because of my excessive sins and my many negligences. But I also know, and with my whole heart believe and confess to you, that you, since you are almighty, can make me worthy; you alone justify the ungodly, and from one unclean you can make one clean. Therefore, by your omnipotence I pray you: grant to me, your unworthy servant, true contrition for my sins, pure devotion, and a most fervent compunction in your love, so that I may be able to offer this most holy sacrifice to you with fear and reverence, with purity of heart and a fountain of sweet tears, with spiritual gladness and heavenly joy, with humility and the fervor of charity.

O sweetest Lord Jesus, grant me in this hour, by your mercy, that my mind may feel the sweetness of your most blessed fullness, and the devotion of the holy angels around me, and a peaceful lifting up into you.

Take away from me, Lord Jesus, all my iniquities, and mercifully kindle in me the fire of your love. Be not angry with me, O Jesus, ineffable good, nor restrain over me the multitude of your mercies. For I do not pour out my prayers before your face, Lord, in my own justifications, but in your many mercies. Take from me, Lord Jesus, a heart of stone, hard and unyielding, and give me a heart of flesh, contrite, which may fear you, love you, love you above all things, delight in you alone, follow you, and enjoy you forever.

O most merciful Lord Jesus, I beg you by the most sacred mystery of your body and blood, by which in your holy Church we are daily fed and given drink, washed and sanctified, and made sharers in your one supreme divinity: give me your holy virtues, adorned with which, in a good conscience, I may be able to approach your altar, so that these heavenly sacraments may become for me salvation and life. For you said with your holy and most blessed mouth: The bread which I shall give is my flesh, for the life of the world. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever. O sweetest bread, heal the palate of my heart, that I may taste the sweetness of your love.

Heal my heart, Lord, of every weakness, so that it may feel no sweetness apart from you, seek no love apart from you, and love no consolation apart from you. O most holy Jesus, bread of life and understanding, having in yourself every delight and every sweetness of fragrance, you who always refresh us with yourself and are never lacking in yourself: let my heart, I beseech you, eat you, and let my soul be filled with the sweetness of your delight. O holy bread, O living bread, beautiful bread, pure bread, you who came down from heaven and give life to the world: come into my heart, and cleanse me from every defilement of mind and spirit. Enter into my soul; heal and sanctify me at every time. Be the protection and continual health of my body and soul. Drive away from me the enemies who lie in wait for me, so that, fortified by the sacrament of your body and blood, I may advance through you on the right path under regular discipline, and after this life may come joyfully to your kingdom.

An excuse for the length.

If this prayer seems too long to anyone, let him read whatever part he wishes, since for this reason we have divided it into short paragraphs, so that we might remove weariness. But the one who wishes to read neither the whole nor a part complains of its length in vain, since he will be shown to be unwilling to pray either a long prayer or a short one.

Meditation before approaching the altar.

By a devout meditation on the Lord’s passion, or at least on one of its sacred articles, or on several if the devotion and opportunity of the time allow, the mind of a devout person is wondrously pierced with compunction, if the practice is held as [unclear]. I would call meditation on the Lord’s passion truly savory when a person, purified through true mortification, begins to revolve in thought the death and passion of the Lord, and is dissolved into tears without violence, from love alone, and through the excessive fervor of desire is prepared as it were for a certain rapture of mind. Whoever has received this gift from the Lord will never be able to prepare himself better for celebrating than if, before approaching the altar, he always passes through at least one article of the Lord’s passion in meditation, with tears. For since the celebration of Mass was instituted by our Redeemer himself in memory of the Lord’s passion, a person never prepares himself for it better or more fruitfully than when he is more fervently kindled by meditation on that same most bitter passion.

The elevation of the priest’s mind to God during the celebration.

With how great reverence, devotion, and purity of mind we ought to stand before the almighty Lord at the altar, what speech could express, or what understanding grasp and penetrate? For there the true body and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are consecrated in an ineffable manner; there the Lord of majesty is truly present and is adored; there the army of invisible angels, standing by its king, rejoices together; there the whole heavenly court adores the Lord and man. Therefore the greatest purity of mind, the greatest reverence and humility are needed when we must stand before so great a majesty, lest the Lord Jesus, who searches the kidneys and hearts, be able to find in us anything that offends him. Let all worldly anxieties depart far from here; let all thoughts withdraw. Let nothing be thought here except what belongs to the consummation of so great a mystery; let nothing be turned over in the mind except what befits the presence of so great a majesty and glory. For here no office of human strength is performed, but the miracle of divine majesty is enacted: the Son of God is offered to the Father; the body of our Redeemer is truly received; the mystery of our reconciliation is celebrated. Therefore, standing at the altar, let the priest remember that he stands before invisible majesty, and let him beware of thinking of anything else.

After celebration, careful custody of the mind is to be kept.

After the celebration, or after communion of the Lord’s body and blood, let the devout monk offer thanksgiving to almighty God, and throughout the whole day let him keep himself, by spiritual exercise, in the purity and devotion of mind he has conceived. Let him direct his affections to God with fiery rays, and not grow lukewarm from his holy purpose. Above all, let him strive to love nothing in this world, but to raise his heart continually, stripped completely of all earthly affections, toward the fire of divine love. Let him always consider how from now on he may order his life as though anew, in the holy fervor of his way of life, and let him humbly dispose himself for the more frequently repeated reception of so great a Guest. Then, during the day, in the labors enjoined on him, let him quite often offer some prayer to God the Father in the power and union of that sacrament, so that through the exercise of holy communion and regular obedience he may kindle himself more fully in divine love. And we attain this divine love especially through the power of this venerable sacrament, if, in memory of the Lord’s passion, we are renewed by the grace of union through communicating in it more often. For truly the devout mind of a person is kindled, through communion of this most sacred sacrament, into the fervor of divine love by its effective working; and, having utterly denied itself, it is transformed, united by grace into Christ. Therefore the more each person, denied to himself through true resignation, has offered himself to the Lord as a living sacrifice in memory of the Lord’s passion, the more disposed he will be to celebrate worthily.

After private Masses. Returning to the cell.

When the celebration of Masses has been finished, and the thanksgivings have been completed according to custom, let the monk return to his cell; and, after first saying the customary prayer as above at Matins, let him recollect himself for a little while, and kindle himself more fully from his holy purpose toward perseverance. Then, turned toward the Lord, let him say:

Prayer.

I beseech you, sweetest Lord Jesus, through the power of your most holy body and blood which I have received, though unworthy: grant me the sweetness of your love, sincerity of brotherly affection, strength in temptation, purity in heart, and discipline in conduct, so that, by your bounty, I may satisfy my profession, and make vigorous progress in your most holy love. Then, until the first signal for choir, let him read something good, meditate, or pray, or certainly write, and let him fervently apply himself to the work enjoined on him by obedience.

At the first signal before choir, before High Mass.

When the first signal has sounded for the hour which, according to custom, precedes High Mass, let the monk at once put aside everything he has in his hands and read the preparatory prayers for choir, just as they are set out above before Matins. Afterward let him go to choir with reverence and maturity, bowing and praying according to the rite set down above.

At High Mass.

At the ringing for High Mass you may read the proper hour of the Holy Cross, and afterward, as time permits, recall to mind something from the preface set before the private Masses. For the sum of our salvation is placed in the merit of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor is any good work of ours believed meritorious unless it is offered in his power. The memory of this passion is carried out in the celebration of Masses, where the innocent Lamb, slain for us, is offered to God the Father in an ineffable mystery. Therefore from our Savior alone, the Lord Christ, whom we believe to have suffered for us, do we truly hope for salvation. And so whatever the Church asks in the collects, she humbly asks God the Father that it be given to her through him. This regard

Let our devout cenobite keep in his heart the merit of the Lord’s passion, upon which the whole office of the Mass may sweetly return, as upon a foundation stone. For every Mass, of whatever kind it may be, which is said in the holy Church of God, is at all times referred to the merit of the Lord’s passion.

On the Introit of the Mass.

We do not intend to explain the office of the Mass point by point, since each of us can find many expositions by others; rather, we wish to give the devout brothers an occasion for meditation, whom we know to be inflamed with inward desires. You may, however, in meditation refer the first part of the introit and the verse to the incarnation of the Lord, and refer the repetition with the Gloria to his nativity. Nevertheless, you must diligently consider what the introit contains according to the literal sense, so that you may be able to find a spiritual understanding suitable for yourself. For nothing is done in vain in the divine office; rather, all things are filled with mysteries and sacred actions.

On the Kyrie eleison.

Kyrie eleison is Greek, composed of a noun and a verb, and among them they are two words. The first is from kyrios, which means “Lord”; kyrie is said in the vocative. The second is from eleeo, which means “I have mercy”; eleeson, “have mercy,” is pronounced in the imperative. From this comes Kyrie eleison, that is, “Lord, have mercy,” by elision for Kyrie eleison, since a vowel before a vowel can be elided for a better sound.

Three times, therefore, he says Kyrie eleison to the Father, so that he who, out of exceeding charity, willed his Son to be incarnate of the Virgin and to die for us, may also be willing to come to our aid by his mercy in our necessities.

To the Son also we say Christe eleison three times, in which we pray him to come to our aid.

Three times also we utter Kyrie eleison to the Holy Spirit, in which we humbly call upon him for our help, according to his ineffable goodness.

On the Gloria in excelsis.

Then Gloria in excelsis Deo is said in the singular number, in which we confess the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit to be one sole true God in a Trinity of persons and a unity of substance.

Accordingly, during that angelic hymn the cenobite ought to be very devout, and, so to speak, especially attentive to each word; in it the gift of peace is promised to men of good will, and God is humbly adored by us in various expressions.

At the Collects.

When the collects or prayers are offered by the priest to God, the devout cenobite should think of nothing else, but, listening to the priest’s words, should present his own desire to God in agreement with them.

At the Epistle.

When the epistle is read, you must attend diligently to everything, and give spiritual thanks to God with the greatest fervor, because, leaving behind the Jewish people, he so mercifully willed to call you and your forebears from Gentile error to his faith.

At the Gradual.

At the gradual, alleluia, sequence, and tract, think how long a desire the holy fathers had, who before the incarnation of Christ longed for his coming. Then consider with how many labors and injuries your Savior was wearied for you in this world for thirty-three years, who voluntarily gave himself up to death for your salvation. Then call to mind the long exile of your soul in the flesh and amid dangers, so that by this abundant meditation, full of misery, you may inflame your affection toward divine love.

During the Gospel.

At the holy Gospel, with your mind lifted up to the Lord, give thanks with rejoicing, because the merciful Father willed you to be born of Christian parents, and because he made you a sharer in his holy and most sweet teaching.

During the Creed.

When the symbol of the catholic faith is sung, consider all its words and mysteries with humble fervor of spirit, [unclear].

hasten at once to recollect yourself within yourself, so that you may be able to give thanks worthily to him who called you to the faith without any merit of your own, and to raise yourself up in the inward love of the spirit. Consider, if you can, or rather as much as you can, how great, exalted, and immeasurable is the Son of God, who for your sake willed to become incarnate; how hard and bitter were the things he endured for you.

At the Offertory.

When the offertory is taking place, apply your mind, together with the host to be consecrated, to the offering, and ponder what is being done there mystically. For the host is round and white. In its whiteness are set forth the purity, innocence, and suffering humanity of our Savior, to be offered to God the Father for us against all our impurities; in its roundness his immeasurable divinity is offered to us as the appointed reward. Say therefore to the Lord:

Prayer.

I have no worthy gift to offer you, almighty God; I hand myself over to you as a sacrifice. Receive, therefore, holy Father, in union with the most holy offering of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your only-begotten Son, me as an eternal gift to you and as a perpetual servant; and give me the continual fire of your holy love, that I may always be able to render you pleasing service. Through the same.

Prayer.

I offer you, almighty God, the life, passion, and death of the same our Lord Jesus Christ, for my sins, for the holy Roman and universal Church, for the supreme pontiff, for our bishop, for our abbot, for all my brothers, for the union of our observance, for our whole order wherever it may be, for the salvation of all the faithful, for the conversion of unbelievers, and for the redemption of the souls of the faithful existing in the pains of purgatory. Receive, I beseech you, holy Father, this offering of mine in union with that charity with which you received the same our Lord Jesus Christ dying for us on the cross, and may it be pleasing to you.

During the Preface.

When the preface is being said, take care to raise your mind from all earthly things to heavenly things, and to prepare it to praise the Lord with the holy angels. Remember that through the merit of his holy passion you have been called to the fellowship of the angels, and take care that through observance of the commandments you may come to it.

At the Sanctus.

With your mind lifted upward, glorify the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God and Lord, to whom the Sanctus is sung, and humbly adore his majesty with the holy angels at all times.

During the Canon.

After the Sanctus, during the canon, you may take up meditation on the Lord’s passion, and offer it, article by article, especially the greater and principal ones, to God the Father for yourself, or for others, or for any necessity. Say, therefore, in this or a similar manner:

O holy Father, I offer you the bloody sweat and tears of our Lord Jesus Christ, your most beloved Son, in that charity and union in which he voluntarily offered himself to you in death for us: for my sins, or for that brother, or for that servant-girl, or for that necessity. And I ask you, through the pain of the wounds of that same sweetest Son of yours, and through the pouring out of his most holy blood and the power of his most innocent death: have mercy on me, or on that person, or grant us this or that, and so forth. Through the same our Lord.

With the other articles of the Lord’s passion you will be able to proceed in the same way, and to enlarge upon them in offering according to the intention of your affection.

At the Elevation.

If, at the elevation of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your mind is not occupied with higher things, you may pray to the Lord, who is truly present, in this way:

You are the King of glory, O Christ. You are the everlasting Son of the Father. You, to deliver man, did not shrink from the Virgin’s womb, and so on to the end. For this part of the hymn, Saint Thomas Aquinas is read to have prayed to the Lord during the elevation.

At the Agnus Dei.

When the Agnus Dei is sung, lift up your mind to the Lord Jesus with singular trust, and humbly pray that he may receive you into perpetual peace. To him, for whose love all things...

Delectione mensalt.
